i.x: Matthew demonstrates that Jesus of Nazareth is the long-awaited Messiah, the king of Israel, who fulfills the Old Testament promises yet turns the expectation of his contemporaries on its head. The Gospel of Matthew shows how both Jewish and non-Jewish people fit together in God’s unfolding Kingdom. It challenges the reader to live with total commitment to Jesus Christ as king.
Setting

Matthew wrote his Gospel when the early Christian community was at a crossroads. Would it remain a sect of Judaism or separate itself from Judaism and become a separate faith? Matthew’s Gospel derives from a Christian community near Jerusalem, surrounded by Jews who had not left their Jewish faith. This community, unlike the Christians of Paul’s churches, had to answer socially to the stipulations of Jewish law on a daily basis.

The Christians reading Matthew’s Gospel were challenged to live as Jewish Christians among Jews who were fully committed to the Torah. The letter from James similarly evokes a Christianity that is still firmly attached to the synagogue (see [Jas 2:1-26](Jas.2.1-Jas.2.26)). Here is a Jewish Christianity that remains as firm in its commitment to the Jewish community as to its glorious Lord (cp. [Acts 15:1-41](Acts.15.1-Acts.15.41)).

Matthew’s Gospel tells how the life of Jesus affected Jewish Christians who were struggling with ritual, legal, social, and political concerns. For those early Christians, Matthew answered the pressing question, “How are we to follow Jesus in our day, surrounded as we are by Judaism, while seeking to declare the Good News of the Kingdom to all?”
Summary

Matthew’s story follows Jesus from before his birth until after his death and resurrection. Jesus experiences a series of potential dangers as a child ([ch 2](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.23)). As an adult, he embarks on a very short career, proclaiming God’s righteousness ([chs 5–7](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29)) and performing astounding miracles ([8:1–9:34](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.34)); he broadens his reach by sending out twelve apostles ([9:35–11:1](Matt.9.35-Matt.11.1)). Most of Jesus’ experience, however, is utter rejection at the hands of Galilean and Judean Jews ([chs 11–17](Matt.11.1-Matt.17.27)). He confronts the Jewish leaders in the Temple during his last week ([chs 21–22](Matt.21.1-Matt.22.46)), announces a final series of woes against authority figures who lead people astray ([ch 23](Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39)), and predicts that God will judge and destroy Jerusalem ([chs 24–25](Matt.24.1-Matt.25.46)). Jesus is arrested, tried, and executed by crucifixion ([chs 26–27](Matt.26.1-Matt.27.66)) for opposing the Jewish leaders and challenging the status quo. Then he is vindicated by his resurrection and gives the great commission to his disciples, to make disciples of all the nations ([ch 28](Matt.28.1-Matt.28.20)).

Matthew shapes his Gospel according to two structural principles. First, following an introduction ([chs 1–4](Matt.1.1-Matt.4.25)), Matthew alternates teaching material with narrative material. Thus, we have discourse and teaching in [chs 5–7](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29); [10](Matt.10.1-Matt.10.42), [13](Matt.13.1-Matt.13.58), [18](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.35), [23–25](Matt.23.1-Matt.25.46); and we have narrative in [chs 8–9](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.38); [11–12](Matt.11.1-Matt.12.50), [14–17](Matt.14.1-Matt.17.27), [19–22](Matt.19.1-Matt.22.46), [26–28](Matt.26.1-Matt.28.20). Second, Matthew records Jesus’ confrontation of Israel with God’s message about the arrival of his Kingdom in the last days ([4:12–11:1](Matt.4.12-Matt.11.1); see [4:17](Matt.4.17)), followed by the responses this message evoked from various people ([11:2–20:34](Matt.11.2-Matt.20.34)). Matthew then tells of Jesus Christ’s death and resurrection ([chs 21–28](Matt.21.1-Matt.28.20)) for the salvation of humankind.
Authorship

Matthew was a tax collector whom Jesus befriended and called to a life of justice and obedience ([9:9](Matt.9.9)). Matthew invited many friends to spend an evening with Jesus ([9:10-13](Matt.9.10-Matt.9.13)), and Matthew is named among the twelve apostles ([10:2-4](Matt.10.2-Matt.10.4); see also [Mark 3:16-19](Mark.3.16-Mark.3.19); [Luke 6:13-16](Luke.6.13-Luke.6.16); [Acts 1:13](Acts.1.13)). Early church tradition reports that after he composed his Gospel, Matthew moved from Palestine in the AD 60s to evangelize India (Eusebius, *Church History* 3.24.6).

In the early AD 100s, Papias, Bishop of Hierapolis, made the statement, “Matthew therefore composed the oracles in the Hebrew language \[or, ‘in a Hebrew style’\] and each interpreted them as he was able.” Papias’s statement is traditionally understood to mean that the apostle Matthew wrote a Gospel in Hebrew or Aramaic, and that this Gospel was later translated into Greek, perhaps by someone who also knew the Gospel of Mark. Recent studies suggest that Papias was referring to Matthew’s Jewish style, not to his language (Hebrew or Aramaic), because Matthew’s Gospel does not appear to be “translation Greek” (i.e., the type of Greek that is often found in materials translated from other languages).

In the 1800s, scholars became convinced that Matthew had used Mark’s Gospel as a source. These scholars argued that since an apostle would not have used another Gospel (and one written by a non-apostle at that!) to record Jesus’ life, Matthew was not the author of the Gospel bearing his name. But early tradition connects the Gospel of Mark with the apostle Peter, a fact that makes Matthew’s dependence on Mark more understandable. There is no conflict with one apostle (Matthew) using the accounts of another apostle (Peter) as a convenient source from which to shape his own report.
Occasion of Writing

Unlike the letters of Paul or the Revelation of John, the settings of the Gospels must be inferred from comments and emphases within the books themselves (see [24:15](Matt.24.15); [27:46](Matt.27.46); [28:15](Matt.28.15)), since direct evidence is unavailable. Matthew appears to have been written at a time when Christians and Jews were fiercely debating such issues as how to obey the law ([5:17-48](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.48); [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20)), who the Messiah is ([chs 1–2](Matt.1.1-Matt.2.23)), who the true people of God are (Israel or the church; [21:33-46](Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46)), who the rightful leaders of God’s people are ([4:18-22](Matt.4.18-Matt.4.22); [10:2-4](Matt.10.2-Matt.10.4); [21:43](Matt.21.43); [23:1-36](Matt.23.1-Matt.23.36); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)), and how Gentiles are related to the church and to Israel ([2:1-12](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.12); [3:7-10](Matt.3.7-Matt.3.10); [4:12-16](Matt.4.12-Matt.4.16); [8:5-13](Matt.8.5-Matt.8.13); [15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)).

There is serious debate as to whether Matthew’s Gospel sprang from a community that was still within Judaism or one that was already outside Judaism. In other words, had Matthew’s Christian community separated from Judaism, or was it still within Judaism’s umbrella? Or, was Matthew written for a general audience rather than a specific community? Early Christianity was diverse; some Christian leaders, such as James, maintained a long-term relationship with the Jewish communities. In discussing this question, scholars examine the following passages: [2:1-12](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.12); [4:12-16](Matt.4.12-Matt.4.16); [8:5-13](Matt.8.5-Matt.8.13); [10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6); [15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28); [17:24-27](Matt.17.24-Matt.17.27); [19:28](Matt.19.28); [21:43](Matt.21.43); [22:7](Matt.22.7); [23:1-39](Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39).
Date and Location

Matthew was probably written sometime between AD 65 and 80. Those who argue that Matthew used Mark’s Gospel as a source usually date Matthew after AD 70; those who claim it is independent tend to date it earlier. Some have suggested that Matthew’s Gospel was written in the AD 50s. Many today think that Matthew was written at Antioch in Syria, which is more probable than any other proposed setting.
Meaning and Message
Matthew argues the case that Jesus fulfills the ancient faith of Israel and the hope of the Old Testament: In Jesus, the Messiah and the day of the Lord have come.

Some people do follow Jesus. In following the instruction of Jesus, these disciples would evangelize the Roman world and build a community (the church) that would include both Jews and Gentiles. In general, however, Israel refuses to follow its Messiah, and Jesus utters disastrous warnings that they will experience the judgment of God ([chs 23–25](Matt.23.1-Matt.25.46)) unless they repent.

Matthew’s Gospel is distinctive in its presentation of Jesus as Messiah and Teacher, its emphasis on the Kingdom of Heaven, its strong call to discipleship, its constant pattern of Old Testament fulfillment, its incisive criticism of the Jewish religious leaders, and its universal outlook that includes Gentiles in the Kingdom.

**The Messiah (Christ).**  Matthew emphasizes Jesus as the Messiah (Christ) ([1:1](Matt.1.1), [16-18](Matt.1.16-Matt.1.18); [11:2-3](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.3); [16:16](Matt.16.16), [20](Matt.16.20); [23:10](Matt.23.10)). He focuses on Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament expectations, though not in the manner his Jewish contemporaries expected. For Matthew, Jesus is clearly the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary in order to bring salvation to his people ([1:21](Matt.1.21)). In short, Jesus is “Immanuel, which means ‘God is with us’” ([1:23](Matt.1.23); [28:20](Matt.28.20)).

**The Kingdom of Heaven.**  The expression “Kingdom of Heaven,” used thirty times by Matthew, is a roundabout way for Jews to say “Kingdom of God.” Matthew uses this term to evoke (1) the invisible but present rule of God on earth through the saving work of Jesus the Messiah; (2) the fulfillment of Old Testament promises ([4:17](Matt.4.17); [11:11-15](Matt.11.11-Matt.11.15)); (3) the saving activity of God, often through quiet and humble means ([11:25](Matt.11.25); [13:24-30](Matt.13.24-Matt.13.30), [36-43](Matt.13.36-Matt.13.43)); (4) the power and strength of God’s activity ([11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6), [12-13](Matt.11.12-Matt.11.13); [12:28](Matt.12.28)); (5) the coming of the Kingdom within a “generation” ([10:23](Matt.10.23); [16:28](Matt.16.28); [24:34](Matt.24.34)); (6) the final, climactic judgment of God ([25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)); and (7) the final, perfect fellowship of all God’s holy people with the Father ([8:11-12](Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12); [13:43](Matt.13.43); [22:1-14](Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14); [26:29](Matt.26.29)). The Kingdom of Heaven shows God’s perfect reign through Jesus the Messiah among his people, beginning with the church and consummated in the eternal Kingdom of glory and fellowship.

**Discipleship.**  Matthew’s Gospel stresses Jesus’ call to men and women to be baptized, to follow him as disciples, to obey his teachings ([28:20](Matt.28.20)), and to enjoy fellowship with him. Jesus summarizes the requirements of discipleship in his Sermon on the Mount ([chs 5–7](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29)), and this theme recurs throughout Matthew (e.g., [10:1-42](Matt.10.1-Matt.10.42); [16:24-26](Matt.16.24-Matt.16.26)). Matthew shows the disciples overcoming their failures through Christ’s help (see [14:28-33](Matt.14.28-Matt.14.33); [16:5-12](Matt.16.5-Matt.16.12)).

**Fulfillment of the Old Testament.**  More than any other Gospel, Matthew highlights the deep correspondence between Old Testament expectations and promises and their fulfillment in Jesus. In the style of a Jewish commentary, Matthew links Old Testament texts to events in the life of Jesus that fulfill those texts and frequently draws out analogies between the Old Testament and the New Testament. Matthew’s procedure is anchored in the belief that what God has done once in Israel, he is doing again, finally and fully, in Jesus the Messiah.

**Universal Outlook.**  In a book so strongly Jewish in orientation, it is surprising to find such an emphasis on the inclusion of Gentiles in the Messiah’s saving work. More than any other, this Gospel emphasizes that the Good News is for all, including Gentiles. This stance put Matthew at odds with the Jewish community of his time on two fundamental questions: Who are the people of God? What future is there for the nation of Israel? The birth narratives show that God saves Gentiles, and throughout the book Gentiles are portrayed positively. Since God is sovereign, his Messiah is King of all creation. Though God has worked especially in and through the nation of Israel (see [10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6); [15:24](Matt.15.24)), the inauguration of the Kingdom of Heaven shares God’s good favor with the nations as well (see [28:18-20](Matt.28.18-Matt.28.20)).

b.x: This account demonstrates that Jesus’ lineage and birth (ch [1](Matt.1.1-Matt.1.25)), as well as the geography of his early years (ch [2](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.23)), fulfilled Old Testament expectations, and that attempts to thwart God’s will do not succeed ([2:1-15](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.15); see also [27:62-66](Matt.27.62-Matt.27.66)).
The phrase **a record of the ancestors** introduces [1:1-17](Matt.1.1-Matt.1.17). A similar phrase is used in Genesis to introduce each section of that book.

**Jesus . . . David . . . Abraham:** These names are repeated in reverse order in the genealogy, an example of a literary form known as *chiasm* (arrangement of elements in mirror-image). Being identified as a **descendant of David** introduces Jesus as Messiah (see [Matt 12:23](Matt.12.23); [22:42-45](Matt.22.42-Matt.22.45)), while the connection to **Abraham** emphasizes God’s covenant with Israel and the extension of that covenant to include all nations (see [Matt 28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20); [Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3)).

**Rahab** was the Gentile prostitute who risked her life to harbor Joshua’s two spies in Jericho ([Josh 2:1-21](Josh.2.1-Josh.2.21)). Her inclusion in the ancestry of the Messiah emphasizes the grace of God. Elsewhere she is commended for her faith in the God of Israel and for righteous deeds ([Heb 11:31](Heb.11.31); [Jas 2:25](Jas.2.25)).

**Asa** (Greek *Asaph*): Probably the Old Testament king ([1 Kgs 15:9-24](1Kgs.15.9-1Kgs.15.24); [1 Chr 3:10](1Chr.3.10)) and not the psalmist (Asaph; [1 Chr 6:39](1Chr.6.39); [25:1-2](1Chr.25.1-1Chr.25.2); [Pss 50](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.23), [73-83](Ps.73.1-Ps.83.18)). Matthew’s focus is on the ancestral line from David to the Messiah.

**father of** (or *ancestor of*): The term includes several generations here ([2 Chr 21:1–26:1](2Chr.21.1-2Chr.26.1)), as it does in the case of Josiah ([Matt 1:11](Matt.1.11)) and Shealtiel ([1:12](Matt.1.12)). The genealogy omits Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah ([2 Kgs 8:24](2Kgs.8.24); [1 Chr 3:11](1Chr.3.11); [2 Chr 22:1](2Chr.22.1), [11](2Chr.22.11); [24:27](2Chr.24.27)), perhaps because of their association with Ahab and Jezebel.
**father:** Josiah was the grandfather of **Jehoiachin**.
Although the Old Testament is clearly the source for [1:1-11](Matt.1.1-Matt.1.11), Matthew is probably also dependent upon royal archives and oral traditions for [1:12-16](Matt.1.12-Matt.1.16).
**Shealtiel:** See [1 Chr 3:17-19](1Chr.3.17-1Chr.3.19); [Ezra 3:2](Ezra.3.2).
This genealogy is traced through **Joseph***,* who stands in David’s line (see also study note on Luke 3:23-38).

Matthew states that each period has **fourteen generations***,* but the first and third periods list only thirteen. A legitimate Jewish and Old Testament approach would count David in both the first and second groupings and include Jesus in the third grouping. This suggests that Matthew is probably stressing the *gematria* (letters representing numbers): The letters in the Hebrew word *dawid* (“David”) also add up to fourteen. Matthew is highlighting Jesus’ credentials as the Messiah ([1:1](Matt.1.1)).
**Jesus the Messiah** (literally *Jesus the Christ*): Using *Messiah* in the translation accurately communicates that it is a title rather than a personal name (“Jesus Christ”).

**engaged to be married:** In Judaism, engagement (or betrothal) meant a permanent relationship ([Mal 2:14](Mal.2.14)) that could be broken only by legal process; thus, Mary was considered Joseph’s wife and he her husband (see [Matt 1:20](Matt.1.20); [Deut 22:23-24](Deut.22.23-Deut.22.24)), even though they had not had sexual relations. Mary’s status as a **virgin** at the time of Jesus’ conception **through the power of the Holy Spirit** helps authenticate Jesus’ divinity.

As a **righteous man**—that is, as one who obeyed the law (see [Luke 1:6](Luke.1.6))—Joseph could not take Mary as his wife since she was a suspected adulteress. He could exonerate himself by publicly exposing Mary to trial and having her put to death ([Deut 22:23-27](Deut.22.23-Deut.22.27); cp. [Num 5:11-31](Num.5.11-Num.5.31)), or pay a fine and **break the engagement** (see also *Mishnah Sotah* 1:1-5). Joseph mercifully decided to do the latter **quietly**.

The **angel of the Lord** declared to Joseph **in a dream** (see [2:12-13](Matt.2.12-Matt.2.13), [19](Matt.2.19), [22](Matt.2.22)) that Mary had been neither seduced nor violated; instead, the baby **was conceived by the Holy Spirit** ([Luke 1:34-35](Luke.1.34-Luke.1.35)), who often has a creative and life-generating role ([Gen 1:2](Gen.1.2); [Ezek 37:1-14](Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.14); [John 3:5-8](John.3.5-John.3.8)).
**Jesus** is the Greek form of the Hebrew name *Yeshua,* which means “The LORD saves.” The name appropriately describes his role: **he will save his people from their sins**.

**His people** may refer either to Israel as a nation ([2:6](Matt.2.6)) or to the Messiah’s people, the church, which is comprised of both Jews and Gentiles ([4:15-16](Matt.4.15-Matt.4.16); [16:18](Matt.16.18); [28:18-20](Matt.28.18-Matt.28.20)).

Jesus’ birth from a **virgin** fulfills [Isa 7:14](Isa.7.14). The Hebrew term *‘almah* (*virgin* or *young maiden*) was translated *parthenos* (“virgin”) in the Greek Old Testament that Matthew quotes. Matthew understands the *‘almah* of Isaiah as foreshadowing the Virgin Mary.
**Until** probably implies that Joseph had **sexual relations** with Mary after the birth of Jesus.
**And Joseph named him Jesus***,* thus showing his acceptance of the child as his own.

Attentiveness to the **star** indicates that the **wise men** were astrologers; their awareness of the Old Testament (perhaps [Num 24:17](Num.24.17)) suggests that they were from Babylonia, where Jews were numerous. The men were Gentiles, which anticipates Gentile acceptance into the Kingdom of God ([Matt 8:11-12](Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12); [15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)). Throughout the entire Gospel, unlikely Gentiles worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish leaders (Herod, high priests, teachers of religious law, Pharisees) oppose him.
**Bethlehem** was David’s hometown ([1 Sam 16:1-13](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.13); [John 7:42](John.7.42)).

**King Herod***,* or Herod the Great, had a meteoric career; he rose from being governor of Galilee to being king of Galilee, Judea, and Samaria (37–4 BC). His career was marked by unflinching loyalty to Rome, magnificent building enterprises (including a substantial renovation of the Temple in Jerusalem), family hostility, suspicion, and ruthless murder of his own family members (Josephus, *Antiquities* 15.7.1-5) and of innocent children ([Matt 2:16-18](Matt.2.16-Matt.2.18)).

Matthew regularly describes Jesus as receiving **worship** ([2:2](Matt.2.2), [8](Matt.2.8), [11](Matt.2.11); [8:2](Matt.8.2); [9:18](Matt.9.18); [14:33](Matt.14.33); [15:25](Matt.15.25); [20:20](Matt.20.20); [28:9](Matt.28.9), [17](Matt.28.17)), thus identifying Jesus as God.
**Herod was deeply disturbed** because he feared this child would rival him as king of the Jews.

**The leading priests** had political and religious clout and ministered predominantly in the Temple (see [21:23](Matt.21.23)). Herod gathered the **teachers of religious law** because they were trained to know Old Testament prophecies and were often influential Pharisees.
**Bethlehem**, a small village, had a privileged status as the birthplace of King David. The religious leaders knew from the prophets ([1:22](Matt.1.22)) that the Messiah would be born there.

King David had been a **shepherd** in his youth, and as king he became the shepherd of Israel ([2 Sam 5:2](2Sam.5.2)). [Micah 5:2-4](Mic.5.2-Mic.5.4) foresees the Messiah as a shepherd (cp. [Ps 23:1](Ps.23.1)).
The **star** was placed by God to guide the **wise men** to the Messiah (see [Num 24:17](Num.24.17)); the details are unknown.

The wise men offered extravagant **gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh** to the King (see [Ps 72:10-17](Ps.72.10-Ps.72.17); [Isa 60](Isa.60.1-Isa.60.22)). The tradition that there were three wise men originated from the number of gifts, but the text does not specify how many wise men there were.

**Flee to Egypt . . . until I tell you to return:** This fulfills [Hos 11:1](Hos.11.1) (see study note on Matt 4:1-11; see also [Gen 15:13-16](Gen.15.13-Gen.15.16); [46:1-5](Gen.46.1-Gen.46.5); [Exod 15:1-21](Exod.15.1-Exod.15.21)).
**I called my Son out of Egypt:** See [Hos 11:1](Hos.11.1), which refers to the Exodus.

**kill all the boys:** Herod was notorious for his viciousness—he killed his own son to protect his throne, which led to the saying, “It is safer to be Herod’s swine \[Greek *hus*\] than his son \[Greek *huios*\],” because Herod kept kosher.
**two years old and under:** Herod calculated the probable age of the child from the **wise men’s report**.
**Ramah**, a village near Bethlehem, is the place of **Rachel**’s burial ([Gen 35:18-20](Gen.35.18-Gen.35.20); [Jer 31:15-17](Jer.31.15-Jer.31.17)).

After **Herod** the Great **died** in 4 BC, Caesar split up his kingdom. Herod’s son Archelaus ([2:22](Matt.2.22)) was appointed over Judea, Samaria, and Idumea, while Antipas ([14:1-12](Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12); [Luke 13:31-32](Luke.13.31-Luke.13.32)) was appointed over Galilee and Perea.
Jesus’ return to Israel fulfills [Hos 11:1](Hos.11.1) (see [2:13-15](Matt.2.13-Matt.2.15)).
**Archelaus***,* like his father, governed brutally, immorally, and tyrannically.
Joseph fulfilled prophecy in moving to **Galilee** to avoid Archelaus’s jurisdiction (cp. [4:12-16](Matt.4.12-Matt.4.16)).

**“He will be called a Nazarene”:** Matthew associates the name **Nazareth** with words in **the prophets** (see [Isa 11:1](Isa.11.1), where the Messiah is called a “Branch,” \[Hebrew *netser*\]; and [Judg 13:5](Judg.13.5), where Samson is called a “Nazirite”).

**John the Baptist** announced Jesus’ coming (see [Mark 1:1-11](Mark.1.1-Mark.1.11); [Luke 3:1-22](Luke.3.1-Luke.3.22); [John 1:6-8](John.1.6-John.1.8), [19-34](John.1.19-John.1.34)) and prepared people to receive him ([Matt 3:3](Matt.3.3)). John attracted large crowds ([3:5](Matt.3.5)) and a group of disciples ([9:14](Matt.9.14)). This group continued for a short time as a movement, even as the Christian church emerged (see [Acts 18:24-28](Acts.18.24-Acts.18.28)).

John’s locale in **the Judean wilderness** had symbolic significance: The wilderness was associated with the giving of the law (see [Exod 19:1](Exod.19.1)) and with God’s final redemption of Israel at the end of history (see [Isa 40:3](Isa.40.3)).

The prophetic call to return to God in repentance (cp. [Isa 1:16-20](Isa.1.16-Isa.1.20)) involves total reorientation from pride and sin to humble obedience to God (see [Jer 3:11-22](Jer.3.11-Jer.3.22)). John’s message included specific practical application ([Luke 3:11-14](Luke.3.11-Luke.3.14)).

**Isaiah** had spoken of a messenger preparing a highway in the wilderness for Israel’s God to return to the land ([Isa 40:1-11](Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11)). John’s ministry prepared the way for Jesus’ arrival (see [Matt 11:10](Matt.11.10); cp. [John 12:41](John.12.41)).
**John’s clothes** and **food** correspond to those of his prophetic predecessor, Elijah ([2 Kgs 1:8](2Kgs.1.8); [Mal 4:5](Mal.4.5); *Sirach* 48:10-11).
John’s ministry became so popular that many **people from Jerusalem** and **Judea** came to hear him.
**they confessed their sins:** Those who responded to John’s preaching and turned away from sin were prepared to receive Jesus’ ministry ([Luke 7:27](Luke.7.27), [29](Luke.7.29)).
**he baptized them:** John’s practice of baptism may have originated with the Old Testament idea of purification (see [Isa 1:16](Isa.1.16); [4:4](Isa.4.4); [Ezek 36:25](Ezek.36.25)).
The **Pharisees***’* name derives from the Hebrew term *perushim*, meaning either *separated ones* or *exact interpreters*.
The **Sadducees***,* a priestly class, probably derive their name from Zadok the priest ([2 Sam 15:24-29](2Sam.15.24-2Sam.15.29); [Ezek 44:10-16](Ezek.44.10-Ezek.44.16)).

**Prove . . . that you have . . . turned to God** (literally *make fruit that accords with repentance*): John calls for action and true ethical change; mere lip service will not do (see [Luke 3:10-14](Luke.3.10-Luke.3.14); cp. [Matt 5:19-20](Matt.5.19-Matt.5.20), [46](Matt.5.46); [7:21](Matt.7.21); [23:3](Matt.23.3)).
**We’re safe:** Some had wrongly assumed that, since they were **descendants of Abraham***,* they were exempt from judgment.

A prominent theme in Matthew is how **God** will **create** new **children of Abraham** by bringing the Gentiles into God’s people and removing from his people Jews who reject the Messiah (see [8:11-12](Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12); [21:43](Matt.21.43); [22:1-14](Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20); [Rom 4:9-25](Rom.4.9-Rom.4.25); [Gal 3:6-14](Gal.3.6-Gal.3.14), [29](Gal.3.29)).
**who is greater than I am:** Despite his popularity and growing following, John had a clear sense of his role as subordinate to the Messiah.

**I’m not worthy even to be his slave:** In Jewish culture, to remove and carry someone’s sandals, even those of a rabbi, was too lowly a task even for the rabbi’s disciple. It was a job reserved for slaves.

**with the Holy Spirit and with fire:** This happened at Pentecost (see [Joel 2:28-29](Joel.2.28-Joel.2.29); [Acts 2:1-47](Acts.2.1-Acts.2.47)); the ministry of Jesus, empowered by the Holy Spirit (see [Matt 12:28](Matt.12.28); [Luke 4:14](Luke.4.14)), may also be included. **Fire** may refer to purification ([Zech 13:9](Zech.13.9)) or judgment ([Mal 4:1](Mal.4.1); see [Isa 1:25](Isa.1.25); [4:4](Isa.4.4); [Mal 3:2-3](Mal.3.2-Mal.3.3)). It is a “Spirit-and-fire baptism”; the Messiah puts into effect what John could only prepare—thoroughgoing judgment and purification.

Farmers would use a **winnowing fork** to toss harvested grain into the air, allowing the useless husks (**chaff**) to blow away. The Messiah’s ministry divides all humanity into two groups: (1) **the wheat**, that is, those who respond, forming the new people of God; and (2) **the chaff,** the unrepentant (see [3:8](Matt.3.8)).
As John had already confessed ([3:11-12](Matt.3.11-Matt.3.12)), he was lesser than the Messiah, so he felt unfit to baptize him.

**for we must carry out all that God requires:** Or *for we must fulfill all righteousness.* This statement refers to accomplishing what the Old Testament demanded or foreshadowed (e.g., [Jer 31:31-34](Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34)). “Righteousness” in Matthew refers to behavior that conforms to God’s will (see [Matt 5:20](Matt.5.20); [6:1](Matt.6.1), [33](Matt.6.33); [21:32](Matt.21.32)).

The **Spirit of God descending like a dove** was anointing Jesus, through whom salvation would come. This event was like a king’s being anointed with oil at his coronation. The Holy Spirit empowered Jesus to accomplish God’s salvation and defeat Satan (see [12:18](Matt.12.18), [28](Matt.12.28)). This same Spirit empowers Jesus’ followers ([10:20](Matt.10.20); [Acts 1:8](Acts.1.8)).

**my dearly loved Son** (see [Ps 2:7](Ps.2.7)): The title “Son of God” reveals and clarifies Jesus’ nature and role (see [Matt 4:3](Matt.4.3), [6](Matt.4.6); [14:33](Matt.14.33); [16:16](Matt.16.16); [17:5](Matt.17.5); [26:63](Matt.26.63); [27:54](Matt.27.54); [28:19](Matt.28.19)). In his unique relationship to the Father, Jesus accomplishes salvation as the trusting and obedient Son.
**who brings me great joy:** God the Father confirmed his Son’s ministry with language from Isaiah ([Isa 42:1](Isa.42.1)) and so prepared Israel for his ministry.

Parallels between Adam and Jesus are obvious in this account of Jesus’ temptation. Jesus is the second Adam (see [Rom 5:12-19](Rom.5.12-Rom.5.19)) and the second Israel ([Matt 2:15](Matt.2.15)). In contrast to the ancient Israelites, he fulfilled Israel’s history by successfully wandering through the desert without sinning. He proved himself the obedient Son of God by defeating Satan in spiritual combat. And because he underwent temptation himself as a human, Jesus is able to sympathize with the temptations we face (see [Heb 2:14-18](Heb.2.14-Heb.2.18); [4:15](Heb.4.15)) and help us overcome them as he did ([1 Cor 10:13](1Cor.10.13)).
**Jesus was led by the Spirit:** The temptation was providentially arranged by God as a test of the Messiah’s character (see [Deut 8:2](Deut.8.2)).

**to be tempted there by the devil:** This test of character, initiated by God (who tempts no one; see [Jas 1:13-14](Jas.1.13-Jas.1.14)), was accomplished through the devil’s own desire to lure Jesus into sin.

**forty days and forty nights** (see [Exod 24:18](Exod.24.18); [34:28](Exod.34.28); [1 Kgs 19:8](1Kgs.19.8)): Israel was tested in the wilderness for forty years ([Exod 16:35](Exod.16.35); [Deut 1:3](Deut.1.3)).

Jesus refused to use his supernatural power to obtain the food that he trusted God to provide. Unlike the people of Israel, who sorely tested God through complaint and unbelief (see [Exod 16](Exod.16.1-Exod.16.36)), Jesus refused to question God’s faithfulness. Instead, he trusted God to provide for his true need, the sustenance of **every word that comes from the mouth of God**.
Jesus refused to test God by presuming upon God’s protection.
**The Scriptures also say:** Countering the devil’s appeal to Scripture, Jesus invoked a deeper scriptural principle of honoring God, which the devil ignored.

Satan, called the ruler of this world ([John 12:31](John.12.31)), offered to hand over **all the kingdoms of the world and their glory** to Jesus to keep him from accomplishing the will of his Father.

**Glory** refers to political power and dominion (e.g., [Matt 6:29](Matt.6.29)). Satan’s strategy was to get Jesus to abuse his sonship, thus diverting him from the path of suffering and obedience that climaxed at the cross.

**Then the devil went away:** Jesus’ rebuff of Satan here foreshadows his victory over demons ([12:28](Matt.12.28)), Satan’s defeat through the Cross ([Col 2:14-15](Col.2.14-Col.2.15)), and the final victory at the end of history ([Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20); [Rev 12:7-17](Rev.12.7-Rev.12.17); [20:2-3](Rev.20.2-Rev.20.3), [10](Rev.20.10)).

**Angels***,* who had already been involved in the Messiah’s arrival and protection ([Matt 1:20](Matt.1.20), [24](Matt.1.24); [2:13](Matt.2.13), [19](Matt.2.19)), now **came and took care of Jesus** after his temptation, in fulfillment of the Old Testament ([4:6](Matt.4.6); see [Ps 91:11-12](Ps.91.11-Ps.91.12)).

Having been announced by John and the Father ([3:13-17](Matt.3.13-Matt.3.17)), and having obediently endured the testing in the wilderness ([4:1-11](Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11)), the Messiah was prepared for his ministry. He first confronted the Galilean Israelites with the message of the Kingdom.
**John had been arrested** by Herod Antipas (see [14:1-12](Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12)). Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, where John was probably working at the time.

**When Jesus heard . . . he left Judea** (near Perea, where John was arrested) **and returned to Galilee:** Jesus withdrew to avoid martyrdom before finishing his work of revealing the Kingdom. As in Joseph’s flight to Nazareth ([2:22-23](Matt.2.22-Matt.2.23)), an escape from danger can also be God’s providential direction and the fulfillment of prophecy ([4:14-16](Matt.4.14-Matt.4.16)).

**Capernaum** was in Galilee, a district viewed negatively by the religious establishment in Judea and Jerusalem (see [John 1:46](John.1.46); [7:41-42](John.7.41-John.7.42), [52](John.7.52)). Many Judeans considered Galileans to be uncultured, with a lazy command of the language (cp. [Matt 26:73](Matt.26.73)), a factor sometimes thought to affect the accuracy of their teachings. Galilee also had a proportionately larger Gentile population than Judea did.
Jesus’ message centered on the imminent arrival of the **Kingdom of Heaven** and the repentance that it necessitates (see [Matt 3:2](Matt.3.2); [10:7](Matt.10.7)).
The call of the first disciples illustrates one of the purposes of Jesus’ ministry: to call people to follow him in self-denying obedience (cp. [4:17](Matt.4.17), [23-25](Matt.4.23-Matt.4.25)).

**Simon, also called Peter***,* became the leader of the apostles (see [14:28](Matt.14.28); [15:15](Matt.15.15); [16:16](Matt.16.16)) and the representative disciple ([14:29-30](Matt.14.29-Matt.14.30); [16:15-19](Matt.16.15-Matt.16.19), [22-23](Matt.16.22-Matt.16.23)).
**Come, follow me:** This involved accepting the beliefs and lifestyle of a master as one’s own ([16:24](Matt.16.24); [Deut 5:33](Deut.5.33); [1 Kgs 19:19-21](1Kgs.19.19-1Kgs.19.21)).

**fish for people:** The disciples would participate in the saving and judging work of the Kingdom (see [Matt 10:5-15](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15); [13:47-51](Matt.13.47-Matt.13.51); [Ezek 29:4-5](Ezek.29.4-Ezek.29.5); [Amos 4:2](Amos.4.2)).

**leaving the boat and their father:** Following Jesus as his disciples involved both commitment and cost on the part of the brothers (see [8:18-22](Matt.8.18-Matt.8.22); [10:38](Matt.10.38); [16:24](Matt.16.24); [19:21](Matt.19.21)).

This summary marks the central theme of the section ([4:23–9:38](Matt.4.23-Matt.9.38)): the ministry and message of the Messiah. In ancient writings, chapter divisions were unknown; authors would instead begin and end a section with the same expression (called an *inclusio*; see [9:35](Matt.9.35)).
The Messiah’s ministry has three main features: **teaching***,* **announcing . . . the Kingdom***,* and healing.

**The synagogues** were centers for prayer, study, and exposition of Scripture and tradition. They were the social centers of many Jewish villages. The hypocrisy and hostility of the Jewish leaders was evident at the synagogues ([6:2](Matt.6.2), [5](Matt.6.5); [10:17](Matt.10.17); [12:9-14](Matt.12.9-Matt.12.14); [13:54](Matt.13.54); [23:6](Matt.23.6), [34](Matt.23.34)).

**Announcing the Good News** means presenting the message **about the Kingdom** of Heaven ([9:35](Matt.9.35); [24:14](Matt.24.14); [26:13](Matt.26.13); also [Mark 1:1](Mark.1.1); [Rom 1:16](Rom.1.16)). Most often, the message evokes hostility (see [Matt 9:32-34](Matt.9.32-Matt.9.34); [10:27-28](Matt.10.27-Matt.10.28); [13:1-9](Matt.13.1-Matt.13.9), [18-23](Matt.13.18-Matt.13.23)).

During Jesus’ day, much of Palestine was in the Roman jurisdiction of Syria (a term that could refer to the entire eastern shore of the Mediterranean). Matthew mentions **Syria** to show how widespread the news of Jesus was.
The word translated **epileptic** refers to epilepsy or demonic oppression. In [17:15](Matt.17.15), one so described “falls into fire and water,” that is, the boy was unable to control himself.

The **Ten Towns** was a federation of ten cities, most of which were east of the Jordan and southeast of the Sea of Galilee (Damascus, Raphana, Hippos, Abila \[or Canatha\], Gadara, Scythopolis, Pella, Dion, Gerasa, and Philadelphia \[Amman\]). These cities were predominantly Gentile and Hellenistic in culture.

This is the first of five lengthy discourses in Matthew (see also [9:35–11:1](Matt.9.35-Matt.11.1); [13:1-53](Matt.13.1-Matt.13.53); [18:1–19:2](Matt.18.1-Matt.19.2); [23:1–26:1](Matt.23.1-Matt.26.1)). The theme of the Sermon on the Mount is the Messiah’s call to righteousness. Paul understood righteousness in terms of God’s saving acts and of a person’s standing before God. Jesus uses the term for moral behavior that conforms to God’s will, as James does. Specifically, righteousness is doing the will of God as Jesus reveals it. This “revelation of righteousness” unifies the entire Sermon.

**poor and realize their need for him** (literally *poor in spirit*; cp. [Luke 6:20](Luke.6.20), [24](Luke.6.24)): In the Old Testament, the poor are often depicted as especially pious because oppression by the wealthy leads them to trust in the Lord for salvation and deliverance rather than relying on the power of wealth ([Matt 11:5](Matt.11.5); [Pss 37:14-15](Ps.37.14-Ps.37.15); [40:17](Ps.40.17); [69:28-33](Ps.69.28-Ps.69.33); [Isa 61:1](Isa.61.1); [66:2](Isa.66.2)). In both Matthew’s and Luke’s accounts, the “poor” are indeed physically poor, but their trust in God, not their poverty, is what makes them blessed ([Isa 57:15](Isa.57.15); [66:2](Isa.66.2)).

**Those who mourn** were those who lamented the spiritual and national condition of Israel (see [23:37-39](Matt.23.37-Matt.23.39); [Isa 61:2-3](Isa.61.2-Isa.61.3); [Joel 1:8-13](Joel.1.8-Joel.1.13); [2:12-13](Joel.2.12-Joel.2.13), [18-19](Joel.2.18-Joel.2.19); [Rom 9:1-5](Rom.9.1-Rom.9.5); [1 Cor 5:2](1Cor.5.2); [Jas 4:9](Jas.4.9)). Personal grief, whether caused by sin or tragedy, may also be in view ([Mark 16:10](Mark.16.10); [Rev 18:11](Rev.18.11), [19](Rev.18.19)).

**will be comforted:** The passive voice is used out of reverence for the holy name of God; the phrase could also be rendered *God will comfort them* (see also [Matt 5:6-7](Matt.5.6-Matt.5.7), [9](Matt.5.9)). Comfort will accompany the fulfillment of all that God has promised ([Isa 40:1-2](Isa.40.1-Isa.40.2); [61:2-3](Isa.61.2-Isa.61.3)).

**those who are humble:** See [Ps 37:11](Ps.37.11), which Jesus practically quotes here. Elsewhere, Jesus describes himself in similar terms—in contrast to other teachers ([Matt 11:29](Matt.11.29)) and as one who shuns pride ([12:17-21](Matt.12.17-Matt.12.21); [21:5](Matt.21.5)). This trait of Jesus is exemplified in his death on the cross ([1 Pet 2:23](1Pet.2.23); [3:9](1Pet.3.9)).

**The whole earth** could also be rendered *the land*, thus referring to God’s promise of land to Abraham and his descendants ([Gen 12:7](Gen.12.7); [17:8](Gen.17.8); see [Isa 60:21](Isa.60.21)). A wider sense may also be intended, such as God’s reign over the entire earth ([Matt 19:28](Matt.19.28); [28:18-20](Matt.28.18-Matt.28.20); [Ps 115:16](Ps.115.16)).

**those who hunger and thirst for justice** (or *for righteousness*): This refers either to the follower of Jesus whose driving purpose in life is to obey the Lord (cp. [3:15](Matt.3.15); [5:10](Matt.5.10), [20](Matt.5.20)) or to the disciple’s desire to see justice for all people ([Pss 11:7](Ps.11.7); [85:10-12](Ps.85.10-Ps.85.12); [Isa 11:1-4](Isa.11.1-Isa.11.4); [Jer 23:5-6](Jer.23.5-Jer.23.6); [33:16](Jer.33.16)). One with such a longing often prays, “May your will be done on earth” ([Matt 6:10](Matt.6.10)).

Christ has brought **justice** and righteousness ([Rom 3:21-22](Rom.3.21-Rom.3.22); [5:1](Rom.5.1)); the disciples **will be satisfied** with it (cp. [Pss 42:1-2](Ps.42.1-Ps.42.2); [63:1-2](Ps.63.1-Ps.63.2)).

Jesus made a cardinal virtue of being **merciful***,* that is, showing kindness to those in distress (see [6:12](Matt.6.12), [14-15](Matt.6.14-Matt.6.15); [9:13](Matt.9.13); [12:7](Matt.12.7); [18:23-35](Matt.18.23-Matt.18.35); [23:23](Matt.23.23); [25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)). Those who are merciful now will find God’s mercy in the final judgment.

**Those whose hearts are pure** (see [Pss 24:3-5](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.5); [51:7](Ps.51.7); [Isa 6:5](Isa.6.5)) are contrasted with those who thought that they had satisfied God’s will through ceremonial conformity to tradition ([Matt 23:25-26](Matt.23.25-Matt.23.26)). Jesus insisted on simple, true heart-righteousness (see [6:1-24](Matt.6.1-Matt.6.24); [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20); [23:23-28](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.28); [Deut 6:5](Deut.6.5)).
**They will see God** and thereby attain even more than Moses did (see [Exod 33:18-23](Exod.33.18-Exod.33.23); [34:5-7](Exod.34.5-Exod.34.7); see also [Ps 73:1](Ps.73.1)).
This beatitude probably targeted zealots—Jewish revolutionaries who advocated the overthrow of Roman domination through violent resistance. The Messiah’s Kingdom would be established by other means.
**those who work for peace:** Jesus is not calling for pacifism per se, but rather a different kind of activism.

**Peace** is the absence of enmity and the presence of God’s salvation ([Lev 26:6](Lev.26.6); [1 Sam 16:4-5](1Sam.16.4-1Sam.16.5); [Isa 9:5-6](Isa.9.5-Isa.9.6); [Zech 8:16](Zech.8.16); [Eph 2:14](Eph.2.14); [Col 1:20](Col.1.20)). Jesus’ disciples are to work for justice, righteousness, reconciliation, and mercy as the *effects* of God’s salvation through Christ ([Matt 5:43-47](Matt.5.43-Matt.5.47); [Luke 10:5-6](Luke.10.5-Luke.10.6)).

Jesus’ first disciples were **persecuted** by hostile Jewish leaders who were offended by Jesus’ new and authoritative revelation (see [10:17-23](Matt.10.17-Matt.10.23); [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6); [12:1-8](Matt.12.1-Matt.12.8); [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20); [23:34-36](Matt.23.34-Matt.23.36)). Since then, **doing right** by associating with Jesus and obeying his teachings has often been a source of persecution ([10:24-25](Matt.10.24-Matt.10.25); [2 Tim 3:12](2Tim.3.12)).

The **great reward** Jesus mentions is not something earned by suffering for doing right; it is God’s blessing to those who have expressed his grace to others (see [10:41-42](Matt.10.41-Matt.10.42); [20:1-16](Matt.20.1-Matt.20.16)).
The **ancient prophets** are closely connected with the New Testament apostles (see also [13:16-17](Matt.13.16-Matt.13.17); [23:29-36](Matt.23.29-Matt.23.36); [Eph 2:20](Eph.2.20)).

The disciples’ good deeds will have profoundly positive effects on the world around them, to the glory of God. With this comes a warning from Jesus: Do nothing that might jeopardize that positive influence.

**Salt** was used for cleansing and preservation from decay ([Ezek 16:4](Ezek.16.4)), in forming covenants ([Lev 2:13](Lev.2.13); [Num 18:19](Num.18.19); see study note on 2 Chr 13:5), and as flavor ([Job 6:6](Job.6.6); [Mark 9:50](Mark.9.50)).
Salt that **lost its flavor** became useless, insipid, or dull (see [Mark 9:50](Mark.9.50); [Luke 14:34](Luke.14.34)).

**light of the world . . . city on a hilltop:** The attractive quality of the disciples’ lives will draw other people to live similarly and to glorify God (see [Isa 2:2-5](Isa.2.2-Isa.2.5); [42:6](Isa.42.6); [49:6](Isa.49.6); [51:4](Isa.51.4); [56:6-8](Isa.56.6-Isa.56.8); [60:1-3](Isa.60.1-Isa.60.3); [Phil 2:15](Phil.2.15)).
**praise your heavenly Father:** Religious hypocrites seek praise for themselves; Jesus’ disciples should seek praise for God (see [1 Pet 2:12](1Pet.2.12)).
**Abolish** would mean to eliminate and replace **the law of Moses** and **the writings of the prophets** (i.e., the whole Old Testament) as the revelation of God’s will.

**Accomplish their purpose** might mean to obey them perfectly, to complete their teaching, or to bring about the fulfillment of their prophecies (see [1:22](Matt.1.22); [2:15](Matt.2.15), [17](Matt.2.17), [23](Matt.2.23)). Jesus himself is the realization of all that both the Prophets and the Law taught and expected. Now that Christ, the fulfillment, has come, the Old Testament must be understood in light of him ([Luke 24:26](Luke.24.26), [44](Luke.24.44)).
The realization of the law in Christ means that obedience to all of his commands (see [28:20](Matt.28.20)) is the only acceptable response for his disciples.
**Commandment** refers to the Old Testament commands ([5:18](Matt.5.18)) as now fulfilled in Christ’s teaching (see [5:21-48](Matt.5.21-Matt.5.48)).

**the least in the Kingdom of Heaven:** Jesus may mean that such an individual will enter the Kingdom, but only barely and with low status; alternatively, some Jewish evidence suggests that he is referring to damnation (cp. [8:12](Matt.8.12), where “those for whom the Kingdom was prepared” are eternally excluded).

**unless your righteousness is better:** Jesus’ disciples must have the substantially new kind of righteousness that Jesus teaches and makes possible (illustrated in [5:21-47](Matt.5.21-Matt.5.47) and summed up in [5:48](Matt.5.48)); it is both quantitatively and qualitatively distinct. Just as Jesus is greater than the Temple ([12:6](Matt.12.6)) and Jonah ([12:41](Matt.12.41)), so the righteousness of his followers far outstrips that of the **teachers of religious law and the Pharisees** (see [3:7-9](Matt.3.7-Matt.3.9)).

**You have heard. . . . But I say:** Jesus contrasts his own teaching to six misinterpretations of the law. Each antithesis provides an example of the surpassing righteousness of Jesus. Jesus reveals the will of God as it contrasts with traditions.

**our ancestors were told:** The expression refers to the traditional interpretation of the teachers of religious law and Pharisees. Though their traditions prohibited **murder***,* they did not prohibit hatred. The surpassing righteousness of Jesus demands reconciliation ([5:23-24](Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24)); merely refraining from committing murder is not sufficient ([5:22](Matt.5.22)).

**judgment . . . the court . . . hell:** The second and third punishments are more severe than would have been typical in Jesus’ day, emphasizing the surpassing righteousness of Jesus and his followers (see [5:20](Matt.5.20)). They did not tolerate unreconciled relationships or any devaluation of others.

**If you call someone an idiot:** The Aramaic term *reqa’* (transliterated as *raca*) means something like “empty head,” and the clause probably means the same as **if you curse someone** (literally *if you say, ‘You fool’*; cp. [Jas 2:20](Jas.2.20)). Devaluation of people is a sin that manifests itself in various ways.
Jesus gives two illustrations of reconciliation in community and society.
Jesus’ righteousness uncovers sin at a deeper level than the external; he reveals the true intent of the law.

**good eye . . . gouge it out . . . stronger hand . . . cut it off:** These graphic images call for radical separation from sin. But even self-mutilation, radical as it would be, cannot stop a lustful mind. Jesus is calling for the surpassing righteousness that only he can bring.

**hell** (Greek *Gehenna*): Gehenna originally referred to a valley outside Jerusalem where some of the kings of Judah worshiped idols and performed human sacrifice by fire ([2 Chr 28:3](2Chr.28.3); [33:6](2Chr.33.6); [Jer 7:31](Jer.7.31); [32:35](Jer.32.35)). The site was eventually destroyed by Josiah ([2 Kgs 23:10](2Kgs.23.10)). In the New Testament, Gehenna describes the place of punishment by God. Unless disciples have surpassing righteousness, they will not enter the Kingdom ([Matt 5:20](Matt.5.20)) but will be punished eternally ([5:22](Matt.5.22); [23:33](Matt.23.33)).

Jesus challenges the misapplication of the Old Testament provision for **divorce** (see [Deut 24:1-4](Deut.24.1-Deut.24.4); cp. [Matt 19:3-9](Matt.19.3-Matt.19.9)): Following the rules does not make divorce acceptable. Jesus allows only one legitimate reason for divorce, sexual infidelity, and forbids casual divorce (see also [1 Cor 7:10-11](1Cor.7.10-1Cor.7.11)).

A **notice of divorce** is a document stating the legality of a divorce. Evidence suggests that such a document permitted remarriage. “The essential formula in the notice of divorce is, ‘Lo, you are free to marry any man.’ . . . The essential formula in a writ of emancipation is, ‘Lo, you are a freedwoman: lo, you belong to yourself’” (*Mishnah Gittin* 9:3).

The exception clause permits but does not demand divorce when one partner has **been unfaithful** (see also [19:9](Matt.19.9)). Notably, Jesus does not demand death for the guilty party (see [Deut 22:21-22](Deut.22.21-Deut.22.22)).

The implication seems to be that by divorcing his wife for illegitimate reasons, the man **causes her to commit adultery** by wrongly putting her in a situation where she remarries and so breaks the law.

**anyone who marries a divorced woman:** It is not clear whether Jesus is referring to any woman who is divorced, regardless of the reason, or only to a woman who is divorced without an acceptable reason (unfaithfulness). The underlying assumption in Jewish divorce law was simple: Legitimate divorces permitted remarriage.

Jesus here summarizes the Old Testament teaching on oaths ([Lev 19:12](Lev.19.12); [Num 30:2-4](Num.30.2-Num.30.4); [Deut 23:21-23](Deut.23.21-Deut.23.23); [Ps 50:14](Ps.50.14); [Zech 8:17](Zech.8.17)). The Pharisees had degrees of commitment for oaths—for example, ones that did not mention God were not as binding. Jesus shows that because God is related to all things (**heaven***,* **earth***,* **Jerusalem***,* **my head**; see also [Matt 23:16-22](Matt.23.16-Matt.23.22)), breaking any oath breaks God’s command (see [Exod 20:7](Exod.20.7)). The point is that one must be altogether truthful. Jesus’ righteousness elevates the disciple’s everyday yes and no to the level of binding oath. Oaths become superfluous to the honest person ([Jas 5:12](Jas.5.12)).

The Old Testament permitted proportionate retribution ([Exod 21:24-25](Exod.21.24-Exod.21.25); [Deut 19:16-21](Deut.19.16-Deut.19.21)), which was to prevent punishments from far exceeding the severity of the offense. Jesus, however, does not permit personal retaliation at all among his followers. Jesus’ way is not to insist on justice but to find victory through suffering and the cross ([1 Pet 2:23](1Pet.2.23)). Some have taken this passage as a guide for all of life (including politics). Others understand it merely as the willingness to forgo one’s personal rights and to forgive as God has forgiven (see [Matt 5:48](Matt.5.48); [18:23-35](Matt.18.23-Matt.18.35)). Like the servant in [Isa 50:4-9](Isa.50.4-Isa.50.9) and [53:7](Isa.53.7) (see also [Matt 12:15-21](Matt.12.15-Matt.12.21)), Jesus’ followers are to apply the same virtue to honor, possessions, time, or property. Righteousness does not insist on its own way.

Forced labor was a humiliating fact of Roman occupation (see [27:32](Matt.27.32)); Jesus turned it into an occasion for exuberant service to God. This saying shows Jesus’ opposition to Jewish revolutionaries, who advocated violent resistance (see [5:9](Matt.5.9)).

**hate your enemy:** Jesus is opposing not the Old Testament, but a traditional, though mistaken (cp. [Exod 23:4-5](Exod.23.4-Exod.23.5)), interpretation of the Old Testament. The “hate” clause is not in the Old Testament (but see [Ps 139:21-22](Ps.139.21-Ps.139.22)).

By loving all people, Jesus’ followers would not *become* children of God; they would show by their actions that they are indeed God’s **true children,** according to his nature and will (see [Deut 10:18-19](Deut.10.18-Deut.10.19)).

**If you are kind only to your friends** (literally, *If you greet only your brothers*): Jews were instructed to greet Gentiles for the sake of maintaining peaceful relations, but such greetings were not the same as those for “brothers”—i.e., fellow Jews.
This verse ties [5:20-48](Matt.5.20-Matt.5.48) together as a unit (see study note on 4:23-25).

**you are to be perfect:** The term rendered “perfect” means maturity and wholeness in response to Jesus’ proclamation of the Kingdom, and complete consecration to God ([19:21](Matt.19.21); [Eph 4:13](Eph.4.13); [Phil 3:15](Phil.3.15); [Col 1:28](Col.1.28); [4:12](Col.4.12); [1 Jn 4:18](1John.4.18)). Perfection has love at its core (see [Luke 6:36](Luke.6.36)).
This verse introduces the theme of [6:2-18](Matt.6.2-Matt.6.18), that righteousness should not be done for public recognition but as a service to God.

**Good deeds** are acts that conform to God’s pattern for proper behavior: e.g., gift giving ([6:2-4](Matt.6.2-Matt.6.4)), prayer ([6:5-15](Matt.6.5-Matt.6.15)), and fasting ([6:16-18](Matt.6.16-Matt.6.18)). Jesus urges secrecy to counteract the human propensity to seek praise for oneself rather than for God (cp. [5:16](Matt.5.16)).
**the hypocrites:** See study note on 23:13.
The **blowing** of **trumpets** accompanied major rituals, including public fasts.
**your Father . . . will reward you:** Both now and at the final judgment at the end of history ([25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)).

**When you pray:** Jews prayed regularly at 9 AM and 3 PM (see [Acts 3:1](Acts.3.1)) and had frequent times of public prayer. Hypocrites deliberately sought to be in public places at such times, to be seen by all.

**go away by yourself:** Jesus is not prohibiting corporate prayer (see [18:19-20](Matt.18.19-Matt.18.20); [Luke 11:2-4](Luke.11.2-Luke.11.4)) but is instructing his followers to avoid using prayer as a means of drawing attention to themselves.
God cannot be coaxed by endless repetition. The Lord’s Prayer ([6:9-13](Matt.6.9-Matt.6.13)) is a model of simplicity in contrast with pagan wordiness.
The Lord’s Prayer is similar in form to a common Jewish prayer (the *qaddish*). Jesus gave this prayer to his followers as a succinct expression of their new faith.
**Pray like this:** In contrast to the vain repetition of pagan prayers ([6:7-8](Matt.6.7-Matt.6.8)), “the Lord’s Prayer” is a model of simplicity.
Jews rarely addressed God as **Father***,* but Jesus did so in every prayer but one ([Mark 15:34](Mark.15.34)).

**may your name be kept holy:** God’s name is profaned by the sin of his people ([Isa 29:22-24](Isa.29.22-Isa.29.24); [Jer 34:15-16](Jer.34.15-Jer.34.16); [Ezek 39:7](Ezek.39.7); [Amos 2:7](Amos.2.7)).
In praying for God’s **Kingdom** to **come soon***,* Jesus’ disciples pray for his justice, righteousness, peace, and mercy to be established.
Outside God’s **will***,* no person will be permitted into God’s presence ([7:21](Matt.7.21); [12:50](Matt.12.50); [21:28-32](Matt.21.28-Matt.21.32)).
**on earth, as it is in heaven:** This probably refers to all of the first three petitions, not just the third.
**Give us today the food we need:** The disciple, after confidently asking God to provide for daily needs, can go about Kingdom ministry relieved of care ([6:25-34](Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34)).

**as we have forgiven** (see also [6:14-15](Matt.6.14-Matt.6.15); [18:21-35](Matt.18.21-Matt.18.35)): Forgiving others is a reflection of a repentant, regenerate heart, which makes our own forgiveness possible. Those who have experienced God’s forgiveness will forgive. Jesus implies that those who are unwilling to forgive have not perceived God’s mercy, and perhaps have never truly repented.

**And don’t let us yield to temptation:** Just as Jesus was tested ([4:1-11](Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11)), temptation will test the disciple’s character. Jesus urges prayer for God’s enabling to stand the test (see [26:41](Matt.26.41); [Ps 141:4](Ps.141.4)).
**from the evil one:** Or *from evil.* The alternate reading refers to sin in general; the NLT reading refers to Satan, the tempter (see [Jas 1:13](Jas.1.13)).
The doxology appended to some manuscripts was added later (probably based on [1 Chr 29:11-13](1Chr.29.11-1Chr.29.13)) to tailor the prayer to the liturgy.

Prayer and fasting are frequently connected ([Lev 23:27-32](Lev.23.27-Lev.23.32); [Neh 9:1-2](Neh.9.1-Neh.9.2); [Zech 7:3-5](Zech.7.3-Zech.7.5); [8:19](Zech.8.19); [Luke 18:12](Luke.18.12)). The practice had been abused before Jesus’ time ([Isa 58:3-12](Isa.58.3-Isa.58.12)).

**treasures in heaven:** This was a common image for Jews of Jesus’ day; doing God’s commands became virtually equivalent to accumulating treasures with God. The context ([6:19](Matt.6.19); [Luke 12:33](Luke.12.33)) suggests that Jesus primarily had acts of charity in mind.
**Your eye is like a lamp:** It gives **light** to the **body** and so enlightens the entire person.
**Healthy** means morally healthy, with simple, wholehearted devotion to God ([6:24](Matt.6.24)). Here it connotes generosity.

The term for **money** (traditionally *mammon*) is an Aramaic term for profits or material possessions. Since God tolerates no rivals, Jesus repeatedly warns of the danger of accumulating riches ([13:22](Matt.13.22); [19:16-30](Matt.19.16-Matt.19.30); [26:14-16](Matt.26.14-Matt.26.16); [27:3-10](Matt.27.3-Matt.27.10); [28:11-15](Matt.28.11-Matt.28.15)), which can be an idol (see [Eph 5:5](Eph.5.5); [Col 3:5](Col.3.5)). We must trust God to meet our needs ([Matt 4:3-4](Matt.4.3-Matt.4.4); [6:8](Matt.6.8), [11](Matt.6.11), [25-34](Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34); [7:7-11](Matt.7.7-Matt.7.11); [10:9-14](Matt.10.9-Matt.10.14); [14:15-21](Matt.14.15-Matt.14.21); [15:32-38](Matt.15.32-Matt.15.38)), and the community of disciples is to be mutually supportive ([6:2-4](Matt.6.2-Matt.6.4); [10:40-42](Matt.10.40-Matt.10.42); [19:21](Matt.19.21); [23:23-24](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.24); [25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46); [26:6-13](Matt.26.6-Matt.26.13); [27:57-61](Matt.27.57-Matt.27.61)).

Jesus taught an anxiety-free existence of simple trust in God for provisions. Jesus’ disciples had abandoned all ([4:18-22](Matt.4.18-Matt.4.22); [9:9](Matt.9.9); [10:5-14](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.14)); Jesus gave them comforting reassurance that God would provide for their needs.

Jesus’ logic progresses from lesser to greater: If the Father tends to **birds** (the lesser), and the disciple is **far more valuable to him** (the greater), then he will certainly tend to the disciples’ needs (see also [10:29-31](Matt.10.29-Matt.10.31)).
**Little faith** results from the failure to understand one’s value to God and the extent of God’s providential protection.
**unbelievers** (literally *Gentiles*): Those who fail to know God and follow his will (see also [20:19](Matt.20.19)).
**your heavenly Father already knows:** Prayer does not inform God about **needs***;* it expresses trust in his provision.

Here Jesus gives the positive alternative to worrying. Single-minded commitment to God and seeking his reign through Christ (see [6:19-24](Matt.6.19-Matt.6.24)) must be the primary concern of Jesus’ disciples.

Mercy is a dominant theme in Jesus’ teaching and practice ([9:9-13](Matt.9.9-Matt.9.13); [12:1-7](Matt.12.1-Matt.12.7)), but not at the expense of clear opposition to sin (see [18:15-20](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.20); [23:13-33](Matt.23.13-Matt.23.33)). At the same time, Jesus calls for people to stop oppressively controlling others in the name of pastoral concern. The judgment Jesus prohibits often involves rigorous scrutiny of trivial matters (see [23:23-24](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.24)). God alone has the right to judge (see [Jas 4:11-12](Jas.4.11-Jas.4.12)).

**you will not be judged:** This might refer to God’s judgment at the end of history (see [Matt 5:7](Matt.5.7)). God measures us by our treatment of others (see [6:12](Matt.6.12); [18:21-35](Matt.18.21-Matt.18.35)).

Jesus exhorts his disciples to minister to others rather than condemning them. Reference to a **speck** (speck of dust, chip of wood) versus a **log** in the **eye** is hyperbolic imagery, intended to heighten the contrast (see [5:29](Matt.5.29); [23:23-24](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.24); cp. [Mic 6:6-8](Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8)).

Rabbis often referred to important ideas or Scripture verses as **pearls**. The mysteries of the Kingdom ([13:11](Matt.13.11)) are **holy** (see [Exod 29:33](Exod.29.33); [Lev 2:3](Lev.2.3); [22:10-16](Lev.22.10-Lev.22.16); [Num 18:8-10](Num.18.8-Num.18.10)).

**Don’t waste what is holy on people who are unholy:** Literally *Don’t give the sacred to dogs.* Jews often referred to Gentiles as dogs (see [Matt 15:26](Matt.15.26); see [Ps 22:16](Ps.22.16), [20](Ps.22.20)) or **pigs** because those animals were unclean ([Lev 11](Lev.11.1-Lev.11.47)). Some interpreters understand this statement as warning that the message of the Kingdom would not be well received by many Gentiles. Others see it as a warning about offering the message of the Kingdom to the resistant Jewish leaders (see [Matt 5:20](Matt.5.20); [10:11-14](Matt.10.11-Matt.10.14); see also [Heb 10:29](Heb.10.29)) or to unbelievers in general (see [Matt 18:17](Matt.18.17); see also [1 Cor 2:13-16](1Cor.2.13-1Cor.2.16); [2 Pet 2:21-22](2Pet.2.21-2Pet.2.22)).

This passage teaches persistence in prayer, but Jesus does not teach that God will grant extravagant desires. God’s people are to seek daily provision and spiritual blessing ([6:10-11](Matt.6.10-Matt.6.11)).

**the law and the prophets:** The teaching of Jesus in [5:21–7:6](Matt.5.21-Matt.7.6) is the goal and true expression of the law of Moses. Love is at the core of discipleship (see also [Gal 5:13-14](Gal.5.13-Gal.5.14), [18](Gal.5.18)).

The Sermon on the Mount closes with a call to decide about Jesus and his teaching (see [4:23](Matt.4.23); [9:35](Matt.9.35)). Those who hear Jesus’ message regarding the Kingdom must follow him to obtain eternal life or disown him and experience God’s condemnation. There is no middle way ([Deut 30:15-20](Deut.30.15-Deut.30.20); [Ps 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6); [Prov 12:28](Prov.12.28); [Jer 21:8](Jer.21.8)).
Entering **through the narrow gate** refers to the decision to follow Jesus as the Messiah. The **wide** gate and **broad** highway refer to the decision not to follow Jesus and his teachings.
**Hell** refers to being thrown into the fire, not entering the Kingdom of Heaven, being banished from the presence of Jesus, and being ruined ([7:19-23](Matt.7.19-Matt.7.23), [27](Matt.7.27)).
**Few** people come to the light that is revealed in Christ (see [19:23](Matt.19.23); [20:16](Matt.20.16); [22:14](Matt.22.14); see also [John 3:19](John.3.19); [6:66-71](John.6.66-John.6.71)).

**False prophets** speak what people want to hear rather than calling people to live according to God’s will. [Deuteronomy 13:1-5](Deut.13.1-Deut.13.5) and [18:21-22](Matt.18.21-Matt.18.22) set standards for evaluating a prophet’s truthfulness: His words must conform to God’s word, and his predictions must come true. Jesus unpacks the first requirement: A prophet’s actions must match his words in order to be believable; accordingly, a true prophet’s actions will also match God’s word. Just as the **fruit** indicates the nature of a **tree***,* so one’s life indicates either a regenerate or unregenerate heart. False prophets are expected at the end of the age (see [Matt 24:11](Matt.24.11), [24](Matt.24.24); [Acts 20:28-35](Acts.20.28-Acts.20.35); [Rev 13:11-18](Rev.13.11-Rev.13.18); [16:13](Rev.16.13); [19:20](Rev.19.20); [20:10](Rev.20.10)). In order not to be deceived, Christians must be discerning (see [1 Cor 12:10](1Cor.12.10); [14:29](1Cor.14.29); [1 Thes 5:21](1Thess.5.21); [1 Jn 4:1-3](1John.4.1-1John.4.3); [Rev 2:20](Rev.2.20)).

Spiritual rebirth is absolutely necessary if one is to **produce** the **good fruit** that Jesus demands. Good works flow from faith; good works and faith cannot be separated (see [Jas 2:14-26](Jas.2.14-Jas.2.26)).
**The will of my Father** is expressed in Jesus’ teachings (see also [12:50](Matt.12.50); [21:28-32](Matt.21.28-Matt.21.32); [Rom 2:13](Rom.2.13); [Jas 1:22-27](Jas.1.22-Jas.1.27)).

**judgment day:** The Old Testament concept behind this notion is the “day of the Lord,” when God will come to rescue the faithful and judge the oppressors ([Isa 13–14](Isa.13.1-Isa.14.32); [Joel 2:1-32](Joel.2.1-Joel.2.32); [Zeph 1:14-16](Zeph.1.14-Zeph.1.16)). In Jesus’ teaching, this day is when all will be judged for their response to him (see [Matt 10:15](Matt.10.15); [11:20-24](Matt.11.20-Matt.11.24); [12:36](Matt.12.36); [24:19-50](Matt.24.19-Matt.24.50); [25:13](Matt.25.13), [31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46); [Acts 17:31](Acts.17.31); [Rom 2:16](Rom.2.16)).
Neither charismatic gifts nor public accomplishments in Jesus’ **name** will necessarily bring God’s acceptance; the decisive issue is obedience ([Matt 7:21](Matt.7.21)).

**I never knew you:** These people were never converted, even though they did great things in God’s name. They **break God’s laws** through rejection of the Father’s will as taught by Jesus. Having never known Christ, they never learned to do what he commanded.

The emphasis in this whole sermon ([5:3–7:27](Matt.5.3-Matt.7.27)) is on doing what Jesus teaches by walking in righteousness ([5:20](Matt.5.20)). To hear and not obey is to choose the wide gate and the broad highway that lead to destruction ([Jas 1:22-25](Jas.1.22-Jas.1.25); [2:14-26](Jas.2.14-Jas.2.26)). Decision is necessary in light of what has been revealed. See [Lev 26](Lev.26.1-Lev.26.46); [Deut 28](Deut.28.1-Deut.28.68), [30](Deut.30.1-Deut.30.20).

A **wise** . . . **person** perceives that Jesus is the fulfillment of Old Testament promises, willingly submits to him, and walks the path that ultimately leads to blessing ([5:3-12](Matt.5.3-Matt.5.12); [7:13-14](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.14)).
Building a **house** directly on **rock** provides a much stronger foundation than would a dry, sandy riverbed or floodplain ([7:26](Matt.7.26)).
The storm is a metaphor for God’s all-knowing judgment (see [Jer 23:19](Jer.23.19); [Ezek 1:4](Ezek.1.4)).
Jesus began teaching only his disciples ([5:1](Matt.5.1)), but **crowds** had followed up the mountainside as well.

Unlike the **teachers of religious law***,* whose authority was derived from the Scriptures they quoted or from the teachings of previous scholars, Jesus taught **with real**—that is, direct—**authority**. He quoted Scripture in the Sermon, but his teaching was based on his own authority as the Messiah.

Here the Kingdom of God is manifested with supernatural power (see [4:23-25](Matt.4.23-Matt.4.25); [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6)). It reaches people who had been excluded from the blessing of God: Gentiles, lepers, blind people, sick women, demoniacs, tax collectors, those with a chronic hemorrhage, and the dead. Jesus shows compassion, but the religious leaders are provoked to opposition. Jesus calls his followers to faith and discipleship.

**Leprosy** refers to various skin diseases. Lepers were ceremonially unclean; they were excluded from society unless they became symptom-free and a priest pronounced them **clean** (see [8:4](Matt.8.4); [Lev 14:2-32](Lev.14.2-Lev.14.32)). On some occasions, leprosy was a judgment from God ([Num 12:9-15](Num.12.9-Num.12.15); [2 Kgs 5:27](2Kgs.5.27); [15:5](2Kgs.15.5)).
**Be healed:** Jesus’ healing of lepers was tangible evidence of the Kingdom in his person and ministry ([11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6)).

The leper’s healing would be **a public testimony**—either that the religious leaders were wrong not to trust in the Messiah ([10:18](Matt.10.18)) or that Jesus was not against the **law of Moses** ([5:17](Matt.5.17)).

Jesus once again ministered to the marginalized or ostracized. The centurion was a Gentile soldier, and ministry to him would have evoked strong resentment from both the nationalistic and the separatist wings of Jewish society.

**Capernaum** is located on the Sea of Galilee, about two and a half miles west of the Jordan River outlet. In Jesus’ day, it was a prosperous fishing village. Standing at a crucial junction on the Great Trunk Road linking Mesopotamia and Egypt, it was an international village, and much of Jesus’ Galilean ministry was based there (e.g., [4:13](Matt.4.13); [8:14-17](Matt.8.14-Matt.8.17)).

**a Roman officer** (Greek *a centurion*): A centurion, one of sixty commanders in a legion, commanded 100 Roman soldiers (see also [Mark 15:39](Mark.15.39); [Acts 10:1](Acts.10.1); [27:1](Acts.27.1)).

**I will come** (cp. [Acts 10:9-35](Acts.10.9-Acts.10.35); [Gal 2:11-14](Gal.2.11-Gal.2.14)): Some have rendered this as a question: *Shall I* \[a Jew\] *come* \[into the house of a Gentile, risking defilement\] *and heal him?*

The centurion recognized Jesus’ **authority**. From his own experience, he knew that when he gave orders, they were quickly obeyed. He perceived that God had entrusted Jesus with authority to work miracles. The centurion’s **faith** shows that the Kingdom of God includes Gentiles ([8:11](Matt.8.11)).

The influx of **Gentiles** fulfills Old Testament promises ([Isa 2:2-3](Isa.2.2-Isa.2.3)). God’s promise to **Abraham** included being a blessing to many nations ([Gen 18:18](Gen.18.18)). Christ fulfills this promise ([Gal 3:8](Gal.3.8), [16](Gal.3.16)).
Jesus is the authoritative Lord over every disease and demon.
**with a simple command:** Jesus’ authority extended beyond touch; his words brought healing and life.

**He took our sicknesses and removed our diseases:** When he took the sins of humanity, the Messiah also took our sickness. Sickness exists because sin is in the world, and one of the effects of Jesus’ taking our sin on the cross is physical healing ([1 Pet 2:24](1Pet.2.24)). Jesus’ healings and exorcisms demonstrated, in fulfillment of Scripture, that he is the Messiah (see [Matt 11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28); [1 Cor 11:29-30](1Cor.11.29-1Cor.11.30); [Jas 5:13-16](Jas.5.13-Jas.5.16)).
Jesus confronted two would-be followers with what it truly means to follow him.

The **teachers of religious law** had a prestigious vocation of preserving, learning, and interpreting the Scriptures for the good of society. The way to God was thought to be through them ([15:13-14](Matt.15.13-Matt.15.14); [23:13](Matt.23.13)).
Following Jesus is not easy; it involves more than intellectual mastery. Following Jesus entails being willing to forgo life’s normal comforts.
**Another of his disciples:** This statement suggests that the teacher of [8:19](Matt.8.19) was a disciple as well. **Lord** suggests a stronger commitment to Jesus.
**bury my father:** This was one of the highest religious duties in Judaism, but Jesus requires total commitment to him.

**Let the spiritually dead bury their own dead:** Jesus’ opponents would have misconstrued this instruction as blatant disregard for the fifth commandment to honor one’s parents ([Exod 20:12](Exod.20.12)), but in essence it is a restatement of the first commandment ([Exod 20:1-3](Exod.20.1-Exod.20.3)). It was warranted by Jesus’ messianic authority and the impact of the Kingdom upon normal human life, including family ties and commitments (see [Matt 10:34-39](Matt.10.34-Matt.10.39); [12:46-50](Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50); [19:29](Matt.19.29); [Zech 13:3](Zech.13.3); [Luke 14:26-27](Luke.14.26-Luke.14.27)).

The episode at sea extends the theme of what true discipleship involves. The storm challenged the disciples to entrust their very lives to Jesus for protection and deliverance. Jesus even has authority over dangerous weather and the sea (see [Job 38:8-11](Job.38.8-Job.38.11); [Pss 29](Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11); [65:1-13](Ps.65.1-Ps.65.13); [89:9](Ps.89.9); [107:23-32](Ps.107.23-Ps.107.32)).
**a fierce storm struck the lake:** Sudden squalls are common on the Sea of Galilee, which is among mountains.
**Who is this man?** Salvation requires a proper answer to this question and active faith in him. Jesus’ disciples had still failed to understand.
This episode focuses on Jesus’ authority as well as on the cost of following him; those who walk by faith will, like the Messiah, also experience opposition.

**possessed by demons . . . so violent:** Demon-possession was often accompanied by violence, revulsion at the presence of the Son of God ([8:29](Matt.8.29)), inability to speak ([9:32](Matt.9.32); [12:22](Matt.12.22)), blindness ([12:22](Matt.12.22)), seizures ([17:15](Matt.17.15)), and self-destructive behavior ([17:15](Matt.17.15)). With Jesus’ exorcisms, the power of the Kingdom broke into human history ([12:28](Matt.12.28)).

Those controlled by Satan immediately recognized Jesus’ true identity as the **Son of God** (see [Mark 1:24](Mark.1.24)) and answered the question asked by Jesus’ disciples when he had calmed the storm ([Matt 8:27](Matt.8.27)). Elsewhere, Jesus’ true nature and identity are acknowledged by the Father ([3:17](Matt.3.17); [17:5](Matt.17.5)), Satan ([4:3](Matt.4.3), [6](Matt.4.6)), humans ([14:33](Matt.14.33); [16:16](Matt.16.16); [27:54](Matt.27.54)), and Christ himself ([11:27](Matt.11.27); [24:36](Matt.24.36); [28:19](Matt.28.19)).
**God’s appointed time** is the final, eternal damnation of all who oppose God (see [Jude 1:6](Jude.1.6); [Rev 20:10](Rev.20.10)).
The **demons** were no match for Jesus’ authority; they desperately **begged** to avoid imminent doom.
Jesus’ word had sufficient authority to expel demons.
**drowned:** Jesus had begun to defeat the enemy ([12:28](Matt.12.28); [Luke 10:17-20](Luke.10.17-Luke.10.20); [Rom 16:20](Rom.16.20); [Col 2:15](Col.2.15)).
The tragedy of the incident is that those who witnessed the Son of God’s power to give salvation feared having their world upset, so they rejected him.
Controversy ensued among Jesus’ opponents, the teachers of religious law and Pharisees ([9:1-13](Matt.9.1-Matt.9.13)), and among the disciples of John the Baptist ([9:14-17](Matt.9.14-Matt.9.17)).
**His own town** was Capernaum ([Mark 2:1](Mark.2.1)), where he apparently relocated from Nazareth after being rejected there ([Matt 4:13](Matt.4.13); [Luke 4:16-31](Luke.4.16-Luke.4.31)).

**Does he think he’s God?** God alone could forgive sins ([Ps 103:3](Ps.103.3); [Isa 43:25](Isa.43.25); [Jer 50:20](Jer.50.20)). The **teachers of religious law** failed to comprehend Jesus’ mission as God’s incarnate Son ([Matt 3:17](Matt.3.17); [11:25-27](Matt.11.25-Matt.11.27)). As God’s Messiah ([1:1](Matt.1.1); [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6)), he was saving mankind ([8:17](Matt.8.17); [26:26-28](Matt.26.26-Matt.26.28)).

It is **easier** for Jesus to pronounce forgiveness, since that might have no verifiable effects; it is harder to enable a paralytic to **walk**. The miracle, visible to all, corroborates Jesus’ authority to forgive sins and forces all who witness it to decide about Jesus.
**So I will prove:** Jesus performed the miracle to reveal his authority and identity as God’s Messiah (see [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28)).

The mixture of **fear** and praise in the crowd’s response corresponds to the awesome truth they perceived about Jesus. He is indeed the Son of God who has **authority** on earth to forgive sins ([9:6](Matt.9.6)).
Jesus, as Lord and Messiah, tore down the barriers that prevented righteous Jews from intermingling with those who were unclean or sinful.
**Matthew** was also called Levi ([Mark 2:14](Mark.2.14)). Matthew might have had two names, or he might have been given a new name by Jesus.

The Jewish people despised Jewish **tax collectors** ([5:46-47](Matt.5.46-Matt.5.47); [18:15-20](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.20)), who cooperated with Roman oppressors and were considered betrayers of the Israelite nation. Many also considered them unclean because of their frequent contact with Gentiles and because of the idolatrous images on Roman coins. Tax-collection was a private enterprise. In each district, Rome granted the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder (cp. [Luke 19:1-10](Luke.19.1-Luke.19.10)). Anything collected above the bid was profit for the collectors, who, driven by greed, often used extortion.

**I want you to show mercy, not offer sacrifices:** God’s desire is applied to the question of table fellowship with sinners; Jesus’ **mercy** in eating with sinners contrasts with the Pharisees’ separation from sinners (symbolized as **sacrifices**).

Jesus revealed the true spiritual condition of the Pharisees, **who think they are righteous***;* they failed to recognize that they were in fact unrighteous and in need of the Messiah’s salvation. See [7:1-5](Matt.7.1-Matt.7.5); [8:11-12](Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12); [19:30](Matt.19.30); [20:16](Matt.20.16); [21:43](Matt.21.43).

**fast:** Fasting expressed personal humility and repentance ([2 Sam 12:16-23](2Sam.12.16-2Sam.12.23); [Dan 9:3](Dan.9.3)). It called attention to the national need for repentance ([Lev 16:29-31](Lev.16.29-Lev.16.31); [Neh 9:1](Neh.9.1)) and probably sought to hasten the arrival of the Messiah through purification. The fact that **Jesus** and his **disciples** did not fast ([Matt 11:18-19](Matt.11.18-Matt.11.19)) subtly proclaimed that the Messiah had already arrived (see also [6:16](Matt.6.16)).

**wedding guests . . . groom:** John the Baptist had also described the Messiah and his disciples in this way ([John 3:29](John.3.29)), drawing on Old Testament imagery to reveal Jesus’ status (see [Matt 25:1-13](Matt.25.1-Matt.25.13); [Isa 54:5-6](Isa.54.5-Isa.54.6)).

**taken away:** This is Jesus’ first prediction of his violent death (see [Matt 16:21](Matt.16.21); [17:12](Matt.17.12), [22-23](Matt.17.22-Matt.17.23); [20:18-19](Matt.20.18-Matt.20.19); [26:2](Matt.26.2), [26-35](Matt.26.26-Matt.26.35); [Isa 53:8](Isa.53.8)).

**then they will fast:** Jesus may be referring to the disciples’ sorrow immediately after his crucifixion, or to the disciples’ lifestyle after his death and resurrection (see [Acts 9:9](Acts.9.9); [13:2-3](Acts.13.2-Acts.13.3); [14:23](Acts.14.23); [27:9](Acts.27.9), [33](Acts.27.33)).

These riddle-like parables contrast the new covenant that Jesus has established ([26:26-29](Matt.26.26-Matt.26.29)) with the old covenant, especially in relation to such rituals as fasting. Jesus consummates, but does not abolish, the law ([5:17-20](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.20); see [Gal 2:21](Gal.2.21); [5:4](Gal.5.4)). Yet the new covenant requires new practices.
Jesus is the Messiah whose power knows no boundaries. He calls people to have faith in him.

**lay your hand on her:** The laying-on of hands is a visible symbol of prayer for God’s power to flow into someone, often resulting in new life or ministries ([19:13](Matt.19.13); [Num 27:18-23](Num.27.18-Num.27.23); [Deut 34:9](Deut.34.9)).
The man believed that Jesus had the power to raise the dead (cp. [1 Kgs 17:8-24](1Kgs.17.8-1Kgs.17.24); [2 Kgs 4:18-37](2Kgs.4.18-2Kgs.4.37)).

The woman’s **constant bleeding** rendered her always ceremonially unclean and made whoever she touched unclean as well ([Lev 15:25-30](Lev.15.25-Lev.15.30)). But instead of rendering Jesus unclean, her touching him made her clean, a stunning reversal that illustrates Jesus’ power to redeem and sanctify (see [Matt 14:36](Matt.14.36); [Mark 3:10](Mark.3.10)).
**fringe:** The tassels at the bottom of a tunic ([Matt 23:5](Matt.23.5); [Num 15:37-41](Num.15.37-Num.15.41)) reminded Jews to live in accord with God’s law.
**Your faith has made you well** (literally *has saved you)*: Physical healing demonstrated her spiritual salvation (see [8:17](Matt.8.17)).

**noisy crowd . . . funeral music:** Sorrow over the death of a family member was publicly expressed, with musical accompaniment and dirges by professional mourners. “Even the poorest in Israel should hire not less than two flutes and one wailing woman” (*Mishnah Ketubbot* [4:4](Matt.4.4)).

Though she was physically dead, from Jesus’ perspective **the girl** was just **asleep**—she would soon be raised back to life (see [Isa 26:19](Isa.26.19); [John 11:11-14](John.11.11-John.11.14), [25](John.11.25); [1 Thes 4:14](1Thess.4.14)).

Eye diseases were common in the ancient world. Blindness was often considered to be divine punishment (see [Exod 4:11](Exod.4.11); [Deut 28:28](Deut.28.28); [2 Kgs 6:18](2Kgs.6.18); [John 9:2-3](John.9.2-John.9.3)). The Old Testament predicts that the Messiah’s coming would bring restoration of sight for the blind ([Matt 11:4-5](Matt.11.4-Matt.11.5); [Isa 29:18-19](Isa.29.18-Isa.29.19); [35:5-6](Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6)).

**Son of David** is a messianic title particularly associated with miraculous healings (see [Matt 1:1](Matt.1.1); [12:23](Matt.12.23); [15:22](Matt.15.22); [20:30-31](Matt.20.30-Matt.20.31); [2 Sam 7:12-16](2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16)).
Jesus intended his question to elicit confessions of faith from the two men.
The Messiah’s acts invoke faith, astonishment, and derisive rejection.
