Enabling the deaf to hear and the mute to speak is a sign of the Kingdom of God ([11:4-5](Matt.11.4-Matt.11.5); [Isa 35:5-6](Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6)).

Jesus here extends his ministry (shown in [4:23–9:34](Matt.4.23-Matt.9.34)) to others within Israel through his disciples ([10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6)). Jesus’ instructions to his disciples ([10:5-42](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.42)) focus on missionary activity and its consequent opposition and hardship.

This verse connects with the section begun at [4:23](Matt.4.23). Matthew has presented Jesus to his readers as the Messiah who teaches, preaches, heals, casts out demons, and calls for a decisive response of faith.

**like sheep without a shepherd:** Jesus lamented the Pharisees’ pastoral negligence (see [12:11-12](Matt.12.11-Matt.12.12); [18:12](Matt.18.12)). Their attacks against Jesus were a clear indication of their hard-hearted rejection of God. The crowds languished due to pastoral neglect and mistreatment ([10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6); [15:12-14](Matt.15.12-Matt.15.14); [23:4](Matt.23.4); [Zech 11:16](Zech.11.16)).

**the Lord who is in charge of the harvest:** All ministries are ultimately under God’s call (see [Matt 23:8-10](Matt.23.8-Matt.23.10), [13](Matt.23.13)), so Jesus urges his disciples to pray for God himself to call more **workers**.

**Jesus called his twelve disciples** as workers in the harvest ([9:37-38](Matt.9.37-Matt.9.38)). The choice of twelve is not accidental—it recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus was appointing new leaders for the new people of God under his reign as Messiah ([16:18-19](Matt.16.18-Matt.16.19); [18:18](Matt.18.18); [19:28](Matt.19.28); [21:43](Matt.21.43)).

**gave them authority** ([9:6-8](Matt.9.6-Matt.9.8); [28:18](Matt.28.18)): Jesus enabled the Twelve to perform ministries that the Jewish leaders could not accomplish ([9:32-34](Matt.9.32-Matt.9.34); [10:5-8](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.8)). The authority **to cast out evil spirits** ([8:28](Matt.8.28)) and **to heal** are ascribed to Jesus ([4:23](Matt.4.23); [8:1–9:35](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.35)) in similar terms.

The four lists of the apostles (see also [Mark 3:16-19](Mark.3.16-Mark.3.19); [Luke 6:14-16](Luke.6.14-Luke.6.16); [Acts 1:13](Acts.1.13)) are all different, although the differences are minimal. The order within each list varies slightly, but only the names **Thaddaeus** ([10:3](Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](Mark.3.18)) and Judas son of James ([Luke 6:16](Luke.6.16); [Acts 1:13](Acts.1.13)) differ. They might be two names for the same man.

The **apostles** are ambassadors or messengers, authorized and sent by an authority to represent and accomplish prescribed tasks (see [10:1-8](Matt.10.1-Matt.10.8), [40](Matt.10.40); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)). The term is also used for Paul ([Gal 1:1](Gal.1.1)).

**first, Simon (also called Peter):** Peter had priority in time ([Matt 4:18-22](Matt.4.18-Matt.4.22); [16:17-19](Matt.16.17-Matt.16.19)) and position as the representative leader of the apostles (see [19:27](Matt.19.27); [26:33](Matt.26.33); [Acts 2:14](Acts.2.14)).
**Matthew (the tax collector)** (see [9:9](Matt.9.9)) is also called Levi ([Mark 2:14](Mark.2.14)).

**the zealot:** Zealots were militant Jews who thought violence and war were capable of accomplishing the will of God. As a Jewish nationalist, **Simon** was probably zealous for the law ([Acts 22:3-5](Acts.22.3-Acts.22.5); [Gal 1:14](Gal.1.14); [Phil 3:6](Phil.3.6)). Josephus blamed the Zealot party for the great war with Rome in AD 66–70.
**Iscariot** might refer to someone from Kerioth in southern Judea ([Josh 15:25](Josh.15.25)) or from Kerioth in Perea ([Jer 48:24](Jer.48.24)).

**Don’t go to the Gentiles:** Jesus’ mission was limited to Jews at this stage ([15:24](Matt.15.24)). Through the Jews, God would reach the Gentiles ([Isa 2:2-4](Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4); [42:6-7](Isa.42.6-Isa.42.7); [49:6](Isa.49.6); [60:3](Isa.60.3)).

Jews regarded **Samaritans** as impure Jews ([Luke 17:18](Luke.17.18)) because of their intermarriage with Gentiles during and after the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles ([2 Kgs 17:24-41](2Kgs.17.24-2Kgs.17.41)). Tension was provoked in 128 BC when the Jewish leader John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, *Antiquities* 13.9.1).
Being **lost** is the result of neglect by their shepherds ([9:36](Matt.9.36); [15:24](Matt.15.24)).
By doing these things in the name and authority of Jesus, the apostles demonstrated Jesus’ status as Messiah (see [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6)).

**Give as freely as you have received!** While remuneration is not improper ([1 Cor 9:3-19](1Cor.9.3-1Cor.9.19); [Gal 6:6](Gal.6.6); [1 Tim 5:17](1Tim.5.17)), Jesus urged the apostles to avoid accusations of greed (see [Acts 8:20](Acts.8.20); [20:33](Acts.20.33)).

Jesus’ disciples were to trust in God’s provision ([6:11](Matt.6.11), [25-34](Matt.6.25-Matt.6.34); [7:7-11](Matt.7.7-Matt.7.11)), to avoid greed that would give others the opportunity to defame the Lord’s name, and to encourage the newly formed communities to provide for their leaders’ needs (see [1 Cor 9:3-19](1Cor.9.3-1Cor.9.19)).
**give it your blessing:** Greetings were more significant than a simple hello. Often, a greeting would convey a blessing for those who received it (cp. [Ruth 2:4](Ruth.2.4)).
**A worthy home** would embrace the message about Jesus and the Kingdom ([10:37-38](Matt.10.37-Matt.10.38); [22:8](Matt.22.8)).
The disciples’ **blessing** was an offer of salvation; to **take back the blessing** was a sign of judgment as the offer was withdrawn.

**shake its dust from your feet:** This prophet-like gesture is explained by the Israelite custom of expressing displeasure with ungodliness by shaking off Gentile dust whenever crossing the border into Israel. The gesture signifies the disciples’ rejection of those who oppose God’s work (see [Acts 18:6](Acts.18.6)). Pronouncing judgment on those who reject the message is part of proclaiming the Good News about the Kingdom (see [Matt 11:20-24](Matt.11.20-Matt.11.24); [13:10-15](Matt.13.10-Matt.13.15); [23:37-39](Matt.23.37-Matt.23.39); [24:1-36](Matt.24.1-Matt.24.36)).

God destroyed **Sodom and Gomorrah** for their wickedness ([Gen 18:16–19:29](Gen.18.16-Gen.19.29)). Now, with a more complete revelation in Jesus Christ, a town that rejected the disciples’ preaching would receive a more complete judgment.

**such a town:** An entire village or city is culpable when a significant majority rejects the message (see [Acts 13:45-47](Acts.13.45-Acts.13.47), [50-51](Acts.13.50-Acts.13.51); [14:1-7](Acts.14.1-Acts.14.7)). However, individuals who respond in faith are saved (e.g., Lot; see [Gen 19:1-29](Gen.19.1-Gen.19.29); [2 Pet 2:6-9](2Pet.2.6-2Pet.2.9)).

False leaders who prey upon people’s spiritual vulnerability rather than exercise appropriate pastoral care are often called **wolves** ([Ezek 22:27](Ezek.22.27); [Zeph 3:3](Zeph.3.3); cp. [Prov 28:15](Prov.28.15)).
**be as shrewd as snakes and harmless as doves:** The proverb calls for being astute but not deceitful.

As God gave Moses a spokesman in Aaron ([Exod 4:10-17](Exod.4.10-Exod.4.17)), so God would give Jesus’ disciples the **right words at the right time** through **the Spirit** ([John 14:26](John.14.26); [Acts 4:8](Acts.4.8)).
Jews regularly associated family strife with the last times (see [24:9-10](Matt.24.9-Matt.24.10)). Jesus experienced such conflicts as well ([12:46-50](Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50)).
**Everyone who endures to the end** refers to those who remain faithful to Jesus, to the point of death or until his return ([10:23](Matt.10.23)).
**will be saved:** Though some have taken this phrase to mean temporal deliverance from persecution (such as release from prison), the idea here is eternal salvation for those who remain faithful.

**will return:** Scholars are divided as to whether this refers to the second coming of Christ for his church or an earlier coming in judgment—namely, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see [16:28](Matt.16.28)).

**before you have reached:** Jesus meant either “before you have *fled* through all the towns” or “before you have *evangelized* all the towns.” The focus on persecution in the context (see [10:17-39](Matt.10.17-Matt.10.39)) favors the former, suggesting that the towns were like cities of refuge ([Num 35:9-32](Num.35.9-Num.35.32)). The emphasis is on how widespread the rejection of the message will be—i.e., “not until the whole nation has run you out of town.”

In Jesus’ day, Satan was often called **prince of demons.** The Greek term is *Beelzeboul,* from the name of an Old Testament pagan deity, Baal-zebul (“lord, the prince”). The Latin version reads *Beelzebub,* which is a transliteration of a Hebrew phrase meaning “lord of flies,” which was most likely a Jewish insult of Baal-zebul (see [2 Kgs 1:2](2Kgs.1.2)).
Jesus’ disciples are to **fear only God** by obeying him and testifying of him; in contrast to human authorities, God’s authority and judgment are unlimited.
**hell:** See study note on 5:29.
Because God cares about every sparrow, and because Jesus’ disciples are much more valuable, certainly the disciples need not fear—God will providentially care for them.

God accepts the one **who acknowledges** Jesus **publicly** in the context of trial and persecution ([10:16-25](Matt.10.16-Matt.10.25)). These verses pertain to a person’s pattern of life (see [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27)) and not to a single confession or a single denial. For example, Judas acknowledged Jesus in individual instances yet was damned ([26:23-24](Matt.26.23-Matt.26.24)), whereas Peter denied Jesus (see [26:69-75](Matt.26.69-Matt.26.75)) yet was saved.
Allegiance to Jesus has priority over allegiance to family.

Jesus did bring **peace** ([John 14:27](John.14.27)), but not of a social and political kind. Instead, Jesus calls humans to make a decision about him, which brings a **sword**—i.e., division (see [Matt 8:21-22](Matt.8.21-Matt.8.22); [12:46-50](Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50); [Luke 12:51](Luke.12.51)).

The cross was a Roman instrument of torture and execution ([27:27-55](Matt.27.27-Matt.27.55)). To **take up your cross and follow** Jesus involves loving him above all other things and being willing to follow him regardless of the physical or social consequences.
**The same reward as a prophet** (literally *A prophet’s reward*) means either the same reward a prophet would receive or the benefit of the prophet’s ministry.

**Righteous people** are those who conform their behavior to God’s law as taught by both John the Baptist ([21:32](Matt.21.32)) and Jesus (see [3:15](Matt.3.15)), and therefore are approved by God ([13:43](Matt.13.43), [49](Matt.13.49); [25:37-46](Matt.25.37-Matt.25.46)).

**The least of my followers** probably refers to the low social standing of most of Jesus’ followers (cp. [5:3](Matt.5.3); [18:1-5](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.5) and [6:5](Matt.6.5); [23:5-12](Matt.23.5-Matt.23.12)).

This section begins with John the Baptist’s doubt, but it ends by exalting his faith and ministry ([11:7-19](Matt.11.7-Matt.11.19)). The people’s rejection of John ([11:16-19](Matt.11.16-Matt.11.19)) foreshadows their later rejection of Jesus.

This section highlights the two primary responses to Jesus: acceptance and rejection. The first section ([11:2–12:50](Matt.11.2-Matt.12.50)) features the rejection of Jesus by Jewish leaders while his disciples were learning to understand and accept him.
**John** was arrested ([4:12](Matt.4.12)) by Herod Antipas because he had denounced Herod’s immoral relationship with Herodias, his half-brother’s wife ([14:1-12](Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12)).
**the things the Messiah was doing:** These actions demonstrated that he is the Messiah ([8:1–9:34](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.34)).

Jesus’ miracles of compassion inaugurated the Kingdom of God ([12:28](Matt.12.28); see [Isa 29:18-19](Isa.29.18-Isa.29.19); [35:5-6](Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6); [61:1](Isa.61.1)). Jesus expected John to understand that he was fulfilling Old Testament expectations.

**who do not fall away because of me:** The works listed in [11:5](Matt.11.5) were intended to drive John and his disciples to a decision regarding Jesus. Jesus was aware, however, that certain unexpected elements of his ministry would cause some to reject him.
**a weak reed, swayed by every breath of wind:** An unstable person. The implied answer to Jesus’ rhetorical question is no.

**John the Baptist** was the greatest person ever to have lived. Yet **the least** of Jesus’ followers are **greater** than John because they live in the new covenant of salvation through Christ (see [4:17](Matt.4.17)).

**the Kingdom of Heaven has been forcefully advancing:** Or *the Kingdom of Heaven has suffered from violence.* These alternatives reflect either a positive or negative nuance of the Greek verb. In [Luke 16:16](Luke.16.16), a different verb (“preached”) makes it a clearly positive statement.

**violent people are attacking it:** This phrase may also have a positive or negative sense. If negative, it might refer to those who imprisoned John (see [Matt 11:2](Matt.11.2); [14:1-12](Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12)), and *attacking* might mean either that they were trying to attack the Kingdom but were unable to thwart God’s sovereign plans, or that they were attacking it by persecuting its members. In [Luke 16:16](Luke.16.16) this statement has the positive sense that they were “eager to get in” and were forcefully laying claim to the Kingdom through radical trust and obedience.
**Elijah, the one the prophets said would come:** John is the fulfillment of Old Testament expectations of Elijah’s return ([17:10-13](Matt.17.10-Matt.17.13); see [Mal 4:5](Mal.4.5)).

John’s prophetic message is represented by **funeral songs**—he didn’t drink wine and he often fasted ([11:18](Matt.11.18); see [3:4](Matt.3.4)). Jesus’ message is seen in **wedding songs** and in **feasts and drinks** (see [9:9-17](Matt.9.9-Matt.9.17)). In both cases, **this generation** responds to God’s messenger with indifference and rejection.

Here Jesus describes the specific ways in which **John** and Jesus offended the present generation. John, who stayed in the wilderness and ate locusts and honey ([3:1](Matt.3.1), [4](Matt.3.4)), was accused of being **possessed by a demon***;* while Jesus, who ate and drank freely, was accused of being a rebellious son (see [Deut 21:18-21](Deut.21.18-Deut.21.21)).

The **miracles** Jesus performed confirmed him as Messiah ([11:5-6](Matt.11.5-Matt.11.6)) and demanded repentance ([11:20](Matt.11.20)). Rejecting the Messiah would result in terrible judgment because the evidence of Jesus’ identity was clear.

As Jesus moved through the villages of Galilee—from **Korazin** to **Bethsaida** to **Capernaum**—he gave the people a greater revelation of himself, with a correspondingly more severe judgment when they refused to listen. The severity is indicated by comparison with the pagan cities of **Tyre** ([Isa 23](Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18); [Ezek 26:1–28:19](Ezek.26.1-Ezek.28.19)), **Sidon** ([Ezek 28:20-23](Ezek.28.20-Ezek.28.23)), and **Sodom** ([Gen 18:22–19:29](Gen.18.22-Gen.19.29)).
**the place of the dead:** Greek *Hades,* which corresponds to the Hebrew term *Sheol* (see study note on Ps 6:5).
This passage focuses on the remnant who, despite the present generation’s overall rejection of the Messiah, willingly embrace him and follow his teachings.

**those who think themselves wise and clever:** The Pharisees and teachers of religious law thought their access to God was guaranteed through their knowledge and practice of the law. Jesus’ disciples were more **childlike** (see [21:15-16](Matt.21.15-Matt.21.16)).

Jesus was revealing his intimate relationship to the **Father**. Everything he said and did was rooted in this Father–Son unity (see [John 10:14-15](John.10.14-John.10.15); [14:6-7](John.14.6-John.14.7); [15:23-24](John.15.23-John.15.24); [16:15](John.16.15); [17:25-26](John.17.25-John.17.26)).
The **heavy burdens** were likely caused by the legal requirements of the teachers of religious law and Pharisees (see [23:4](Matt.23.4)).
**rest:** Spiritual refreshment in either a present or a future sense (cp. [1:21](Matt.1.21); [Heb 4:8-11](Heb.4.8-Heb.4.11)).

A **yoke**, which forms a harness between two animals, is a metaphor for the demands of discipleship. In contrast to the “yoke” of the religious leaders, Jesus’ yoke is **easy** and **light**, not because it is less demanding (see [7:13-14](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.14)), but because the power of the Messiah (by the Holy Spirit) makes it possible (see [Acts 15:10](Acts.15.10); [1 Jn 5:3](1John.5.3)). The religious demands of Israel’s spiritual leaders ([Matt 23:4](Matt.23.4); [Acts 15:10](Acts.15.10)) included 613 Old Testament commands and their expansion through tradition. Jesus urged those who were suffering from the burdens of the Pharisees’ stipulations to come to him ([Matt 11:28](Matt.11.28)) in order to find the salvation their hearts desired. It is a call to salvation involving a life of obedience to Jesus’ new teachings. People are invited to enter a relationship with a **humble and gentle** teacher.

Matthew places Jesus’ offer of rest ([11:28-30](Matt.11.28-Matt.11.30)) in close connection with a discussion of the Sabbath. Jesus’ rest liberates people from human traditions concerning the Sabbath (cp. [Heb 4:1-11](Heb.4.1-Heb.4.11)). The Pharisees rejected Jesus because of their commitment to tradition.
This exchange highlights the Pharisees’ lack of compassion as they imposed a burdensome yoke ([11:29-30](Matt.11.29-Matt.11.30)).

The **Sabbath***,* the seventh day of the week, was to be a day of complete rest according to Old Testament laws ([Gen 2:2-3](Gen.2.2-Gen.2.3); [Exod 20:8-11](Exod.20.8-Exod.20.11)). The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (cp. [Heb 4:1-11](Heb.4.1-Heb.4.11)).
The Pharisees did not understand that the Sabbath was designed to benefit people. Their view of the Sabbath placed onerous burdens on people.
Ritual laws were at times rightly suspended for particular people or circumstances ([1 Sam 21:1-6](1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.6)).

Priests worked **on the Sabbath** ([Lev 24:8-9](Lev.24.8-Lev.24.9); [Num 28:9-10](Num.28.9-Num.28.10)), and this was not offensive to Pharisees. If the priests’ work for the **Temple** on the Sabbath is allowed, then certainly Jesus can do the same because he is **greater than the Temple** (see [Matt 4:23](Matt.4.23); [9:35](Matt.9.35); [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6), [20-30](Matt.11.20-Matt.11.30)).
The Pharisees’ view of the Sabbath was unscriptural since it broke the deeper principle of **mercy**.
Jesus is superior to David, the priests, and the Temple. He reigns **even over the Sabbath**.
This second Sabbath controversy castigates the Pharisees for elevating regulations over human needs (see [12:7](Matt.12.7), [11-12](Matt.12.11-Matt.12.12)).
**their synagogue:** A disunion was developing between Jesus and Judaism (also [4:23](Matt.4.23)).
**Does the law permit:** Rabbinic tradition permitted healing on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. Since life was not in jeopardy, the Pharisees thought healing was not permitted.
Their practice of rescuing animals but neglecting fellow humans was inconsistent.
This summary of Jesus’ ministry clarifies Jesus’ nature as the Messiah, the **Servant** of God who will bring salvation **to the nations** (see [Isa 42:1-4](Isa.42.1-Isa.42.4)).
This quotation parallels Jesus’ baptism ([3:13-17](Matt.3.13-Matt.3.17)).
**Justice** (or *judgment*) can have positive or negative implications; the context here favors a positive meaning ([12:20](Matt.12.20); cp. [23:23](Matt.23.23)).
Instead of increasing people’s spiritual burden, Jesus offers compassionate forgiveness and sustenance (see [11:28-30](Matt.11.28-Matt.11.30); [12:1-14](Matt.12.1-Matt.12.14)).
The Messiah was rejected by the Pharisees, the teachers of religious law, and his own generation.
Amazement was a common response to Jesus’ miracles ([Mark 2:12](Mark.2.12); [6:51](Mark.6.51); [Luke 2:47](Luke.2.47); [8:56](Luke.8.56); [24:22](Luke.24.22)).
**Could it be:** The question expected a negative answer: Jesus did not fit their expectations for the Messiah, but his miracles did prompt the question.
**Satan:** Greek *Beelzeboul;* see study note on 10:25.
Jesus argued, in essence, “If I cast out demons under the influence of Satan, then Satan is dividing his camp, which obviously would be a foolish thing for Satan to do.”

**what about your own exorcists** (literally *your sons*): Jesus forced them to think consistently. If demons are cast out under Satan’s influence, then their disciples were equally guilty (see [Acts 19:13-16](Acts.19.13-Acts.19.16)).

The Pharisees were being confronted with and were rejecting the **Kingdom of God** itself (see [Luke 17:20-21](Luke.17.20-Luke.17.21); [1 Jn 3:8](1John.3.8)). Jesus’ miracles brought the power of the Kingdom into the present reality; its ultimate consummation awaits Christ’s second coming.

This parable forced the Pharisees to answer a simple question: Can anyone cast out demons without first binding Satan’s powers and thus opposing him (see [Isa 49:24-26](Isa.49.24-Isa.49.26); [53:12](Isa.53.12))?

**tie him up:** Jesus overcame Satan first at his temptation ([Matt 4:1-11](Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11)), then throughout his ministry (see [Luke 10:17-20](Luke.10.17-Luke.10.20)), and ultimately on the cross (see [Col 2:14-15](Col.2.14-Col.2.15)).

In the face of the Pharisees’ accusations of Satanic influence, Jesus had just argued that he, the Messiah, cast out demons through the power of the Holy Spirit. In this context, **blasphemy against the Holy Spirit** can only mean attributing the ministry and exorcisms of Jesus to Satan’s power.

One may stumble over Jesus’ mysterious revelation of himself as **Son of Man** and be **forgiven***,* but one cannot be forgiven for attributing the work of the Spirit to Satan. The present-day analogy is the outright rejection of the conviction of the **Holy Spirit** concerning Christ—that is, the ultimate rejection of the Good News by an unbeliever (cp. [Heb 6:4-6](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6); [1 Jn 5:16-21](1John.5.16-1John.5.21)).
Jesus got to the heart of the matter: The Pharisees did not accept him or the divine origin of his ministry because they were wicked (see [7:15-27](Matt.7.15-Matt.7.27)).
The **idle word***,* in this context, was the accusation that Jesus had demonic inspiration.
What one says will **acquit** or **condemn***;* one’s words reflect the true condition of the heart.

**a miraculous sign to prove:** A popular expectation of the Messiah, probably fueled by biblical accounts about Moses ([Exod 4:1-9](Exod.4.1-Exod.4.9); see also [Isa 7:11](Isa.7.11), [14](Isa.7.14); [38:7-8](Isa.38.7-Isa.38.8)), was that the Messiah would display spectacular miracles on command (see [Matt 16:1-4](Matt.16.1-Matt.16.4); [Luke 23:8](Luke.23.8); [John 2:18](John.2.18); [4:48](John.4.48); [6:30](John.6.30); [7:31](John.7.31); [9:16](John.9.16); [11:47](John.11.47); [1 Cor 1:22](1Cor.1.22)).
To **demand** a **sign** demonstrates a lack of faith.

The **sign of the prophet Jonah** consisted of Jonah’s “resurrection” from the large fish after **three days and three nights** as well as his preaching ([12:41](Matt.12.41); [Luke 11:32](Luke.11.32)); it was analogous to Jesus’ burial and resurrection and his preaching. Jesus was drawing a parallel between Jonah’s experience and what he himself would experience. He was not predicting an exact chronology of his death and resurrection.
**Heart of the earth** is a euphemism for the grave.

**someone greater:** Jesus is greater than the Temple ([12:6](Matt.12.6)), a prophet (**Jonah**), and a king (**Solomon**); therefore, rejection of him entails greater judgment on this “evil, adulterous generation” ([12:39](Matt.12.39)).
**The queen of Sheba:** See [1 Kgs 10:1-13](1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.13).

The Messiah came in victory over demonic powers, but instead of repenting, the nation as a whole rejected the Messiah. Just as an exorcised demon will return if the house is not properly prepared against it, so judgment would come to **this evil generation** for rejecting the Messiah.
Demons were thought to prefer the arid **desert** (see [Rev 18:2](Rev.18.2); cp. [Isa 13:21](Isa.13.21); [34:14](Isa.34.14)).

Those who are true members in Jesus’ family do **the will of** the **Father***,* as expressed in the commands of Jesus (see [7:21](Matt.7.21)). Obedience does not earn entrance into this family, but one cannot be considered a member if he or she is not obedient (see [3:15](Matt.3.15); [5:17-48](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.48); [6:10](Matt.6.10), [12](Matt.6.12); [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27); [21:31](Matt.21.31)).

In the third major discourse recorded by Matthew (see study note on Matt 5:1–7:29), Jesus here recognized the separation of his followers from others ([13:14](Matt.13.14), [16](Matt.13.16)) and began to reveal the secrets of the Kingdom privately to them through parables.
This parable (interpreted in [13:18-23](Matt.13.18-Matt.13.23)) addresses the mostly negative responses of the Jewish nation to Jesus and his message.

**Parables** (Greek *parabolē*) are stories that usually express an analogy between a common aspect of life and a spiritual truth. To understand a parable, it is necessary to locate the central analogy and understand it in its historical context and in the context of the Gospel text; then the central message can be understood. Speculative allegorical meanings that were not intended should not be found in every element of a parable.

From this point on, Jesus rarely taught the general public. Instead, he focused on teaching those who had committed themselves to him ([13:1–20:34](Matt.13.1-Matt.20.34)), though he would once again confront Israel ([21:1–23:39](Matt.21.1-Matt.23.39)).
**The people** were the unbelieving opponents mentioned again in [13:11](Matt.13.11) (“others”) and [13:12](Matt.13.12) (“those who are not listening”).
Jesus’ answer to the disciples’ question ([13:10](Matt.13.10)) was essentially that the people’s stubborn unbelief and rejection of Jesus had brought God’s condemnation.

**You are permitted to understand:** God had enabled the disciples to comprehend Jesus’ significance and to respond to his message of the Kingdom in faith and obedience (see [13:19](Matt.13.19), [23](Matt.13.23)).
**the secrets of the Kingdom of Heaven:** Namely, that salvation is available to them in Jesus as the fulfillment of Old Testament promises.
Jesus told **parables***,* and those who believed understood while those who had rejected Jesus found that his parables intensified their unbelief.

**they don’t really see . . . listen or understand:** They lacked the faith that perceives the truth ([13:19](Matt.13.19), [23](Matt.13.23)) and acts upon it ([Mark 8:18](Mark.8.18); [John 12:40](John.12.40); see also [Jer 5:21](Jer.5.21)).

Like that of **Isaiah**, Jesus’ message has a dual effect: It judges people for unbelief and disobedience, and it creates a remnant of faithful ones who accomplish the Lord’s will ([21:43](Matt.21.43)).

Jesus brought into reality what the **prophets** and Old Testament saints desired to **see** and **hear***,* that is, the fulfillment of Old Testament promises (see [Isa 52:15](Isa.52.15); [John 8:56](John.8.56); [1 Pet 1:10](1Pet.1.10)).
**don’t understand it:** Responding to the **message** of **the Kingdom** is directly related to discerning its significance.

**don’t have deep roots . . . don’t last long:** The problem is a lack of persevering faith and obedience (see [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27); [10:22](Matt.10.22)), particularly when persecution arises.

Jesus spoke of competing demands in life, (see also [8:18-22](Matt.8.18-Matt.8.22)). **The worries of this life** can become so great that they divert one from the path of faithful obedience (see [6:19-34](Matt.6.19-Matt.6.34)). **The lure of wealth***,* particularly in its ability to deceive, appears often in Matthew (e.g., [4:8-10](Matt.4.8-Matt.4.10); [6:24](Matt.6.24); [13:44-45](Matt.13.44-Matt.13.45)). God does not desire that his people have wealth as much as that they have faith, obey him, and willingly help those in need (e.g., [19:21](Matt.19.21); [25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)).
**produce a harvest:** Probably a general reference to faithful obedience to Jesus’ commands (e.g., [5:1–7:27](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.27); [28:20](Matt.28.20)).
This **story** is explained in [13:36-43](Matt.13.36-Matt.13.43).

**Weeds** (or *tares*, bearded darnel) are almost indistinguishable from **wheat** and so were left until growth revealed their true nature. Malevolent contamination of crops in this manner was punishable by law.

Just as Jesus rebuked the sons of Zebedee for wanting to destroy unbelieving villages ([Luke 9:54-55](Luke.9.54-Luke.9.55)), he prohibited his followers from retaliating against enemies. Judgment is God’s work (see [Matt 7:1-5](Matt.7.1-Matt.7.5)). Jesus urges his followers to wait patiently for God’s righteous judgment (**the harvest**; see [Luke 13:6-9](Luke.13.6-Luke.13.9)).

Jesus used surprising, evocative imagery in these parables, either to emphasize the inevitable growth of **the Kingdom** through proclamation of the gospel or, more probably, to emphasize the contrast between insignificant beginnings and glorious consummation, and to exhort the disciples to patience (see also [16:24–17:13](Matt.16.24-Matt.17.13)).

Normally **yeast** refers to the influence of evil (e.g., [16:6](Matt.16.6); [1 Cor 5:6](1Cor.5.6); [Gal 5:9](Gal.5.9)); here, however, it is positive, speaking of the all-pervasive influence of the **Kingdom**.

Even Jesus’ manner of teaching fulfilled Old Testament predictions. [Psalm 78:2-3](Ps.78.2-Ps.78.3) speaks of passing down the history of God’s revelation to children of the next generation. Jesus’ revelation is the climax of that history ([Matt 13:10-17](Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17); [1 Cor 2:7](1Cor.2.7)).

These verses are the interpretation of the parable told in [13:24-30](Matt.13.24-Matt.13.30). The **people of the Kingdom** (**wheat**) coexist with nonmembers (**weeds**) in the world (**field**) until the end of history. The mystery of the Kingdom is that it is present in the world without weeding out the wicked in judgment; Jesus’ disciples must learn patience.
They **went into the house** (see [13:1](Matt.13.1)). Jesus taught in parables publicly, but the interpretations were reserved for his **disciples** in private.
**Please explain:** Though the disciples were privileged to know the mysteries of the Kingdom ([13:11-17](Matt.13.11-Matt.13.17)), they did not understand the parables until Jesus explained them.
**The field is the world:** The Kingdom includes all nations ([28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)).
The **people of the Kingdom** are those who follow Jesus ([13:11-17](Matt.13.11-Matt.13.17), [23](Matt.13.23); [21:43](Matt.21.43)).
The harvest of judgment, which began with the first coming of **the Son of Man** ([3:12](Matt.3.12)), will be completed when he returns ([Rev 14:14-16](Rev.14.14-Rev.14.16)).
**his Kingdom:** Not until the “end of the world” ([13:40](Matt.13.40)) will the rule of the **Son of Man** be visible over all things.
**The righteous** do the will of God as revealed by Jesus, in contrast to those “who do evil” ([13:41](Matt.13.41)).

Another mystery of the Kingdom ([13:11](Matt.13.11)) is that its value exceeds all other treasures, and so everything should be forfeited to acquire it (see [19:21](Matt.19.21), [29](Matt.19.29); [Phil 3:7](Phil.3.7)).
**treasure . . . hidden in a field:** Treasures were buried for protection against thieves and military enemies ([25:25](Matt.25.25)).
**In his excitement:** Those who discover **the Kingdom** find greater joy in it than can be found in any temporal pleasure (see [1 Pet 1:8](1Pet.1.8)).

This parable refers to God’s judgment at the last day ([25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)), which will eternally separate the wicked from the righteous. This note of warning reinforces the urgency of the previous two calls to decision.

The **wicked** are those who do not do the will of God as revealed in Jesus, and the **righteous** are those who do (see [5:21-48](Matt.5.21-Matt.5.48); [6:1](Matt.6.1), [33](Matt.6.33); [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27); [12:33-37](Matt.12.33-Matt.12.37); [16:27](Matt.16.27)).
The ability to **understand** the mysteries of the Kingdom is a gift from God ([13:10-17](Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17), [23](Matt.13.23)).
A **teacher of religious law who becomes a disciple in the Kingdom** has had his allegiance radically altered toward Jesus as the way of salvation.

**new gems of truth as well as old:** The sequence reflects the preeminence of the new covenant inaugurated in Jesus ([5:17-20](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.20); [19:16-22](Matt.19.16-Matt.19.22)) over the old covenant administered under Abraham and Moses.

That Jesus was rejected at home is part of the ongoing theme of the Messiah’s rejection by his own people (see ch [12](Matt.12.1-Matt.12.50); [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20); [16:1-12](Matt.16.1-Matt.16.12)).
**carpenter’s son:** A carpenter (literally *craftsman*) worked with his hands, whether in wood, metal, or stone.
They were **deeply offended**. Dwelling on Jesus’ all-too-common heritage ([John 6:42](John.6.42)), they could not see his uncommon significance.
Faith is required both to understand Jesus’ message ([13:10-17](Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17)) and to experience his miracles.

**Herod Antipas**’s official title was *tetrarch* (ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom) **of Galilee** and Perea (4 BC—AD 39; see [2:19-22](Matt.2.19-Matt.2.22)). Jesus referred to Antipas as “that fox” ([Luke 13:32](Luke.13.32)), and John the Baptist justly condemned him for adultery ([Matt 14:3-12](Matt.14.3-Matt.14.12); [Luke 3:19-20](Luke.3.19-Luke.3.20)).
There was a rumor that **John** had been resurrected (see [16:14](Matt.16.14)).

The popular appeal of John’s message posed a political threat (see Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.5.2). Years after John’s execution, the Jews viewed Herod’s military defeat at the hands of Aretas (AD 36) as a just recompense for putting an innocent man to death.
**John** had continually warned **Herod** of his sin (see [Lev 18:6](Lev.18.6); [20:21](Lev.20.21)).
**Herodias’s daughter** was probably Salome, a daughter from Herodias’s previous marriage to Philip. Sexually provocative dances such as this were a regular occurrence for depraved royalty.
Such an extravagant, foolish oath was consistent with Herod Antipas’s character.
The practice of bringing a **head** . . . **on a tray** was not unknown in the ancient world (see Josephus, *Antiquities* 13.4.8; 14.15.13; 18.5.1; 20.5.1).

Jesus’ actions consistently fulfilled Old Testament promises regarding the Kingdom and the Messiah ([11:5-6](Matt.11.5-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28)). Here Jesus evoked the memory of God’s provision of manna for the Israelites ([Exod 16](Exod.16.1-Exod.16.36); see [John 6:32](John.6.32)), demonstrating that he is the promised end-time prophet (see [Deut 18:15-16](Deut.18.15-Deut.18.16)).
**5,000 men . . . in addition to all the women and children:** The count was of families, denoted by heads of households, rather than individuals.

Jesus’ power over nature presented the disciples with the opportunity to trust in him as the **Son of God** ([14:33](Matt.14.33); see also [8:23-27](Matt.8.23-Matt.8.27); [Ps 8:6](Ps.8.6); [Heb 2:8-9](Heb.2.8-Heb.2.9)).
After the miraculous feeding, the crowds sought to make Jesus king ([John 6:15](John.6.15)), prompting his withdrawal because it was not the appropriate time.

Jesus often sought solitude in order to **pray***,* particularly in conjunction with important events in his life and ministry ([26:36-46](Matt.26.36-Matt.26.46); [Mark 1:35](Mark.1.35); [Luke 5:16](Luke.5.16); [6:12](Luke.6.12); [9:28](Luke.9.28)).
**About three o’clock in the morning:** Literally *In the fourth watch of the night.* This was approximately 3:00–6:00 AM by Roman reckoning.
The fact that **Jesus came** . . . **walking on the water** demonstrates God’s sovereign reign over the stormy waters (see [Job 9:8](Job.9.8); [Ps 77:19](Ps.77.19); [Isa 43:16](Isa.43.16)).
**I am here:** Literally *I am.* This declaration is associated with the appearance of God himself (see also [John 8:24](John.8.24); [18:5-6](John.18.5-John.18.6); cp. [Exod 3:14](Exod.3.14)).
On the purpose of Jesus’ miracles, see study notes on Matt 11:5; 12:28.
Jesus indicted the Pharisees for disobeying God’s law in their zeal to preserve traditions.
**Jerusalem** was the location of the Temple and thus the seat of authority in Judaism; this gave the ambassadors greater leverage in their arguments with Jesus.

The Jewish teachers’ **age-old tradition** sought to apply the written Torah to common circumstances in the ordinary course of life. This **tradition** was memorized and passed on orally from teacher to student (cp. [1 Cor 11:23](1Cor.11.23); [15:1-5](1Cor.15.1-1Cor.15.5)).

To **ignore** the **tradition of** . . . **hand washing** (see [Mark 7:2-4](Mark.7.2-Mark.7.4); [Luke 11:38](Luke.11.38)) was considered disobedient to the Torah and unfaithful to God’s will for Israel (cp. [Matt 23:25-26](Matt.23.25-Matt.23.26)).

**vowed to give to God:** Such a gift was likely donated at the Temple (see [Mark 7:11](Mark.7.11); see also [Prov 28:24](Prov.28.24)) but functioned as a way to dodge financial responsibility for one’s **parents**.
**cancel:** Because of a greater commitment to their traditions, the Pharisees in effect rendered God’s law nonbinding, turning their piety into sinful disregard for the **word of God**.
**You hypocrites!** See study note on Matt 23:13.
**what goes into your mouth:** Jesus was speaking here either of foods that were not permitted (e.g., pork or shellfish) or of food contaminated by unclean hands ([15:20](Matt.15.20)).

That which **defiles** makes a person unfit for communion with God. Jesus pressed the matter beyond ceremonial purity to true inner purity (see [15:18-19](Matt.15.18-Matt.15.19); [23:25-26](Matt.23.25-Matt.23.26); [Acts 10:1-48](Acts.10.1-Acts.10.48); [Rom 14:14](Rom.14.14)).
One’s **words** are a measure of one’s character (see [Matt 15:18-20](Matt.15.18-Matt.15.20); [Jas 3:1-12](Jas.3.1-Jas.3.12)).

**not planted by my heavenly Father:** These Pharisees did not belong to the true people of God (see [3:9-12](Matt.3.9-Matt.3.12); [Isa 5:1-7](Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7); [Jer 45:4](Jer.45.4)). They **will be uprooted** at the final judgment (see [Matt 3:10](Matt.3.10); [8:12](Matt.8.12)).
This encounter highlights another controversial issue: Gentile participation in the Kingdom of the Messiah (see [8:11](Matt.8.11)).
**Gentile woman:** Literally *Canaanite woman.* Matthew uses this archaic Old Testament expression to describe the woman as a pagan.
**Lord, Son of David:** The woman apparently perceived that Jesus was the Messiah (see [1:1](Matt.1.1); [9:27](Matt.9.27); [17:15](Matt.17.15); [20:30](Matt.20.30)).
**no reply:** Jesus’ silence was a test of the woman’s faith ([15:28](Matt.15.28); cp. [8:24](Matt.8.24); [14:16](Matt.14.16)).

Jews often referred to pagans as **dogs***,* which are ceremonially unclean ([Lev 11:27](Lev.11.27)). Jesus was speaking to the woman of her spiritual condition as a Gentile—as unclean and separated from God (cp. [Matt 7:6](Matt.7.6)).

Jesus returned to a predominantly Gentile area and performed many miracles. Though Jesus was sent primarily for Israel’s sake ([15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28)), the new era that he inaugurated is also the beginning of Gentile salvation ([1:3](Matt.1.3), [5-6](Matt.1.5-Matt.1.6); [2:1-12](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.12); [4:12-16](Matt.4.12-Matt.4.16); [8:5-13](Matt.8.5-Matt.8.13); [15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)).
Such healings are signs that the Kingdom has broken into history through Jesus’ ministry ([8:1–9:34](Matt.8.1-Matt.9.34); [11:5-6](Matt.11.5-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28)).
**the God of Israel:** This phrase suggests that **the crowd** ([15:30](Matt.15.30)) was predominantly Gentile.

The previous feeding miracle (see [14:13-21](Matt.14.13-Matt.14.21)) was for Jews, whereas this one extended to Gentiles; it thus develops the theme of [15:27](Matt.15.27). Through this miracle Jesus demonstrated that he is the true bread of life (see [16:5-12](Matt.16.5-Matt.16.12); [John 6](John.6.1-John.6.71)).
**Magadan** is an unknown site, perhaps *Magdala* (as in some Greek manuscripts; see also [Mark 8:10](Mark.8.10)).
Having been warmly received in the Gentile world, Jesus returned to his fellow countrymen only to encounter further rejection.

Jesus made a deliberate play on their words when they sought a “sign from heaven” ([16:1](Matt.16.1)). They were able to read the **weather** in **the sky** (Greek *ouranos*, the same word translated “heaven”), but they failed to discern the Messiah despite the many signs already given (see [11:1-6](Matt.11.1-Matt.11.6)).
The **signs of the times** were Jesus himself ([16:4](Matt.16.4)) and the various miracles that he performed (cp. [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28)).

Jesus had demonstrated to his disciples that he is the true bread of life ([15:32-39](Matt.15.32-Matt.15.39); [John 6:35](John.6.35), [48](John.6.48)), whereas the Jewish leaders, particularly in their teachings, were like yeast in permeating everything they touched with their sinfulness (see study note on Matt 16:11-12).

**Yeast** is often a symbol of sin and evil (see [Exod 12:8](Exod.12.8), [15](Exod.12.15); [Lev 6:16-17](Lev.6.16-Lev.6.17); [Gal 5:9](Gal.5.9)); here it indicates the permeating nature of the **deceptive teaching**.
**Caesarea Philippi***,* located approximately twenty-five miles north of Capernaum, hosted many shrines to the Roman god of nature, Pan.
**Some***,* such as Herod Antipas ([14:1-2](Matt.14.1-Matt.14.2)), thought Jesus was **John the Baptist** resurrected.
**Elijah** was expected as a forerunner to the Messiah ([11:14](Matt.11.14); [17:10-12](Matt.17.10-Matt.17.12); [Mal 3:1](Mal.3.1); [4:5-6](Mal.4.5-Mal.4.6)).

**Jeremiah or one of the other prophets:** Some Jews expected Jeremiah to be raised (see *2 Maccabees* 15:13-16). Jesus’ strong stand on sensitive matters ([Matt 5:17](Matt.5.17); [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20)) may have led some to think Jesus was Jeremiah. Jesus was not yet understood as God’s Messiah.

Peter’s acknowledgment of Jesus as **the Messiah, the Son of the living God** ([3:17](Matt.3.17)) shows that his eyes had been opened by faith (see [11:25-27](Matt.11.25-Matt.11.27); [14:33](Matt.14.33); [27:54](Matt.27.54)).

God **revealed** to Peter his plan of salvation in Jesus, the Messiah. This moment of revelation was a high point in the unfolding of God’s will for humanity (cp. [Gal 1:16](Gal.1.16); [3:23](Gal.3.23); [Eph 3:5](Eph.3.5)).

The phrase **upon this rock** is a pun on **Peter**’s name. Peter was the foundational rock in that he was the first confessor and leader of the apostles—he was the “founding member” of the church (see [Eph 2:20-22](Eph.2.20-Eph.2.22); [Rev 21:14](Rev.21.14)). Some scholars have suggested that Jesus was referring to himself when he said **this rock***,* but it seems clear that Jesus was referring either to Peter or to his confession. However, it is clearly Jesus’ church (**my church**), not Peter’s, and Jesus himself **will build** it. So it is not necessary to conclude that later church leaders must derive their authority from Peter.
Matthew is the only Gospel writer who uses the term **church** (also [Matt 18:17](Matt.18.17)). The idea here is more *the community of God’s people* than an ecclesiastical institution.
**will not conquer it:** The church will not be defeated by the attacks of Satan (see [11:12](Matt.11.12); [13:24-30](Matt.13.24-Matt.13.30), [36-43](Matt.13.36-Matt.13.43)).
**Keys** are an image for access to privileged knowledge that gives one authority (see [13:16-17](Matt.13.16-Matt.13.17); [23:13](Matt.23.13); [Isa 22:22](Isa.22.22); [Rev 3:7](Rev.3.7)).

**forbid . . . permit:** Jesus granted to Peter (and later to the rest of the Twelve, [Matt 18:18](Matt.18.18)) the authority to teach the will of God as revealed in Jesus Christ ([13:52](Matt.13.52); [18:15-20](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.20); [23:2-12](Matt.23.2-Matt.23.12); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)).
**will be:** This could be translated *will have been*, emphasizing that God’s sovereign decision comes first.

Jesus, now officially recognized by his disciples as the Messiah, begins to reveal a startling aspect of his mission: He must suffer before entering his glory ([16:21-23](Matt.16.21-Matt.16.23)), and those who follow him will meet a similar fate ([16:24-28](Matt.16.24-Matt.16.28)).

This is the first of three predictions of Jesus’ *passion*—his suffering through betrayal, crucifixion, and death (see also [17:22-23](Matt.17.22-Matt.17.23); [20:18-19](Matt.20.18-Matt.20.19)). Each prediction gives a lesson on the cost of discipleship ([16:24-27](Matt.16.24-Matt.16.27); [20:20-28](Matt.20.20-Matt.20.28)).
That **he would suffer** was God’s sovereign and necessary purpose for the Messiah (see [17:12](Matt.17.12)).
**began to reprimand him:** Though Peter accurately perceived Jesus’ identity as God’s Messiah, he did not understand that the Messiah must suffer.
As when **Satan** tempted Jesus to assume royal privileges without first enduring the cross (see [4:8-10](Matt.4.8-Matt.4.10)), so now Jesus perceived Peter’s suggestion as incited by satanic forces.
**dangerous trap:** Literally *stumbling block*.

**give . . . take . . . follow:** These three imperatives use different images to speak of the same radical commitment of confessing one’s sinfulness before God in humility, surrendering one’s personal ambition to God, and living according to his will (see also [5:20](Matt.5.20); [10:34-39](Matt.10.34-Matt.10.39); [18:1-5](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.5); [20:20-28](Matt.20.20-Matt.20.28)).

**Take up your cross** is a metaphor for devotion (see [Luke 9:23](Luke.9.23)) rather than a call to martyrdom, although martyrdom is an ever-present possibility for Jesus’ disciples ([Matt 5:10-12](Matt.5.10-Matt.5.12); [10:21](Matt.10.21)).

In Matthew, **follow** is used both literally ([9:19](Matt.9.19); [26:58](Matt.26.58)) and metaphorically. Metaphorically, it indicates interest in a teacher ([4:25](Matt.4.25); [8:1](Matt.8.1), [10](Matt.8.10); [12:15](Matt.12.15); [14:13](Matt.14.13); [19:2](Matt.19.2); [20:29](Matt.20.29); [21:9](Matt.21.9)) or personal allegiance to Jesus involving a call, a commitment, and great ongoing costs ([4:20](Matt.4.20), [22](Matt.4.22); [8:19](Matt.8.19), [22-23](Matt.8.22-Matt.8.23); [9:9](Matt.9.9); [10:38](Matt.10.38); [16:24](Matt.16.24); [19:21](Matt.19.21), [27](Matt.19.27)).

Jesus’ disciples must relinquish control of their lives, even to the point of being willing to suffer and die for Christ. Jesus promised that those who follow him with such radical abandon, though they may suffer now, will be vindicated at the final judgment (see [1 Pet 2:23](1Pet.2.23)).
**your own soul?** “Soul” and “life” ([16:25](Matt.16.25)) both translate the same Greek term (*psuchē*) and refer to the essence of a person—the self.

The exhortation to deny oneself and follow Jesus is rooted in the fact that Jesus will return to **judge all people according to their deeds** (see [19:28](Matt.19.28); [24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31); [25:31](Matt.25.31); [Ps 62:12](Ps.62.12); [Prov 24:12](Prov.24.12)).

This saying has been taken to refer either to (1) the transfiguration that follows ([17:1-13](Matt.17.1-Matt.17.13)); (2) the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ ([27:50-53](Matt.27.50-Matt.27.53); [28:1-10](Matt.28.1-Matt.28.10)); (3) Pentecost ([Acts 2:1-47](Acts.2.1-Acts.2.47)); (4) the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 ([Matt 24:1-31](Matt.24.1-Matt.24.31)); (5) the second coming of Christ in the future ([24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31)); or (6) an unfolding revelation of God’s Kingdom in various ways, including the evangelism of the world. In the fourth view, **coming** would mean “coming in judgment” upon sinful Israel.

The expression **Son of Man** ([16:27-28](Matt.16.27-Matt.16.28)) forms an *inclusio* (bracketing expression) with [16:13](Matt.16.13), unifying [16:13-28](Matt.16.13-Matt.16.28) around the theme of the identity of the Son of Man. He is the Messiah who would suffer and then be exalted by God and return as Judge.
**Peter** . . . **James and John** later accompanied Jesus at Gethsemane ([26:37](Matt.26.37); [2 Pet 1:16-19](2Pet.1.16-2Pet.1.19)).

It is impossible to determine the exact location of this **high mountain**. The traditional site, Mount Tabor, is only about 1,900 feet (580 meters) high and is out of the way for a trip from Caesarea Philippi ([Matt 16:13](Matt.16.13)) to Capernaum ([17:24](Matt.17.24)). Mount Hermon, another possibility, is about 9,200 feet (2,800 meters) high and located in Syria, forty miles north of Capernaum. It is unlikely, however, that “teachers of religious law” ([Mark 9:14](Mark.9.14)) would have congregated at the foot of a mountain in Gentile territory. A strong candidate is Mount Meron, about 4,000 feet (1,220 meters) high and situated between Caesarea Philippi and Capernaum.

**Jesus’ appearance was transformed:** Jesus’ inner, divine nature, previously veiled, was now disclosed so that the three caught a glimpse of his glory (see [Exod 34:29-35](Exod.34.29-Exod.34.35); [Ps 104:2](Ps.104.2); [2 Cor 3:12-18](2Cor.3.12-2Cor.3.18); [Rev 1:16](Rev.1.16)). Jesus’ followers will one day share in this glory ([Matt 13:43](Matt.13.43)).

**Moses** symbolizes the law and **Elijah** the prophets. They appeared as witnesses to Christ, to demonstrate that Jesus, God’s Son, is the fulfillment of everything written in the Law and the Prophets (see [5:17-20](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.20); [11:2-6](Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6); [12:28](Matt.12.28)).
**three shelters as memorials:** Peter probably thought that the Kingdom was about to be ushered in with full glory (cp. [Acts 1:6](Acts.1.6)), and he desired to memorialize the moment.

**a bright cloud overshadowed them:** Such an occurrence accompanied God’s presence among the ancient Israelites during Moses’ ministry (see [Exod 24:15-18](Exod.24.15-Exod.24.18); [25:8](Exod.25.8); [29:45-46](Exod.29.45-Exod.29.46); [40:34-38](Exod.40.34-Exod.40.38)).
**my dearly loved Son:** The Father was confirming what Peter had previously affirmed ([Matt 16:16-17](Matt.16.16-Matt.16.17)).

They should **listen to him** because Jesus is God’s Son, who, as a prophet, reveals God’s will ([11:27](Matt.11.27); see [Deut 18:15](Deut.18.15), [18](Deut.18.18); [Acts 3:22-23](Acts.3.22-Acts.3.23); [7:37](Acts.7.37)).
Such a response is typical for encounters with God’s glory (e.g., [Isa 6:5](Isa.6.5); [Dan 8:17](Dan.8.17); [10:9](Dan.10.9), [15-19](Dan.10.15-Dan.10.19); [Rev 1:17](Rev.1.17)).
Jesus could not be fully understood until all of his work was accomplished, particularly his death and resurrection.

Elijah’s presence at the transfiguration prompted a question about the view **that Elijah must return before the Messiah comes** (see [Mal 4:5-6](Mal.4.5-Mal.4.6)). In pointing to **John the Baptist***,* Jesus reinforced the unexpected idea that the Messiah must **suffer***,* even as his precursor had suffered ([Matt 14:3-12](Matt.14.3-Matt.14.12)).

**faithless and corrupt people:** The expression is often used for moral depravity (see [Deut 32:5](Deut.32.5), [19-22](Deut.32.19-Deut.32.22)). Normally, this exclamation of Jesus was directed at the unbelieving Jewish crowds or leaders who refuse to acknowledge God’s presence in him (see [Matt 12:39](Matt.12.39)). Here, however, it was a sharp criticism of his disciples’ failure to trust Jesus and his saving, healing power.
Here, the expression **don’t have enough faith** is virtually synonymous with *no faith*.

**faith even as small as a mustard seed:** This could mean that if the disciples had even very little faith they would be able to accomplish great things ([21:21](Matt.21.21); cp. [1 Cor 13:2](1Cor.13.2)). It could also mean that if they would allow their faith to grow (see [Matt 13:31-32](Matt.13.31-Matt.13.32)), they could act with courageous belief.
Moving mountains is an adage for overcoming obstacles and fulfilling God’s purposes ([Isa 40:4](Isa.40.4); [49:11](Isa.49.11); [54:10](Isa.54.10); [1 Cor 13:2](1Cor.13.2)).
**betrayed:** See [Matt 20:18](Matt.20.18); [26:14-16](Matt.26.14-Matt.26.16), [45-49](Matt.26.45-Matt.26.49) for the fulfillment of this prediction.
Every adult citizen of Israel was required to pay the **Temple tax** of one-half shekel. In Jesus’ day, priests and some rabbis did not pay the tax.
**Peter** was the spokesman for the Twelve (see [10:2](Matt.10.2)).

As an obedient Jew, Jesus would have paid the tax annually, and he did pay it. Jesus’ point was that as God’s Son, he is greater than the Temple ([12:5-6](Matt.12.5-Matt.12.6)), and he makes a decisive break with it (see [16:18-19](Matt.16.18-Matt.16.19); [21:33-46](Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46)).

This fourth major discourse in Matthew (see study note on Matt 5:1–7:29) focuses on responses to the Messiah—acceptance by the disciples and rejection by the Jewish leaders and most of the populace. In light of this growing polarization, Jesus began to instruct his followers on the nature of community life. For a community to live according to Jesus’ standards, it must live with humility ([18:1-5](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.5)), sensitivity ([18:6-9](Matt.18.6-Matt.18.9)), compassion ([18:10-14](Matt.18.10-Matt.18.14)), discipline ([18:15-18](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.18)), and forgiveness ([18:21-35](Matt.18.21-Matt.18.35)). As with the other discourses, a concluding formula ([19:1-2](Matt.19.1-Matt.19.2)) bridges to the next section.

**About that time:** Matthew connects the disciples’ questions with the previous discussion concerning the Temple. The disciples began to assume that their new freedom in relation to Jewish authority entitled them to authority of their own. In addition, talk of special revelations ([11:25-27](Matt.11.25-Matt.11.27); [13:11-17](Matt.13.11-Matt.13.17)) and roles of leadership ([10:2-4](Matt.10.2-Matt.10.4); [19:28](Matt.19.28)) probably gave rise to jealous comparisons and petty desires for power among the disciples, perhaps revolving around the apparent privilege of Peter ([17:25](Matt.17.25)) or Peter, James, and John ([17:1-3](Matt.17.1-Matt.17.3)).
**Like little children** means to be humble ([18:4](Matt.18.4)). The disciples had been intent on status and ambition.
Jesus moved the discussion toward solidarity within the community; to welcome a humble follower of Jesus is to welcome Jesus himself (see [10:40-42](Matt.10.40-Matt.10.42)).
To **cause one** . . . **to fall into sin** is to lead believing children (or possibly believing adults who become “like children”; see [18:3](Matt.18.3)) to reject Christ and abandon the faith.
The designation **little ones** emphasizes their humility ([5:3-12](Matt.5.3-Matt.5.12); [18:4](Matt.18.4); [19:13-15](Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15)).

Though the thought of being drowned with a **large millstone** around the neck is frightful, Jesus warned that causing another to fall away will bring far greater misery ([18:7](Matt.18.7); [26:24](Matt.26.24); [Rev 18:21](Rev.18.21); see [Matt 22:13](Matt.22.13)).
Concern shifts to the individual: Get rid of whatever **causes you to sin** (see [5:29-30](Matt.5.29-Matt.5.30); [Col 3:5-17](Col.3.5-Col.3.17)).

**Don’t look down on** them, either by refusing to receive them ([18:5-6](Matt.18.5-Matt.18.6)) or by refusing to give pastoral care when needed ([18:12-14](Matt.18.12-Matt.18.14); see [19:13-15](Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15)).
**their angels:** See [4:5-7](Matt.4.5-Matt.4.7); [Heb 1:14](Heb.1.14).
Just as a shepherd will work to recover a lost **sheep***,* the “little ones” ([18:6](Matt.18.6)) must not be despised or neglected.
The shepherd’s joy is also the joy of the Father; the purpose of pastoral care is so God will not lose any of his sheep.

The believing community must not be fractured into rival parties and unreconciled relationships. Its members are to pursue reconciliation ([18:15-20](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.20)) and forgive willingly ([18:21-35](Matt.18.21-Matt.18.35)). At times, however, stern discipline may be necessary ([18:17](Matt.18.17)).
Restoration begins privately and should be made public only as a last resort.

**If another believer sins***,* love requires us to **go privately and point out the offense** ([Lev 19:17](Lev.19.17); [Luke 17:3](Luke.17.3); [Gal 6:1](Gal.6.1); [1 Tim 5:20](1Tim.5.20); [Titus 3:10](Titus.3.10)).

By requiring the presence of **one or two others***,* Jesus prevented slanderous, unsubstantiated accusations from being presented to the congregation (see [John 8:17](John.8.17); [2 Cor 13:1](2Cor.13.1); [1 Tim 5:19](1Tim.5.19); [Heb 10:28](Heb.10.28)).
**The church** is the local Christian community.

The unrepentant person is to be considered a **pagan or a corrupt tax collector**, a wicked transgressor of the law. Church discipline by exclusion (excommunication; see [Acts 5:1-6](Acts.5.1-Acts.5.6); [Rom 16:17](Rom.16.17); [1 Cor 5:1-13](1Cor.5.1-1Cor.5.13); [2 Cor 6:14-18](2Cor.6.14-2Cor.6.18); [Gal 5:7-12](Gal.5.7-Gal.5.12); [2 Thes 3:14-15](2Thess.3.14-2Thess.3.15)) is rooted in the conviction that God’s people are to be holy and that sin corrupts fellowship, both between people and between the people and God. The goal is neither vindictive retribution nor a public display of power, but restoration of the wayward to holiness and fellowship ([Matt 18:10-15](Matt.18.10-Matt.18.15); [Gal 6:1](Gal.6.1); [Jas 5:19-20](Jas.5.19-Jas.5.20)).
These sayings provide the basis for a process of discipline and restoration in the community of disciples.

**forbid . . . permit:** The privilege and authority granted to Peter ([16:19](Matt.16.19)) are here granted to the church (or possibly to the twelve apostles, [18:1](Matt.18.1)). The decisions of the community, when in accord with God’s will, are eternally binding.
**anything you ask:** In the context of church discipline ([18:15-17](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.17)), this suggests that discipline must be done in prayer.
Christ is present in the process of discipline, so the process is a ratification of God’s decision.

Peter’s suggestion of **seven times** was generous, so Jesus’ answer was startling. The disciple’s willingness to forgive should be like God’s forgiving grace, limitless and free (see [18:10-14](Matt.18.10-Matt.18.14)). Those who do not forgive in this way cannot themselves have experienced God’s forgiveness ([18:35](Matt.18.35); see [6:12](Matt.6.12)).
**seventy times seven:** Or *seventy-seven times*; either way, Jesus prescribes limitless readiness to forgive from the heart ([18:35](Matt.18.35); cp. [Gen 4:23-24](Gen.4.23-Gen.4.24)).

**millions of dollars** (Greek *10,000 talents*): The talent was the highest unit of currency, but its value fluctuated. The debt was clearly impossible to pay—this amount exceeded the tax revenue of all Galilee.
**I will pay it all:** The exaggerated debt and the slave’s promise amplify the greatness of the king’s mercy and the slave’s unforgiving attitude ([18:29-30](Matt.18.29-Matt.18.30)).
**a few thousand dollars:** The first servant’s debt was about one million times greater than this sum owed to him.
This is how God responds ([18:35](Matt.18.35)) to anyone unwilling to forgive.
**until he had paid his entire debt:** I.e., permanently, because he could never repay.
**That’s what my heavenly Father will do to you:** Prison and torture ([18:34](Matt.18.34)) is thus a metaphor for hell (see [5:22](Matt.5.22)).
Jesus was now on the move toward Jerusalem ([19:1](Matt.19.1); [20:29](Matt.20.29); [21:1](Matt.21.1)), with a further opportunity for instructing the disciples on various aspects of discipleship.

There were two divergent views on when one was **allowed to divorce** one’s wife. One group of Pharisees, following Rabbi Shammai, argued that divorce was allowed only in the case of adultery or other grave sin, while the other group, following Rabbi Hillel, contended that a man could divorce his wife for **any reason**, such as if she burned his dinner.
The Pharisees were not considering *all* of God’s word. The Creator had made marriage as a permanent union (see [Gen 2:18-25](Gen.2.18-Gen.2.25); see also [1 Cor 7:10-16](1Cor.7.10-1Cor.7.16)).
Since God made marriage a union, humans do not have the right to break that union. Jesus affirmed the indissolubility of marriage.

**why did Moses say** (literally *command*): The Pharisees thought Jesus had contradicted a command of the law (see [Deut 24:1-4](Deut.24.1-Deut.24.4)), but Moses **permitted divorce** **only as a concession** to their **hard hearts**. Jesus introduced the revolutionary principle that God’s permission is not necessarily his desire (see [1 Cor 6:12](1Cor.6.12)). Divorce is never God’s desire ([Mal 2:14-16](Mal.2.14-Mal.2.16)); it is an expression of human sin.

Jesus permits only one legitimate reason for a man to divorce: if **his wife has been unfaithful** (see [5:32](Matt.5.32)). In the face of those who thought divorce could be taken lightly, Jesus affirms God’s created order: Marriage was designed to be permanent (see [Mark 10:11-12](Mark.10.11-Mark.10.12)).
**commits adultery:** This speaks only of the man who divorces his wife unlawfully. In such a case, his remarriage is adulterous. Jesus’ motivation is to reestablish the permanency of marriage.
**This statement** refers to the disciples’ comment ([19:10](Matt.19.10)).

**Eunuchs** are males castrated either by a birth defect or by a surgical operation. Jesus also uses the term metaphorically for those who **choose not to marry** (see [Luke 14:26](Luke.14.26); [18:29](Luke.18.29); [1 Cor 7:7-8](1Cor.7.7-1Cor.7.8)).
**for the sake of the Kingdom:** Jesus was not denigrating marriage; he was simply indicating that the unmarried often have greater potential for ministry (see [1 Cor 7:25-35](1Cor.7.25-1Cor.7.35)).
Jesus would **lay his hands** on others to bless them (see [Luke 4:40](Luke.4.40); [13:13](Luke.13.13); see also [Gen 48:14-15](Gen.48.14-Gen.48.15); [Acts 19:6](Acts.19.6)).
**The disciples***,* motivated to protect Jesus, **scolded the parents***,* demonstrating a wrong attitude toward children (see [Matt 18:5-6](Matt.18.5-Matt.18.6), [10](Matt.18.10)).

**Why ask me?** The man, as a Jew, should have known that God’s standard of goodness is clearly reflected in his commandments. The man’s questions (also [19:20](Matt.19.20)) show that he was not trusting in the adequacy of God’s revealed will.
**only One . . . is good:** The man may have believed he could act with perfect goodness on his own, whereas only God is truly **good** and thus the source of all goodness.

**keep the commandments:** Jesus has in mind either leading the man to see his sinfulness by asking him to do the impossible, or more probably, restating that good works are a telling gauge of the truthfulness of a person’s faith (see [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27)).

By calling the man to **go and sell** and **come, follow me***,* Jesus revealed that the man had not in fact kept the first of the ten commandments ([Exod 20:3](Exod.20.3)). His **possessions**—his wealth and security—had become his god (see [Matt 6:20](Matt.6.20), [24](Matt.6.24); [13:44-46](Matt.13.44-Matt.13.46)).

Jesus draws a lesson for discipleship from the rich man’s tragic denial. It is **hard** for the **rich** to humble themselves, admit their need, and trust in God (see [5:3](Matt.5.3); [Luke 6:24](Luke.6.24); [1 Tim 6:9-10](1Tim.6.9-1Tim.6.10)).

**Kingdom of Heaven** is equivalent here to *eternal life* ([Matt 19:16-17](Matt.19.16-Matt.19.17), [29](Matt.19.29)) or to *salvation* as the result of God’s regenerating work ([19:25-26](Matt.19.25-Matt.19.26)).

**easier for a camel:** This analogy reinforces the difficulty that wealthy people face in entering the Kingdom. A few manuscripts have a Greek word meaning *rope* (Greek *kamilos*) instead of *camel* (Greek *kamēlos*), a difference of only one letter.

**to go through the eye of a needle:** The image makes the wealthy entering the Kingdom an impossibility. The situation is not utterly hopeless, however ([19:26-27](Matt.19.26-Matt.19.27)). See study note on Mark 10:25.
God’s regenerating grace is absolutely essential before the wealthy are able to repent from their idolatry, abandon their possessions if called to do so, and follow Jesus ([19:21](Matt.19.21)).

**you . . . will also sit on twelve thrones:** The disciples’ part in judging is a reversal—those who are wealthy and powerful now will be judged by those who are humble and poor (see [19:30](Matt.19.30)).
**Judging** can mean both ruling and condemning (see [Rev 20:4](Rev.20.4)).
This parable is similar to the parable of the Lost Son ([Luke 15:11-32](Luke.15.11-Luke.15.32)). In both, God’s grace is shown to two parties while one grumbles about unjust treatment.
Payment followed the day’s work ([Deut 24:14-15](Deut.24.14-Deut.24.15)).

Each prediction of Jesus’ suffering in Matthew is connected to instruction on the nature of discipleship in light of that suffering (see [16:24-28](Matt.16.24-Matt.16.28); [17:24–18:5](Matt.17.24-Matt.18.5)). This teaching called the Messiah’s disciples to follow his example of service and sacrifice.
This mother’s question appears to have been inspired by her sons, since Jesus responded to the sons rather than to the mother (cp. [Mark 10:35-37](Mark.10.35-Mark.10.37)).

The promise of sitting in positions of authority **in** God’s **Kingdom** had already been given ([19:28](Matt.19.28)); the brothers’ request seems to have been motivated out of selfish desire for prominence, with no regard for the suffering the Messiah would soon undergo (see [Matt 23:6](Matt.23.6); [Luke 14:7-11](Luke.14.7-Luke.14.11)).

The **cup** refers to Jesus’ duty, calling, and destiny (see [26:39](Matt.26.39); [John 18:11](John.18.11); see also [Ps 75:8](Ps.75.8); [Isa 51:17](Isa.51.17), [22](Isa.51.22); [Rev 16:19](Rev.16.19)).
**You will indeed:** James was eventually martyred ([Acts 12:2](Acts.12.2)), and John suffered significant persecution ([Acts 4:3](Acts.4.3); [5:40](Acts.5.40); [Rev 1:9](Rev.1.9)).
The **other disciples** . . . **were indignant:** Selfish ambition was apparently not unique to **James and John** (see also [21:15](Matt.21.15); [26:8](Matt.26.8); [Luke 13:14](Luke.13.14)).

The desire for power is characteristic of pagan **rulers in this world**. It ought not to be a trait of those who follow the **Son of Man** ([18:1-5](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.5); [19:13-15](Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15); [23:1-12](Matt.23.1-Matt.23.12)).

The word **slave** is a common metaphor for the submissive relationship of a disciple to his master ([8:9](Matt.8.9); [10:24-25](Matt.10.24-Matt.10.25); [24:45-51](Matt.24.45-Matt.24.51); [25:14-30](Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30)). Jesus’ disciples serve others, following Jesus’ example (e.g., [John 13:1-17](John.13.1-John.13.17)).
This expression, the **Son of Man came***,* suggests Jesus’ preexistence (see [Dan 7:13-14](Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14)).

Jesus was describing his voluntary offering of himself as **a ransom for many**, to pay the debt all people owe (see [Matt 26:26-29](Matt.26.26-Matt.26.29); [Isa 53:10-12](Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12); [Rom 3:24](Rom.3.24)), thereby buying them out of slavery (see [Gal 5:1](Gal.5.1)).
The blind men’s expression of faith in the **Son of David** was an acknowledgment of Jesus as the Messiah (see [21:9](Matt.21.9); [22:42](Matt.22.42); [2 Sam 7:12-16](2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16)).
Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem initiates Matthew’s account of how the Messiah’s suffering and resurrection establish salvation.
**Bethphage** (a Hebrew name meaning *house of figs*) was probably located on the eastern slope of the **Mount of Olives** between Bethany and Jerusalem proper.
Jesus was revealing himself as **the Lord** who, as king of Israel, ascends to Mount Zion on a donkey ([21:5](Matt.21.5); see [Zech 9:9](Zech.9.9)).

The Old Testament fulfillment here emphasizes the Messiah’s non-violent, **humble***,* and saving work (see [11:28-30](Matt.11.28-Matt.11.30); [Isa 62:11](Isa.62.11); [Zech 9:9-10](Zech.9.9-Zech.9.10)).
The crowds with Jesus understood him to be a **prophet***,* empowered by God to teach and to perform miracles.
The description **from Nazareth in Galilee** highlights Jesus’ humble origins (see [2:23](Matt.2.23)).

The close association of the Temple cleansing (see [John 2:13-16](John.2.13-John.2.16)) with the cursing of the fig tree ([Matt 21:18-19](Matt.21.18-Matt.21.19)) reveals Jesus as the Messiah who confronted Israel and warned that God judges those who reject the Messiah and his message.
**Buying and selling** took place within **the Temple** complex, in the Court of the Gentiles.

**Money changers** profited from the exchange of money from other currencies into official Jewish currency. Jesus criticized the commercialism that profaned the holiness of the Temple (see [Mark 11:11-18](Mark.11.11-Mark.11.18)).
Jesus’ actions were justified, because God’s glory was being desecrated through financial exploitation.
The Jewish leaders’ stubborn refusal to believe is contrasted with the exuberant faith and **praise** of little **children** (see [18:1-14](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.14); [19:13-15](Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15)).

**Haven’t you ever read the Scriptures?** Jesus put this penetrating question to opponents who did not perceive the fulfillment of messianic promises in his ministry. See also [12:3](Matt.12.3), [5](Matt.12.5); [19:4](Matt.19.4); [21:42](Matt.21.42); [22:31](Matt.22.31).

**there were only leaves:** Mark observes that “it was too early in the season for fruit” (see [Mark 11:13](Mark.11.13)). It was spring (just before Passover); figs form in the spring but ripen in the fall.

**immediately the fig tree withered:** Matthew has apparently compressed the story (cp. [Matt 21:18-22](Matt.21.18-Matt.21.22); [Mark 11:13-14](Mark.11.13-Mark.11.14), [20-23](Mark.11.20-Mark.11.23)). The cursing of the fig tree is a symbolic gesture depicting God’s judgment on Israel for rejecting the Messiah (see [Matt 3:9](Matt.3.9); [8:11-12](Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12)). Like a fig tree that shows promise but no fruit, the Israelites (especially the hypocritical leaders) did not bear the fruit of receiving the Messiah (see [21:33-46](Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46)).
Jesus was exhorting the disciples to trust in God and to pray accordingly. He was not offering God’s unconditional endorsement of all that they might desire ([1 Jn 5:14-15](1John.5.14-1John.5.15)).

This section focuses on the Jewish leaders’ attack on Jesus’ authority. In each case, Jesus’ wisdom revealed the leaders’ spiritual blindness. These debates also revealed Jesus’ status as Messiah and the consequences of rejecting him. Tragically, the leaders grew more resistant with each encounter and plotted to eliminate Jesus ([21:23](Matt.21.23), [46](Matt.21.46); [22:15-17](Matt.22.15-Matt.22.17), [23](Matt.22.23), [34](Matt.22.34), [41](Matt.22.41)).
**Elders** (literally *elders of the people*) were family heads from each tribe who were members of the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem (cp. [Ezra 5:5](Ezra.5.5); [6:14](Ezra.6.14); [10:8](Ezra.10.8)).

Jesus propounded a riddle, the solution to which answered the leaders’ question and forced them into a dilemma that revealed their hearts ([21:25-26](Matt.21.25-Matt.21.26)). Answering by counter-question was typical for such debates.

**John’s** ministry, like Jesus’ (see [3:1](Matt.3.1), [5-6](Matt.3.5-Matt.3.6)), was controversial, especially after John’s public denouncement of the sins of Herod Antipas (see [14:4](Matt.14.4)). The leaders did not want to acknowledge that John’s ministry was from God, since they had refused to **believe John** by repenting of their sins ([3:2](Matt.3.2)) and accepting Jesus as the Messiah ([John 1:29-34](John.1.29-John.1.34)).
The leaders lacked integrity and courage to confess what they believed about John. So Jesus’ refusal to answer their original question was fair.
Three parables expose the guilt of those who had rejected the Messiah and forfeited their privilege as God’s chosen people. The new people of God are only those who embrace the Messiah.
This parable continues the point about John’s significance.
**I won’t go:** This response must have offended Jews who were taught to show outward respect for the authority of a father (see [8:21-22](Matt.8.21-Matt.8.22)).
**The right way to live** is in conformity to God’s will ([3:15](Matt.3.15); [5:20](Matt.5.20); see also [Prov 8:20](Prov.8.20); [12:28](Prov.12.28)).

In this **story** Jesus draws on [Isa 5:1-7](Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7). The people of Israel who rejected God’s Messiah forfeited the privilege of being God’s people. The Christian community, comprised of both Jews and Gentiles, has now been called to be the people of God (cp. [Rom 9:4-8](Rom.9.4-Rom.9.8); [11:1-12](Rom.11.1-Rom.11.12)).

**sent his servants:** The prophets had spoken God’s word to Israel. The tenant **farmers** represented the leaders of Israel, whom Jesus held responsible for the deaths of God’s prophets ([23:29-37](Matt.23.29-Matt.23.37)).
**Finally:** God’s revelation climaxed in Jesus (see [13:16-17](Matt.13.16-Matt.13.17); [Heb 1:1-2](Heb.1.1-Heb.1.2)).
**When the owner of the vineyard returns** refers to the Lord’s coming in judgment (see [16:27](Matt.16.27); [24:1-36](Matt.24.1-Matt.24.36)).
The Jewish **religious leaders** pronounced their own condemnation.

The **cornerstone** was either the first stone of the foundation or the capstone (as of an arch), the last to be laid. The very **stone that the builders rejected** as unworthy of use was, in fact, the most important. Jesus was referring to his own role in the Kingdom of God ([21:43](Matt.21.43)) and to the religious leaders’ rejection of him.

**taken away from you:** Either the privilege of being God’s chosen nation no longer belonged to the Jews, or the religious leaders had lost the privilege of being leaders of God’s people (see [Rom 9–11](Rom.9.1-Rom.11.36)).

The Christian community is **a nation that will produce the proper fruit**—that is, a life of trust and obedience that demonstrates the inauguration of the Kingdom (see [Matt 3:8](Matt.3.8); [7:15-20](Matt.7.15-Matt.7.20); [12:33](Matt.12.33); [13:8](Matt.13.8), [26](Matt.13.26)).

Though in a short while the Messiah’s opponents would gain a brief victory, they would ultimately be **broken** and the **stone** would **crush** them because the cross became the gateway to Jesus’ vindication and triumph (see also [Dan 2:34-35](Dan.2.34-Dan.2.35), [44-45](Dan.2.44-Dan.2.45)).
This explanation fits with Matthew’s theme of God’s judgment on the Jewish leaders who misled the people of Israel (see [23:13-15](Matt.23.13-Matt.23.15)).

In this parable, Israel, having repeatedly rejected God’s word in the past, rejects the Messiah and is judged as a result. In Israel’s place, God raised up the church ([16:17-19](Matt.16.17-Matt.16.19); [21:43](Matt.21.43)), of which righteousness is also expected ([Rom 11:11-24](Rom.11.11-Rom.11.24)).
The **king** represents God, whose **son** is Jesus ([Gal 4:4](Gal.4.4); [Heb 1:1-2](Heb.1.1-Heb.1.2)).
The **feast** represents the Kingdom of the Messiah.
**Those who were invited** refers to the nation of Israel, who **ignored** God’s **servants,** the prophets (see study note on Matt 21:33-46).
Jesus was alluding to the coming destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see [23:37-39](Matt.23.37-Matt.23.39); [24:2](Matt.24.2)).
Those who reject God’s invitation **aren’t worthy** to enter his Kingdom (cp. [3:8](Matt.3.8); [10:13](Matt.10.13), [37-38](Matt.10.37-Matt.10.38)).
**everyone you see:** God’s invitation is no longer restricted to the nation of Israel (see [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20); cp. [10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6); [15:21-28](Matt.15.21-Matt.15.28)).
**good and bad alike:** See [13:24-50](Matt.13.24-Matt.13.50).
The **proper clothes** correspond to spiritual fruit that demonstrates real faith (see [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27)).

**Weeping and gnashing of teeth** express the intense pain and sorrow that result from condemnation for sin and unbelief (see [8:12](Matt.8.12); [13:42](Matt.13.42), [50](Matt.13.50); [24:51](Matt.24.51); [25:30](Matt.25.30)).
**Outer darkness** is a metaphor for eternal punishment.
While many people are **called**—they hear the invitation to the Kingdom—few are actually **chosen** by God and respond in faithful obedience to Jesus.
Roman taxation was a controversial issue in first-century Palestine (see also [17:24-27](Matt.17.24-Matt.17.27)).
The Pharisees, strict nationalists who resented Roman rule, were normally at odds with the **supporters of Herod**. Here, the unlikely alliance arose from a mutual hatred of Jesus.

**Is it right . . . or not?** The question was designed to trap Jesus. If he answered no, he could be arrested for rebellion against Rome. If he answered yes, he could be accused of supporting Roman oppression.
**You hypocrites!** See study note on 23:13.

The poll tax had to be paid using the denarius coin, which bore the **picture and title** of Caesar. Old Testament prohibitions against images ([Exod 20:4](Exod.20.4); [Lev 26:1](Lev.26.1); [Deut 4:15-24](Deut.4.15-Deut.4.24)) made the use of this coin controversial among Jews (see Josephus, *War* 2.9.2-3). Some Roman procurators apparently produced coins without images for use in Palestine in order not to offend the Jewish conscience.

Jesus outwitted his opponents by affirming the honor due to **Caesar***,* while clearly differentiating it from the supreme honor and allegiance due to **God**. Loyalty to God does not necessarily entail disloyalty to the governing authorities. Jesus was acknowledging two dominions, Caesar’s and God’s, the latter having priority ([Acts 4:19](Acts.4.19)).
The **resurrection** was an important issue of Jesus’ day, but the question was raised only to trap Jesus.

The **Sadducees** (see [3:7](Matt.3.7)) described a situation involving *levirate* marriage (see [Gen 38:6-11](Gen.38.6-Gen.38.11); [Deut 25:5-6](Deut.25.5-Deut.25.6)), which they considered proof that **resurrection from the dead** is not possible.
The **power of God** most likely refers to God’s ability to raise the dead.

**like the angels in heaven:** Jesus was not teaching genderlessness (i.e., androgyny) nor disparaging the divine order of marriage and sexuality; rather, he was affirming that people will be transformed into a glorious new existence (see [1 Cor 15:35-49](1Cor.15.35-1Cor.15.49); [2 Cor 5:1-5](2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.5)) in which aspects of the present order, such as marriage, will not be present.
Since God spoke of being **the God of Abraham** in the present tense, this proves that Abraham still lives and thus that there is a resurrection.
Since many strict Jews saw all commandments as equally binding, a careless response to this question could lead to the accusation of undermining the law of God.

Jesus answers from the Shema ([Deut 6:4-9](Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9)), one of the core statements of God’s covenant with Israel (The first Hebrew word of [Deut 6:4-9](Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9) is *shema‘,* “hear”).
**Love your neighbor as yourself:** [Lev 19:18](Lev.19.18); see also [Rom 13:9](Rom.13.9); [Gal 5:6](Gal.5.6), [14](Gal.5.14); [Jas 2:8](Jas.2.8).
**are based on:** Jesus’ statement affirmed the unity and coherence of God’s will, as recorded in Scripture.

Having successfully defended himself against his opponents’ traps ([21:23–22:40](Matt.21.23-Matt.22.40)), Jesus questioned them as to how the Messiah can be called both the son of David and, at the same time, the Lord of David ([Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1)).
