The quotation is from [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1), which is frequently cited by New Testament authors to describe Jesus (see [Acts 2:34-35](Acts.2.34-Acts.2.35); [1 Cor 15:25](1Cor.15.25); [Heb 1:13](Heb.1.13); [2:8](Heb.2.8); [10:12-13](Heb.10.12-Heb.10.13); [Rev 3:21](Rev.3.21)).
**how can the Messiah be his son?** The answer is that Jesus is more than the son of David: He is the Son of God ([14:33](Matt.14.33)).
**No one could answer him** because they had never thought the Messiah would be God as a human being in the flesh (see [John 1:1-14](John.1.1-John.1.14)).
This final extended discourse (see study note on Matt 5:1–7:29) centers on judgment for rejecting the Messiah.

The religious leaders had sought a reason to accuse Jesus publicly ([21:23–22:46](Matt.21.23-Matt.22.46)) but found none. Jesus now turned **to the crowds and to his disciples** to openly indict the religious leaders for their numerous failures to conform to God’s righteous standards.

**the Pharisees are the official interpreters of the law of Moses:** They transmitted the oral traditions that were associated with the law and thought to be from Moses, and they judged religious and social matters on the basis of these traditions (see [15:2](Matt.15.2)).

**practice and obey:** This was not a blanket endorsement of all that the Pharisees **teach** (see [15:1-20](Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20); [16:5-12](Matt.16.5-Matt.16.12); [23:13-39](Matt.23.13-Matt.23.39)). It might refer only to what was in accord with the law of Moses, or it might be bitter irony or sarcasm. Jesus might also have been counseling conformity to the Pharisees’ teachings to avoid giving offense ([17:24-27](Matt.17.24-Matt.17.27)).
**unbearable religious demands:** There were 613 legal prohibitions and commands, according to the rabbis (see [11:28-30](Matt.11.28-Matt.11.30); [Acts 15:10](Acts.15.10), [28](Acts.15.28)).
**never lift a finger:** The religious leaders were unwilling to consider relaxing traditional legal statutes.

**prayer boxes:** Pious Jews wore, on the head and upper left arm, a small pouch or box (phylactery) containing written copies of important Old Testament commands (see [Deut 6:6-9](Deut.6.6-Deut.6.9); [11:18-19](Deut.11.18-Deut.11.19)).

Wearing **tassels** was another custom associated with piety (see [Matt 9:20](Matt.9.20); see also [Num 15:38-41](Num.15.38-Num.15.41)). Lengthening the tassels called attention to their wearer’s pious practices.
The **seats of honor in the synagogues** were near the scrolls of the Torah and facing the congregation.
**Rabbi** was a title of authority and respect.

Jesus does not prohibit the use of titles (especially for one’s own father), but rather the assumption of undue honor by those who transmit knowledge about God. The community of Jesus is a group of equals, each of whom knows God (see [12:46-50](Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50); [18:15-20](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.20)). The terms **Rabbi, Father,** and **Teacher** are roughly equivalent.

**Rabbi:** These men functioned in Judaism as mediators for dispensing knowledge about God (see [23:7](Matt.23.7)). The new covenant, by contrast, has **only one teacher***,* Jesus himself as Messiah (see [Jer 31:31-34](Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34)).
Writings from later Judaism provide ample evidence of revering the teachers by calling them **Father** (see, e.g., *Mishnah Eduyyoth* [1:4](Matt.1.4)).
**God . . . is your Father:** See [6:9](Matt.6.9); [Mal 2:10](Mal.2.10); cp. [1 Cor 4:15](1Cor.4.15).
**Teacher:** This title denotes the function and office of leading others into knowledge about God. Jesus, not the scribes and Pharisees, is the **teacher** of God’s will ([5:17](Matt.5.17)).
Jesus’ disciples should lead by serving, in stark contrast to Israel’s religious leaders (who are described in [23:5-7](Matt.23.5-Matt.23.7)).

Matthew collected seven statements of **what sorrow awaits you** (literally *woe to you*), drawing upon similar Old Testament listings ([Isa 5:8-23](Isa.5.8-Isa.5.23); [Hab 2:6-20](Hab.2.6-Hab.2.20)), and he arranged them to climax in the murder of the prophets.
**What sorrow awaits you:** A stark warning of judgment from God.

**Hypocrites!** In English, hypocrisy describes a contradiction between reality and appearance. But in biblical usage, hypocrisy is misperceiving God’s will, leading people astray, and thus incurring God’s judgment. Coupled with this is often a desire for prestige and power ([23:5-12](Matt.23.5-Matt.23.12)), abuse of teaching authority, false teachings on doctrine or practice ([23:13-22](Matt.23.13-Matt.23.22)), and preoccupation with ethical minutiae ([23:23-28](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.28)). An accurate English term for this combination of factors is *heresy*. The Pharisees and teachers of religious law displayed all of these characteristics. As the Christian church began to grow, these characteristics continued to appear (e.g., [1 Tim 4:1-3](1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.3); [2 Pet 2:1-22](2Pet.2.1-2Pet.2.22)), so God’s children always need to guard against them ([Jas 4:7-10](Jas.4.7-Jas.4.10); [1 Pet 2:1-3](1Pet.2.1-1Pet.2.3)).

**shut the door of the Kingdom:** By their false teaching and opposition to Jesus (see [Matt 9:32-34](Matt.9.32-Matt.9.34); [12:22-37](Matt.12.22-Matt.12.37); [15:12-14](Matt.15.12-Matt.15.14); [21:15](Matt.21.15); [John 9:13-34](John.9.13-John.9.34)), the **teachers of religious law** and **Pharisees** prevented others from hearing and believing the truth about the Messiah.

A **convert** (proselyte) made a full conversion to Judaism, performing such observances as baptism, sacrifice, and circumcision (see [Acts 13:43](Acts.13.43)). A convert was thus distinct from a “God-fearer,” who adopted certain Jewish beliefs, most notably monotheism, without fully converting to Judaism (see [Luke 7:4-5](Luke.7.4-Luke.7.5); [Acts 10:2](Acts.10.2)). It is likely that **to make one convert** means to persuade God-fearers to become full converts to Judaism by undergoing circumcision (cp. [Gal 2:3](Gal.2.3), [14](Gal.2.14); [5:2-12](Matt.5.2-Matt.5.12); [6:12-13](Matt.6.12-Matt.6.13)).
**of hell:** Greek *of Gehenna;* see study note on 5:29.
The religious leaders declared certain oaths less binding in order to commit fraud. Jesus calls for honest fulfillment of commitments (see [5:33-37](Matt.5.33-Matt.5.37)).

The **teachers of religious law** and **Pharisees** thought that meticulous tithing demonstrated their zeal for the law. Without denying the validity of the **tithe***,* Jesus revealed how they had utterly failed to attend to the **more important aspects of the law** ([Isa 1:16-17](Isa.1.16-Isa.1.17); [Jer 22:3](Jer.22.3); [Hos 6:6](Hos.6.6); [Mic 6:8](Mic.6.8); [Zech 7:9](Zech.7.9)).
**gnat . . . camel:** These words form a pun in Aramaic (*qalma* . . . *gamla*), the language Jesus probably spoke.
Internal purity will result in external righteousness, but the reverse is not true ([6:19-34](Matt.6.19-Matt.6.34); [12:33-37](Matt.12.33-Matt.12.37); [15:15-20](Matt.15.15-Matt.15.20)).

It was a Jewish custom to coat limestone **tombs** (perhaps funerary urns or ossuaries) with a mixture of marble and lime to fill their porous surfaces, giving them a more pleasing appearance and helping visitors to Jerusalem to notice the graves and avoid touching them so as not to contaminate themselves. Jesus is not criticizing the adorning of tombs; rather, he points to the similarity between these **whitewashed tombs** and the **teachers of religious law** and **Pharisees.** Both may have looked good on the outside, but both were contaminated and impure within.

By building and decorating the **tombs for the prophets***,* the **teachers of religious law** and **Pharisees** showed outward solidarity with the prophets, while inwardly they were of the same sinful character as their **ancestors** who had murdered the prophets.
**finish what your ancestors started:** By killing God’s Messiah, they would bring to completion Israel’s history of killing God’s messengers (see [1 Thes 2:14-16](1Thess.2.14-1Thess.2.16)).

The span from **Abel** ([Gen 4:8-11](Gen.4.8-Gen.4.11)) to **Zechariah** ([2 Chr 24:15-22](2Chr.24.15-2Chr.24.22)) follows the order of the Hebrew Bible, in which 2 Chronicles is the last book. The implication is that this generation will be guilty of every murder of the righteous in the Old Testament (cp. [Matt 27:25](Matt.27.25)).
Despite the severe judgment Jesus had just leveled against Israel ([23:29-36](Matt.23.29-Matt.23.36)), he truly longed for them to repent and receive God’s grace.

**your house is abandoned and desolate:** God would withdraw his presence from the Temple ([Ezek 10:18-19](Ezek.10.18-Ezek.10.19); [11:22-23](Ezek.11.22-Ezek.11.23); cp. [Matt 1:23](Matt.1.23)), and both the Temple and Jerusalem would be destroyed.

**Blessings on the one who comes in the name of the** **LORD:** This is possibly the prediction of an end-time conversion of the nation of Israel to the Messiah (see also [Rom 11:12-32](Rom.11.12-Rom.11.32)).

Some believe chapter [24](Matt.24.1-Matt.24.51) pertains to the return of Christ at the end of history. Others view the chapter as a prediction of the events of AD 70, when Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed by the Romans. Others believe it refers to both. See also study notes on Mark 13.
The architecture of **the Temple** was a source of pride among Jews—see study note on Mark 13:1.

**Not one stone:** The destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple was a sign of God’s judgment (see [1 Kgs 9:7-9](1Kgs.9.7-1Kgs.9.9); [Jer 7:8-15](Jer.7.8-Jer.7.15); [9:10-12](Jer.9.10-Jer.9.12); [26:6](Jer.26.6), [18](Jer.26.18); [Mic 3:12](Mic.3.12); see also [Isa 64:11](Isa.64.11); [Luke 19:44](Luke.19.44); [Acts 6:14](Acts.6.14)).
The Greek term translated **return** is *parousia*, which can mean *coming* or *appearing*.

**end of the world** (or *end of the age*): This expression refers to the climax and end of an epoch in salvation history (see [13:39-40](Matt.13.39-Matt.13.40), [49](Matt.13.49); also [Heb 9:26](Heb.9.26)). Jesus’ second coming will bring normal history to a close with decisive judgment. The disciples assumed that the destruction of the Temple and the end of history were closely connected.

Jesus warned the disciples not to be deceived by impostors or overwhelmed by catastrophes in hope of a premature end to history. Time must run its predestined course. The signs predicted in [24:4-8](Matt.24.4-Matt.24.8) are not necessarily at the end; rather, they are signs prior to the end.

**claiming, ‘I am the Messiah’:** A series of false prophets and miracle workers evoked messianic images and persuaded the masses to follow them in hope of deliverance during the period between AD 30 and 70 (Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.4.1; 20.5.1; 20.8.6; *War* 6.5.2). The earliest recorded instance of an outright claim to be the Messiah was Bar Kochba’s claim in AD 132. It is not clear whether Jesus is referring only to impostors in the period prior to the destruction of the Temple or to false messiahs throughout the church age or perhaps during a future tribulation.

**these things must take place:** Tumultuous times are part of God’s sovereign plan as he brings history to a close (see [24:7](Matt.24.7), [29-30](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.30); [2 Thes 2:8-12](2Thess.2.8-2Thess.2.12)).

**The end** could refer to the close of an epoch (such as at AD 70) or the end of human history as we now know it (cp. [Matt 24:13-14](Matt.24.13-Matt.24.14); see also [10:22](Matt.10.22); [13:39-40](Matt.13.39-Matt.13.40), [49](Matt.13.49)).

**first of the birth pains:** Intense anguish is expected just prior to Jesus’ second coming (see also [24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31); [Isa 13:8](Isa.13.8); [26:17](Isa.26.17); [Jer 4:31](Jer.4.31); [6:24](Jer.6.24); [Mic 4:9-10](Mic.4.9-Mic.4.10)).

**hated** (see [Acts 28:22](Acts.28.22)): At the end of the first century, the Roman historian Tacitus described Christians as “the hated ones of mankind” (Tacitus, *Annals* 15.44). The affliction of the righteous sometimes has the purpose of inciting repentance and obedience (see [Exod 4:31](Exod.4.31); [Deut 4:30](Deut.4.30); [Judg 10:6-16](Judg.10.6-Judg.10.16); [Pss 34:19](Ps.34.19); [37:39](Ps.37.39); [50:15](Ps.50.15)).
Persecution will lead some to abandon loyalty to Jesus ([10:25](Matt.10.25); [13:21](Matt.13.21); [16:24-28](Matt.16.24-Matt.16.28); [26:33](Matt.26.33)).

**the love of many will grow cold** (see [Rev 2:4](Rev.2.4)): If the love within the community of Jesus’ disciples diminishes to the point of extinction, then the community ceases to be what God has designed it to be.
The one who **endures** maintains faithful allegiance to Jesus despite persecution. Here, **the end** may refer to the end of one’s own life, the judgment on Israel in AD 70, or the end of history.

**throughout the whole world:** This anticipates the expansive Gentile mission (see [21:43](Matt.21.43); [28:16-20](Matt.28.16-Matt.28.20)). There will be a delay prior to **the end***,* however short or long, during which the Good News will spread significantly throughout the nations.

**The end** will be signaled by a “sacrilegious object” ([24:15](Matt.24.15)), furious persecution ([24:16-28](Matt.24.16-Matt.24.28)), and finally the sign of the Son of Man ([24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31)).
**Daniel . . . spoke about** a profaning or desolating of the Temple (see [Dan 8:13](Dan.8.13); [9:27](Dan.9.27); [11:31](Dan.11.31); [12:11](Dan.12.11)).

**the sacrilegious object that causes desecration:** Attempts to identify a specific fulfillment include: (1) a false priest assuming the priesthood (see Josephus, *War* 4.3.6-10); (2) the presence of unlawful images of God or humans, or certain humans themselves (such as Antiochus Epiphanes, Caligula, Vespasian, or Titus) who were not to be allowed within the Temple precincts (see Josephus, *War* 4.4.1–4.7.1); (3) the presence of the antichrist in the Temple (cp. *1 Maccabees* 1:54-64; *2 Maccabees* 8:17).

**Reader, pay attention!** This covert statement reflects a special bond between writer and reader, based on a shared understanding that the events being described fulfill the prophecies of [Dan 9](Dan.9.1-Dan.9.27), [11](Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45), and [12](Dan.12.1-Dan.12.13).
Josephus records the **winter** swelling of the Jordan River, which made it more difficult to cross (see Josephus, *War* 4.7.5). Muddy roads also made travel difficult in winter.

Normally Jews did not travel **on the Sabbath** in order to rest as God had commanded (see [Gen 2:1-3](Gen.2.1-Gen.2.3); [Exod 20:8-11](Exod.20.8-Exod.20.11); [23:12](Exod.23.12); [31:12-17](Exod.31.12-Exod.31.17); [Lev 23:3](Lev.23.3); [Deut 5:12-15](Deut.5.12-Deut.5.15); [Jer 17:19-27](Jer.17.19-Jer.17.27)).

**greater anguish:** Similar language is found in [Neh 9:37](Neh.9.37); [Jer 11:16](Jer.11.16); [Dan 12:1](Dan.12.1); [Joel 2:1-17](Joel.2.1-Joel.2.17). The blatant savagery of the times has been documented by Josephus (see *War* 5.10.2-3).
**God’s chosen ones** endure ([24:13](Matt.24.13)) and remain faithful ([24:37–25:46](Matt.24.37-Matt.25.46); see [Isa 65:8-9](Isa.65.8-Isa.65.9); [Rom 11:7](Rom.11.7)).

**false messiahs and false prophets** (see [7:15](Matt.7.15); [24:4-8](Matt.24.4-Matt.24.8); also [Acts 13:6](Acts.13.6); [2 Pet 2:1](2Pet.2.1); [1 Jn 2:18](1John.2.18); [4:1](1John.4.1)): Revelation describes a particular false prophet (see [Rev 16:13](Rev.16.13)).
**signs and wonders:** Not all miracles are proof of God’s approval (see [Deut 13:1-4](Deut.13.1-Deut.13.4); [Rev 13:13](Rev.13.13)).
These verses are an expansion of [24:23](Matt.24.23). The place and manner of the Messiah’s appearing was disputed among Jews. The Messiah’s glorious appearance and vindication will be unmistakable.
Some Jewish prophets persuaded the masses to follow them into the **desert** to see signs of deliverance (cp. [24:4-8](Matt.24.4-Matt.24.8)).
**hiding here:** This is perhaps a reference to secretive sects, such as those at Qumran, or to the small fellowship groups associated with the Pharisees.

**Lightning** may be an allusion to the astrological phenomena attending the Messiah’s coming (see [24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31); [1 Thes 4:13-18](1Thess.4.13-1Thess.4.18)). It is not the suddenness of **lightning** that is in view but rather the magnitude of its visibility. Very possibly, Jesus gave these sayings to ward off premature excitement regarding **the end** ([1 Thes 4:13–5:10](1Thess.4.13-1Thess.5.10); [2 Thes 2:1-12](2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.12)).

These sayings form the climax of the discourse and answer the second of the disciples’ initial questions (see [24:3](Matt.24.3)). Some take [24:29-31](Matt.24.29-Matt.24.31) to refer to God’s judgment on the Jewish people in AD 70, using apocalyptic images and metaphors to describe it. Others see a reference to the second coming of Christ at the end of history.

**the sun will be darkened . . . will be shaken:** This phenomenon can be taken literally, as befitting the climactic self-disclosure of God’s Son, or metaphorically, as for a cosmically significant event (see [Acts 2:17-21](Acts.2.17-Acts.2.21); [Heb 12:26-27](Heb.12.26-Heb.12.27); [2 Pet 3:10](2Pet.3.10); [Rev 6:12-13](Rev.6.12-Rev.6.13)). Similar apocalyptic language is used frequently in the Old Testament for describing political disasters and the collapse of a government as cosmic judgments from God (e.g., [Isa 13:9-16](Isa.13.9-Isa.13.16); [Ezek 32:1-10](Ezek.32.1-Ezek.32.10); [Joel 2:1-17](Joel.2.1-Joel.2.17); [Amos 8:7-10](Amos.8.7-Amos.8.10)).

**the sign that the Son of Man is coming** (literally *the sign of the Son of Man*): The **sign** is probably the **Son of Man** himself (see [12:38-42](Matt.12.38-Matt.12.42); [16:4](Matt.16.4)). His **coming** expresses his vindication (see [26:64](Matt.26.64)) and will bring **deep mourning** to those who experience God’s judgment.

**All the peoples of the earth** could be translated *all the tribes of the land.* The term used here is not the usual Greek term for Gentile nations (*ethnoi*), but a term used frequently of the tribes (*phulai*) of Israel (*the land*), suggesting that a national disaster in Israel might be in view (see [21:43](Matt.21.43); [Zech 12:10-14](Zech.12.10-Zech.12.14)).

**the Son of Man coming on the clouds:** See [Dan 7:13](Dan.7.13). Many believe that this means a descent of the Son of Man from God’s presence to reside on earth as Judge and Deliverer—i.e., the second coming of Christ. Others have argued that this describes the Son of Man coming in judgment, but not necessarily the second coming of Christ (see [Matt 10:23](Matt.10.23); [16:27](Matt.16.27); [19:28](Matt.19.28); [25:31](Matt.25.31); [26:64](Matt.26.64); [28:18](Matt.28.18)).

Many believe that the rapture of God’s people through **angels** ([13:41](Matt.13.41); [16:27](Matt.16.27); [25:31](Matt.25.31)) is predicted here. Others believe that **angels** (Greek *angeloi,* “messengers”) here are human messengers ([11:10](Matt.11.10); [Luke 7:24](Luke.7.24); [9:52](Luke.9.52); [Jas 2:25](Jas.2.25)) and that Jesus is describing the expansion of the Good News among Gentiles (see [Matt 21:33-46](Matt.21.33-Matt.21.46); [22:1-14](Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14); [Deut 30:1-10](Deut.30.1-Deut.30.10); [Isa 27:13](Isa.27.13); [Zech 2:6-13](Zech.2.6-Zech.2.13)).
**all these things:** This expression, used first in [23:36](Matt.23.36) (“this judgment”), refers to the events associated with the destruction of the Temple (see [24:2](Matt.24.2), [8](Matt.24.8)).

**his return** (literally *he* or *it*): It could mean Jesus’ return (see [Jas 5:9](Jas.5.9); [Rev 3:20](Rev.3.20)), the destruction of the Temple, or the end of history (see [Luke 21:31](Luke.21.31)).

**this generation:** In Matthew, *generation* is used particularly for contemporary, unbelieving Jews, especially focusing on the leaders who have led people away from the Messiah ([11:16](Matt.11.16); [12:39](Matt.12.39), [41-42](Matt.12.41-Matt.12.42), [45](Matt.12.45); [16:4](Matt.16.4); [23:36](Matt.23.36)).
Jesus’ words are as sure as God’s own (see [5:18](Matt.5.18); [Isa 40:8](Isa.40.8); [55:11](Isa.55.11); [59:21](Isa.59.21)).
**The day** is the day of judgment.

**or the Son:** Jesus’ limited knowledge is suggested also in [Acts 1:7](Acts.1.7). Because the day is unknown, Jesus’ hearers should be vigilant and faithful (see [Matt 24:37–25:46](Matt.24.37-Matt.25.46)). This statement ought to deter those who attempt to calculate the date of our Lord’s return.
Jesus now applied his predictions ([24:1-36](Matt.24.1-Matt.24.36)) to his followers so they will be faithful and prepared for his second coming.

Jesus’ second coming, like the flood ([Gen 7](Gen.7.1-Gen.7.24)), will come upon people unawares. The only adequate preparation is a life of consistent vigilance and obedience (cp. [Luke 17:26-27](Luke.17.26-Luke.17.27), [34-35](Luke.17.34-Luke.17.35)).
**When the Son of Man returns:** Jesus’ second coming (see [24:3](Matt.24.3); cp. [Luke 17:26](Luke.17.26)).

**in Noah’s day** (see [Gen 6:9-22](Gen.6.9-Gen.6.22); [2 Pet 2:5](2Pet.2.5); [3:5-6](2Pet.3.5-2Pet.3.6)): The comparison here does not concern the magnitude of sins, but a lack of discernment about what God is doing, accompanied by a preoccupation with life’s festivities ([Matt 6:19-34](Matt.6.19-Matt.6.34)).

The term **taken** most likely means taken in judgment, at AD 70 or at the end of history; **left** would then mean remaining to enter the new era of either the church (see [21:43](Matt.21.43); [22:1-14](Matt.22.1-Matt.22.14)) or the Millennium.
To **keep watch** is to maintain active, energetic, single-minded obedience to the Lord (see [25:13](Matt.25.13); [26:38-41](Matt.26.38-Matt.26.41)).

This parable and the three that follow ([25:1-13](Matt.25.1-Matt.25.13), [14-30](Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30), [31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)) each dramatize the need for faithful obedience during the delay of Jesus’ second coming.

**servant:** It is possible that Jesus’ listeners would have thought of God’s special servants, the prophets and lawgivers; however, Jesus so frequently used *servant* figuratively that it is more likely a description of every disciple’s responsibility (see [10:24-25](Matt.10.24-Matt.10.25); [13:27-28](Matt.13.27-Matt.13.28); [18:23-35](Matt.18.23-Matt.18.35); [20:26](Matt.20.26)).
This parable reinforces the need for individuals to be watchful and to prepare for the return of Christ ([25:13](Matt.25.13); see also [Luke 12:35-36](Luke.12.35-Luke.12.36)).
**To meet the bridegroom** is an image for the coming of the Messiah (see [Mark 2:19-20](Mark.2.19-Mark.2.20)).

Details of wedding customs during the period are not known. Some think that the bride was led to the home of the bridegroom, who would stay away until the time appointed for the wedding feast. The **bridesmaids***,* who had already escorted the bride to the groom’s home, would then wait for news of his arrival and escort him to the feast ([Matt 25:10](Matt.25.10)). Others think the groom may have come late in the night to the bride’s home, where he was announced. Then, after celebrating with the bride’s guests, the groom would take his bride under torches or lamps to his home.

While some have speculated that the **oil** symbolizes something specific (such as the Holy Spirit), it probably merely supports the point that proper preparation for the second coming of Christ is needed.
Both the prudent and the foolish bridesmaids sleep while waiting. The parable criticizes only the foolish bridesmaids’ failure to bring enough oil.

The arrival of the **bridegroom** at **midnight** while the bridesmaids slept further highlights the fact that the second coming of Jesus will come suddenly, at a time that no one can anticipate ([24:42-51](Matt.24.42-Matt.24.51)).

This parable teaches that the Lord expects his servants to be faithful to the task given to them while waiting for his return. The delay of Christ’s return will cause some to turn to evil deeds ([24:48-49](Matt.24.48-Matt.24.49)), some to inactivity ([25:3](Matt.25.3)), and some to fearful passivity ([25:18](Matt.25.18)).
**After a long time:** This highlights the long delay of Christ’s return ([24:45-51](Matt.24.45-Matt.24.51)).

**Let’s celebrate together** is a metaphor for the Father’s approval and perhaps for the messianic banquet (see [Matt 6:1](Matt.6.1), [4](Matt.6.4), [6](Matt.6.6), [18](Matt.6.18); [9:9-17](Matt.9.9-Matt.9.17)).
**I knew you were . . . harsh:** A false understanding of his master becomes this servant’s excuse for laziness.
God gives abundant grace to those who are faithful with what they have already been given (see [13:12](Matt.13.12)).
To **sit upon his glorious throne** is here a posture of judgment (see [19:28](Matt.19.28); [22:44](Matt.22.44); [Dan 7:13-14](Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14)).
The **right hand** is the place of honor ([Gen 48:13-20](Gen.48.13-Gen.48.20); [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1)).

**prepared for you from the creation of the world:** This might be a reference to God’s choosing individuals for salvation in eternity past (see [13:10-17](Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17); [Eph 1:4](Eph.1.4); [Rev 17:8](Rev.17.8)), or it might simply refer to the Kingdom itself as a place (cp. [Matt 25:41](Matt.25.41)).

The deeds described here, often called “deeds of mercy,” were acts of compassion shown to the helpless (see [Isa 58:1-12](Isa.58.1-Isa.58.12); [Ezek 18:7](Ezek.18.7); [Jas 1:26-27](Jas.1.26-Jas.1.27)). These good deeds are not attempts to merit God’s favor; rather, they arise from a love for Christ that results in compassion toward others (see [6:1-4](Matt.6.1-Matt.6.4)).

**These righteous ones** (see [5:6](Matt.5.6), [20](Matt.5.20)) are those who do God’s will as taught by Jesus, expressed most clearly in deeds of love ([7:12](Matt.7.12); [9:9-13](Matt.9.9-Matt.9.13); [22:34-40](Matt.22.34-Matt.22.40); [25:35-40](Matt.25.35-Matt.25.40)).

**my brothers and sisters:** This expresses either Jesus’ solidarity with his disciples (see [10:42](Matt.10.42); [18:1-14](Matt.18.1-Matt.18.14); [Gal 6:10](Gal.6.10)) or Jesus’ solidarity with humanity in general, irrespective of the faith of the one being helped (see [Matt 6:1-4](Matt.6.1-Matt.6.4); [25:43](Matt.25.43); [Prov 19:17](Prov.19.17)). The use of *brothers and sisters* points to the first interpretation ([Matt 12:46-50](Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50); [18:15-35](Matt.18.15-Matt.18.35); [23:8](Matt.23.8); [28:10](Matt.28.10)) but does not invalidate social responsibility for other people in general (see [Luke 10:30-37](Luke.10.30-Luke.10.37)).

The Greek term translated **eternal** can mean either “lasting forever” or “lasting for an age,” in this case “the age to come” ([13:39-40](Matt.13.39-Matt.13.40), [49](Matt.13.49); [24:3](Matt.24.3); [John 17:3](John.17.3); [2 Thes 1:9](2Thess.1.9); [Phlm 1:15](Phlm.1.15); [1 Jn 5:11](1John.5.11), [13](1John.5.13)). Some hold out hope that the punishment of the damned will, after “an age,” be ended by annihilation or forgiveness. The parallel between **eternal life** and **eternal punishment** suggests strongly that it means “lasting forever,” since eternal life does not end (see also [Luke 16:19-31](Luke.16.19-Luke.16.31); [Heb 6:2](Heb.6.2); [Rev 20:10](Rev.20.10)).

The irony is that the Son of Man, who is to judge the nations ([25:31-46](Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46)), must first be wrongly judged and condemned to death by evil people. Jesus’ death was the ultimate Passover sacrifice (see [John 19:31-37](John.19.31-John.19.37); [1 Cor 5:7](1Cor.5.7)).

**The residence of Caiaphas, the high priest***,* was near the Temple in Jerusalem’s Upper City. Since it was not the normal meeting place, this gathering was *ad hoc*, urgent, and probably secretive. The council chamber, the traditional meeting place for the Sanhedrin, was located either at the southern end of the Court of the Israelites in the Temple, or on the western edge of the Temple hill.

Joseph **Caiaphas***,* son-in-law of Annas (see [John 18:13](John.18.13)), was high priest from AD 18 to 36 ([John 11:49](John.11.49)), the longest tenure of any high priest from the time of Herod’s rule until AD 70. His father-in-law, Annas, had been deposed but continued to be called high priest as well (see [Luke 3:2](Luke.3.2); [John 18:13](John.18.13), [19-24](John.18.19-John.18.24)).

Jerusalem was flooded with pilgrims at **Passover***,* and the Jewish leaders worried about having their authority taken away if they caused or allowed anything that resembled revolt against Rome (see [21:8-11](Matt.21.8-Matt.21.11), [14-16](Matt.21.14-Matt.21.16)).

A similar anointing took place earlier in Galilee ([Luke 7:36-50](Luke.7.36-Luke.7.50)). Matthew’s insertion of the episode at this point (cp. [John 12:1-8](John.12.1-John.12.8)) sets the Jewish leaders’ murderous plotting ([Matt 26:3-5](Matt.26.3-Matt.26.5)) and Judas’s betrayal ([26:14-16](Matt.26.14-Matt.26.16)) in sharp contrast to the woman’s praiseworthy actions.
**Simon, a man who had previously had leprosy:** Jesus’ presence in the man’s home exhibited the forgiving, healing love Jesus often showed toward outcasts (see [8:7](Matt.8.7); [9:10](Matt.9.10)).

The **jar of expensive perfume** was a burial ointment (see [Mark 16:1](Mark.16.1); [Luke 23:56–24:1](Luke.23.56-Luke.24.1); [John 12:1-7](John.12.1-John.12.7); [19:38-42](John.19.38-John.19.42)) made of nard, which was harvested in India. The value of this jar of perfume was nearly a year’s wages ([John 12:5](John.12.5)).
**The disciples were indignant:** [John 12:4](John.12.4) indicates that Judas Iscariot incited this reaction.

**to prepare my body for burial:** It is not clear whether the woman fully understood the significance of her actions. In addition to preparation for burial, the anointing also speaks of Jesus as king ([1 Sam 10:1](1Sam.10.1); [2 Kgs 9:6](2Kgs.9.6)) and priest ([Exod 29:7](Exod.29.7)).

Judas sold himself to the authorities (see also [John 11:57](John.11.57)), concealed it ([Matt 26:25](Matt.26.25)), and then took them to Jesus at the appropriate time so they could carry out their plans ([26:47-56](Matt.26.47-Matt.26.56); see [John 18:2](John.18.2)). Later, Judas was overcome by guilt and committed suicide ([Matt 27:3-10](Matt.27.3-Matt.27.10); see [Acts 1:15-22](Acts.1.15-Acts.1.22)). Judas was apparently known for his greed ([Matt 26:14-15](Matt.26.14-Matt.26.15); [John 12:4-6](John.12.4-John.12.6); [13:29](John.13.29)). It is also possible that he was motivated by disappointment over the nature of Jesus’ reign as Messiah, his own humiliation over the anointing of Jesus (see [John 12:1-8](John.12.1-John.12.8)), or resentment over the leadership of the Galilean apostles, Peter, James, and John. Whatever his motivation, Judas’s betrayal was a part of God’s sovereign plan ([Acts 1:16-17](Acts.1.16-Acts.1.17)).
**My time:** The Messiah would now complete the work for which he was commissioned, to die for the sins of the world.

**eaten from this bowl with me:** It was the custom for everyone present to dip their food into a common bowl, which probably contained herbs and fruit puree. Sharing a meal was a sign of friendship and trust, making a betrayer’s presence all the more startling ([26:21](Matt.26.21); but see [John 13:26](John.13.26)).

**as the Scriptures declared:** Jesus might have been referring to [Isa 53:7-9](Isa.53.7-Isa.53.9) or to the broader Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. This verse combines God’s sovereign will with human responsibility.
Judas referred to Jesus as **Rabbi***,* while the other disciples call him “Lord” ([26:22](Matt.26.22)).
**“You have said it”:** This enigmatic statement affirmed that Judas was the betrayer.

The Last Supper derives its significance in part from the Jewish Passover (see [Exod 12](Exod.12.1-Exod.12.51)). The phases of the Jewish liturgy for Passover are as follows: (1) Festal blessing; (2) first cup (see [Luke 22:17-18](Luke.22.17-Luke.22.18)); (3) eating bitter herbs (see [Matt 26:23](Matt.26.23) and corresponding study note); (4) eating unleavened bread ([26:26](Matt.26.26); [Mark 14:22](Mark.14.22)); (5) second cup is mixed; (6) the Passover *haggadah* (reading) is given ([Exod 12](Exod.12.1-Exod.12.51)); (7) first part of the *hallel* ([Pss 113–114](Ps.113.1-Ps.114.8); see study note on Pss 113–118); (8) second cup is taken; (9) blessing and eating of unleavened bread ([Matt 26:26](Matt.26.26); [Mark 14:22](Mark.14.22); [Luke 22:19](Luke.22.19)); (10) the Passover lamb is eaten; (11) third cup ([Matt 26:27-28](Matt.26.27-Matt.26.28); [Mark 14:23-24](Mark.14.23-Mark.14.24); [Luke 22:20](Luke.22.20)); (12) fourth cup (see [Matt 26:29](Matt.26.29)\[?\]; [Mark 14:25](Mark.14.25)\[?\]); (13) time of fellowship; (14) second part of the *hallel* ([Pss 115–118](Ps.115.1-Ps.118.29); see [Matt 26:30](Matt.26.30)). None of the New Testament accounts of the Last Supper includes every aspect of a typical Jewish Passover. However, the most important aspects of the Passover that gave meaning to the early Christian celebration of the Lord’s Supper are included (see [1 Cor 11:23-25](1Cor.11.23-1Cor.11.25)). Jesus, the Lamb of God, is the ultimate Passover lamb and the perfect sacrifice for sin.

**this is my body . . . my blood:** Ever since the Reformation, there have been three dominant interpretations of Jesus’ statements concerning the bread and the wine: (1) that the bread and wine change into the actual body and blood of Jesus Christ (*transubstantiation*); (2) that Christ is mysteriously present in the sacrament either spiritually (*real presence*) or “in, with, and under” the bread and wine (*consubstantiation*); (3) that the bread and wine symbolize the body and blood of Christ, benefiting the recipient through the Spirit by faith (*symbolism*).
The unleavened **bread** of the Passover ([Exod 12:18](Exod.12.18)) is also described as the “bread of suffering” ([Deut 16:3](Deut.16.3)), referring to hardships in Egypt.
The customary blessing over the bread in the Passover meal was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.”

He **gave thanks**. The traditional blessing for the Passover cup was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.” An early Christian variant is, “We give thanks to you, our Father, for the Holy Vine of David, your child, whom you made known to us through Jesus your child; glory be to you forever” (*Didache* 9.2).

The four cups of the Passover meal correspond to the fourfold promise of [Exod 6:6-7](Exod.6.6-Exod.6.7), with two for deliverance, one for redemption (see [Matt 26:27-28](Matt.26.27-Matt.26.28)), and one for fellowship (see [26:29](Matt.26.29)).

**the covenant:** Under God’s covenant with Israel, the blood of sheep or goats ([Exod 12:5](Exod.12.5), [13](Exod.12.13); [24:8](Exod.24.8)) was shed and placed on the two doorposts and on the lintel at Passover ([Exod 12:7](Exod.12.7)). The blood of Jesus, the sinless Lamb of God, establishes a new covenant (see [Jer 31:31](Jer.31.31)). The idea of the *covenant* is God’s unilateral commitment to establish salvation for mankind, fulfilling the promise to Abraham (see [Gen 12](Gen.12.1-Gen.12.20); [Gal 3:15-29](Gal.3.15-Gal.3.29); [4:12-31](Gal.4.12-Gal.4.31)).

**to forgive the sins of many:** Jesus shed his **blood** as a sacrifice for sin (see [Jer 31:31-34](Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34); [Mark 14:24](Mark.14.24)). Some have understood *many* to refer only to God’s chosen people, while others have understood *many* to be an expression meaning “all” (cp. [Matt 20:28](Matt.20.28)).
**until the day:** Though the **Kingdom** had been inaugurated in Jesus’ ministry, it awaits final consummation (see [1 Cor 15:20-28](1Cor.15.20-1Cor.15.28); [Rev 19–22](Rev.19.1-Rev.22.21)).
**until the day I drink it new:** The final consummation of the Kingdom is pictured as a feast like the Passover, symbolizing an eternal fellowship of love and peace.
**they sang a hymn:** Some have suggested that the *Great Hallel* ([Ps 136](Ps.136.1-Ps.136.26)) was sung.

**God will strike:** In [Zech 13:7-9](Zech.13.7-Zech.13.9), the **Shepherd***,* God’s partner, is struck down (understood by Jesus as a prediction of his own death), and out of the scattered **sheep** emerge a purged, purified remnant of faithful ones ([Zech 13:8-9](Zech.13.8-Zech.13.9)). In the short term, the disciples would soon **be scattered** and deny association with Jesus ([Matt 26:34](Matt.26.34), [56](Matt.26.56), [69-75](Matt.26.69-Matt.26.75)).
Jesus foresaw a time of restoration for the disciples despite their imminent abandonment of him (see ch [28](Matt.28.1-Matt.28.20); [John 21](John.21.1-John.21.25)).
While Peter’s denial receives the most attention, **all the other disciples** denied or avoided association with Christ as well (see [26:56](Matt.26.56)).

This scene reveals the depth of Jesus’ awareness of the suffering that awaited him on the cross, as well as his utter commitment to God’s will (see [20:28](Matt.20.28)). Expressions in [26:41-42](Matt.26.41-Matt.26.42) echo the Lord’s Prayer ([6:9-13](Matt.6.9-Matt.6.13)).

**Gethsemane** is the name of an olive orchard approximately 250 yards east of Jerusalem’s Golden Gate, overlooking the Kidron Valley on the edge of the Mount of Olives. Jesus and his disciples apparently met there often ([Luke 22:39-40](Luke.22.39-Luke.22.40); [John 18:1-2](John.18.1-John.18.2)).

**He took Peter . . . James and John:** These three, apparently the leaders of the apostles, received special revelation ([17:1-13](Matt.17.1-Matt.17.13)) and accompanied Jesus in this difficult hour.
Jesus **became anguished and distressed** from contemplating the Father’s plan for him, to absorb God’s wrath toward humans for their sin (see [27:45-46](Matt.27.45-Matt.27.46)).
**If it is possible:** Jesus’ heart’s desire was for uninterrupted communion with the Father instead of coming under God’s wrath.
**Yet I want your will to be done:** His resolution to do the Father’s will was firm ([4:1-11](Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11); [16:23](Matt.16.23); [John 6:38](John.6.38)).
**Judas . . . gave him the kiss:** Judas’s use of a sign of affection to betray Jesus amplifies the heinousness of his betrayal.
**one of the men with Jesus:** This was Peter ([John 18:26](John.18.26)).

**thousands** (literally *twelve legions*): Jesus used Roman military language (a legion consisted of approximately 6,000 soldiers) to describe the aid he could receive from God. Jesus was not a helpless victim; he permitted his own arrest.
For Jesus to have resisted would have impeded the fulfillment of God’s saving work (see [16:21-23](Matt.16.21-Matt.16.23)).
The leaders’ clandestine behavior was driven by fear of the masses who revered Jesus (see [21:26](Matt.21.26), [46](Matt.21.46); [26:3-5](Matt.26.3-Matt.26.5)).
It is not clear which of **the Scriptures** Jesus was alluding to—perhaps [Isa 53](Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12), or perhaps the Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah in general.
As Jesus had predicted earlier that evening, **all the disciples deserted him** ([Matt 26:31-35](Matt.26.31-Matt.26.35)).

The Gospels record Jesus as undergoing five hearings: (1) an informal hearing before Annas ([John 18:13-24](John.18.13-John.18.24)); (2) a night hearing before the Sanhedrin ([Matt 26:59-66](Matt.26.59-Matt.26.66)); (3) a morning hearing before the Sanhedrin ([27:1-2](Matt.27.1-Matt.27.2)); (4) a hearing before Herod Antipas ([Luke 23:6-12](Luke.23.6-Luke.23.12)); and (5) a two-stage trial before Pilate ([Matt 27:11-31](Matt.27.11-Matt.27.31); see [Luke 23:6-12](Luke.23.6-Luke.23.12)). It all amounts to two trials, a Jewish trial and a Roman trial.

This hearing might have been little more than an unofficial preliminary hearing designed to establish consensus on the terms of the charges. The Jewish leaders were under considerable pressure to keep this incident secret, lest their actions cause a riot (see [21:26](Matt.21.26), [46](Matt.21.46); [26:5](Matt.26.5), [55](Matt.26.55); [John 11:45-53](John.11.45-John.11.53)).
**the high priest’s courtyard:** This location suggests an *ad hoc* meeting of the Sanhedrin at the palace of the high priest ([26:3](Matt.26.3)).

**were trying to find witnesses:** The verb tense suggests an extended, perhaps desperate, attempt to find any testimony that could lead to a formal accusation (see [Mark 14:55-56](Mark.14.55-Mark.14.56)).

**could not use anyone’s testimony:** The evidence was too insubstantial or inconsistent to meet their goal of a death sentence until **two men came forward** ([Deut 17:6](Deut.17.6); [19:15](Deut.19.15)) with testimonies that did not conflict.
The charge is either a misunderstanding or a deliberate distortion of Jesus’ prediction of his death and resurrection (see [John 2:19-21](John.2.19-John.2.21)).

**if you are the Messiah:** This question from **the high priest** was prompted by [Zech 6:12](Zech.6.12), which had predicted that the Messiah would rebuild the Temple (cp. [Matt 26:61](Matt.26.61)).
**You have said it:** This purposefully enigmatic response is essentially an affirmative answer (see [26:25](Matt.26.25); [27:11](Matt.27.11)); Mark has “I AM” ([Mark 14:62](Mark.14.62)).
**you will see:** By quoting [Dan 7:13](Dan.7.13), Jesus affirmed that he was the Son of Man who would be vindicated and exalted by God.

**seated in the place of power at God’s right hand:** Literally *seated at the right hand of the power;* see [Ps 110:1](Ps.110.1). Jews were reluctant to name God directly (see study note on Matt 5:4).
The expression **coming on the clouds of heaven** could refer either to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or to Jesus’ second coming at the end of history.

**Blasphemy!** Caiaphas evidently understood Jesus’ claim to be the exalted Son of Man as a blasphemy against God’s majesty. The Son of Man ([Dan 7:13-14](Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14)) was closely associated with this majesty.

Such abuse fulfills [Isa 50:6](Isa.50.6); [53:4-9](Isa.53.4-Isa.53.9) and Jesus’ own predictions ([Matt 16:21](Matt.16.21); [17:22-23](Matt.17.22-Matt.17.23); [20:18-19](Matt.20.18-Matt.20.19); [26:2](Matt.26.2); see also [Mark 14:65](Mark.14.65)).
Peter’s denials fulfill Jesus’ prediction ([26:34](Matt.26.34)).
**your Galilean accent:** Jews from Galilee had a distinctive accent, compared with those from Judea (cp. [4:13](Matt.4.13) and corresponding study note).
When the crowing of the **rooster** reminded Peter of Jesus’ prediction ([26:34](Matt.26.34)), he was struck with sorrow.
The Jewish leaders were ready to level charges against Jesus before Pilate so that he would order Jesus’ execution. Pilate, a Gentile, fulfills Jesus’ prediction ([20:19](Matt.20.19)).

The charge of blasphemy ([26:65-66](Matt.26.65-Matt.26.66)), though sufficient for the death penalty among Jews, would not convince a Roman judge. Hence, **the leading priests and the elders** conspired together to prepare a more political charge consistent with capital offenses in Roman law (see [27:11-26](Matt.27.11-Matt.27.26); [Luke 23:2](Luke.23.2)).

Tiberius Caesar appointed **Pilate** to be the **governor** (or *prefect*) of Judea. Pilate ruled primarily from Caesarea, not Jerusalem, from AD 26 to AD 36. Though he had sovereign power in Judea, Pilate was ultimately responsible to the legate of Syria, the central authority in the eastern portion of the Roman Empire. Josephus records several instances where Pilate’s disregard for the sanctity of Jewish customs led to revolt.

There are two accounts of Judas’s death—this one and [Acts 1:18-19](Acts.1.18-Acts.1.19). There are differences between the two: (1) Matthew states that the priests bought the field ([Matt 27:6-7](Matt.27.6-Matt.27.7)), while Acts seems to suggest that Judas bought it ([Acts 1:18](Acts.1.18)); (2) Matthew reports that Judas committed suicide by hanging himself ([Matt 27:5](Matt.27.5)), while Acts enigmatically refers to a fall and an abdominal rupture ([Acts 1:18](Acts.1.18)); (3) Matthew implies that the field of blood was so named because it became a place of burial ([Matt 27:7-8](Matt.27.7-Matt.27.8)), while Acts suggests that it was because of Judas’s violent death there ([Acts 1:19](Acts.1.19)). The two accounts are compatible if one takes the account in Acts as describing the effects of the actions described in Matthew.

Judas **was filled with remorse** (Greek *metamelomai*), but he did not repent (Greek *metanoeō*), which would have changed his heart and resulted in obedience and a relationship with God based on faith.

**an innocent man:** Jesus’ innocence is a dominant theme in the narrative of his suffering (see [23:35](Matt.23.35); [26:55-56](Matt.26.55-Matt.26.56), [59-60](Matt.26.59-Matt.26.60); [27:18-19](Matt.27.18-Matt.27.19), [24](Matt.27.24); see also [Luke 23:47](Luke.23.47)).

**hanged himself:** Judas’s suicide resulted from a guilt-stricken, unrepentant conscience. His death satisfied Old Testament law regarding the punishment of a false witness (see [Deut 19:16-21](Deut.19.16-Deut.19.21)).

**Foreigners** were Gentiles who died in Jerusalem. An asset whose owner could not be traced was used for public charity. In this instance, unclean money was used to buy an unclean place for unclean people.
**Field of Blood** is a way of describing a cemetery (cp. [Acts 1:18-19](Acts.1.18-Acts.1.19)).

**the prophecy of Jeremiah:** The citation is from [Zech 11:12-13](Zech.11.12-Zech.11.13). Matthew might merely have been conforming to the Jewish custom of citing books by referring to the first book in the particular scroll—the first book in the scroll containing Zechariah would have been Jeremiah. Or, Matthew might have thought of similar passages in Jeremiah ([Jer 19:1-13](Jer.19.1-Jer.19.13); [18:2-6](Jer.18.2-Jer.18.6); [32:6-15](Jer.32.6-Jer.32.15)) along with [Zech 11:12-13](Zech.11.12-Zech.11.13).
Matthew sees a striking resemblance between Zechariah’s actions and those of the leading priests. Both contexts deal with the rejection of God’s messenger who was to be king of God’s people.

The Roman trial included an initial hearing before Pilate ([27:11-14](Matt.27.11-Matt.27.14)), one before Herod Antipas ([Luke 23:6-16](Luke.23.6-Luke.23.16)), and a second hearing before Pilate ([Matt 27:15-26](Matt.27.15-Matt.27.26)).

**king of the Jews:** The Sanhedrin’s original charge of blasphemy ([26:65-66](Matt.26.65-Matt.26.66); [27:1](Matt.27.1)) held no interest to the Romans, who saw it as a Jewish religious question (cp. [Acts 25:18-20](Acts.25.18-Acts.25.20)). The charge was therefore changed to incriminate Jesus in Roman eyes as a political rebel (see [Luke 23:2](Luke.23.2)).

Pilate’s **custom** seems out of character; he was not known for wanting to please his Jewish subjects. However, if Pilate’s position with Caesar was precarious at this point (see study note on John 19:12; see Philo, *On the Embassy to Gaius* 159–161), then this gesture may have been to keep the peace and thus avoid negative attention from Rome.

**notorious prisoner . . . named Barabbas:** Elsewhere he is called a “revolutionary” ([Mark 15:7](Mark.15.7); [John 18:40](John.18.40)), a term that also denotes a robber or insurrectionist (see [Luke 23:19](Luke.23.19)). To the zealots, Barabbas was a hero.
**through a terrible nightmare** (cp. [1:20](Matt.1.20)): It is ironic that a pagan recognizes and takes a stand for Jesus’ innocence, while the Jewish crowd does not.
**The responsibility is yours!** The priests had said the same thing to Judas ([27:4](Matt.27.4)).

**all the people** (see [21:43](Matt.21.43)): This does not mean every living Jew. Instead, those urging Jesus’ condemnation are representative of all of unbelieving Israel, whose actions bring consequences for the nation as a whole (e.g., the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70).

**We will take responsibility for his death—we and our children** (see [23:35](Matt.23.35); [2 Sam 1:16](2Sam.1.16); [14:9](2Sam.14.9); [Jer 51:35](Jer.51.35); [Acts 5:28](Acts.5.28); [18:6](Acts.18.6); [20:26](Acts.20.26)): Christians have at times misunderstood and misused this verse in persecution of Jews, but it is not an indictment against Jews in general.

When a man was **flogged***,* he was beaten with whips that had leather thongs at the end, some with sharp bone, **lead***,* or rock fragments stuck to the ends of the thongs (see also [Deut 25:1-3](Deut.25.1-Deut.25.3); [1 Kgs 12:11](1Kgs.12.11), [14](1Kgs.12.14); [Acts 16:22](Acts.16.22); [22:25](Acts.22.25); [2 Cor 11:24-25](2Cor.11.24-2Cor.11.25)).
In the Jewish trial Jesus was mocked as a prophet ([26:67-68](Matt.26.67-Matt.26.68)); here he is mocked as a king.
The **governor’s soldiers** were auxiliary troops recruited from non-Jewish residents of Palestine.
**Their headquarters** was located at the official residence of the governor in Jerusalem (the Antonia Fortress on the northwest corner of the Temple compound).
The **scarlet robe** was probably the cloak of a soldier meant to emulate royal garb solely for the purpose of ridiculing Jesus.
Weaving **thorn branches into a crown** was a mockery of Jesus as king.
Ironically, the taunts and ridicule of the crowd express the truth about Jesus: He is the Son of God and King of Israel, the Messiah.

Normally, the victim carried his own **cross**. Only the crossbeam was carried; the vertical pole would be waiting at the crucifixion site. **Simon** might have been **forced** because Jesus was weak from the effects of scourging. The act of enlisting Simon might also have been a further mockery. Jesus was treated as one who deserved a servant even though he was being marched to his death.

Giving Jesus **wine mixed with bitter gall** was probably intended for ridicule (see [Ps 69:21](Ps.69.21)). It was also a sedative—Jesus probably rejected it in order to suffer fully for our sins (see [Isa 53:10](Isa.53.10)).
**Gall,** otherwise known as wormwood, is a bitter narcotic made from the oil of Artemisia (cp. [Mark 15:23](Mark.15.23)).

**they . . . nailed him to the cross:** Crucifixion, though not generally practiced by Jews, was a widespread Roman punishment for military and political offenders, particularly slaves, rebels, and insurrectionists. The sheer cruelty and the public spectacle of crucifixion worked as a powerful social deterrent. Victims were flogged and then crucified naked, adding to the humiliation. It was seen as the most painful of all possible deaths; it involved intense suffering, exposure to weather and insects, suffocation, and often a final violent thrust of a spear to end life. Further, since crucifixion was a curse from God ([Deut 21:22-23](Deut.21.22-Deut.21.23)), the act was particularly heinous to Jewish sensibilities. Paradoxically, what was so despicable among humans has become the instrument of our salvation. Jesus previously had instructed his disciples to take up their crosses and follow him ([Matt 16:24](Matt.16.24)).
The official charge was **fastened** to the cross above the criminal’s **head**; Jesus was crucified for political sedition.
Crucifying Jesus between **two** convicted **revolutionaries** added further humiliation and guilt by association.

**if you are the Son of God:** This taunt recalls Jesus’ temptation at the very beginning of his public ministry ([4:1-11](Matt.4.1-Matt.4.11)), in which the devil appealed to Jesus’ privileged status in order to tempt him to avoid suffering (see also [16:21-23](Matt.16.21-Matt.16.23)).

**Darkness** symbolizes the judgment of God or, more specifically, the arrival of the day of the Lord (see [Amos 5:18](Amos.5.18), [20](Amos.5.20); [8:9-10](Amos.8.9-Amos.8.10); also [Jer 4:27-28](Jer.4.27-Jer.4.28); [13:16](Jer.13.16); [15:9](Jer.15.9)).
**Eli, Eli:** This cry means *My God, my God,* but the similarity in sound accounts for the people’s confusion ([27:47](Matt.27.47)).
**My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?** Jesus was experiencing God’s wrath for the sins of humanity.
It was widely believed that **Elijah** would return before the day of the Lord ([11:14-15](Matt.11.14-Matt.11.15); [17:10-13](Matt.17.10-Matt.17.13); [Mal 4:5](Mal.4.5)).

The **sour wine** was vinegar. The drink was probably designed to mock Jesus (cp. [Ps 69:21](Ps.69.21) with [Matt 27:34](Matt.27.34)) by pretending to help assuage his thirst. Others have suggested that it was given as an act of genuine kindness.
Each of the four Gospels highlights different aspects of Jesus’ last moments.
**released his spirit:** This emphasizes the sovereignty of Jesus in that he released himself to death (see also [John 19:30](John.19.30)).
**shouted out again** (see [Matt 27:46](Matt.27.46)): This cry was Jesus’ final prayer (see [Luke 23:46](Luke.23.46)).

The significance of the splitting of the **curtain** in **the Temple** is that the wall dividing people from God has been torn down by the death of Jesus Christ (see also [Eph 2:11-22](Eph.2.11-Eph.2.22); [Heb 6:19](Heb.6.19); [9:1–10:25](Heb.9.1-Heb.10.25)).

**The earth shook, rocks split apart:** These are portents of the arrival of judgment (see [Exod 19:18](Exod.19.18); [Judg 5:4](Judg.5.4); [Ps 18:7](Ps.18.7); [Joel 3:14-17](Joel.3.14-Joel.3.17); [Amos 8:8-10](Amos.8.8-Amos.8.10)). Josephus records the appearance about AD 30 of a star resembling a sword and a spontaneous opening of the gates of the Temple (Josephus, *War* 6.5.3-4).

**tombs opened:** Jesus’ climactic death inaugurated the Kingdom of God by breaking the powers of death and establishing the final resurrection (see [Isa 26:19](Isa.26.19); [Dan 12:2](Dan.12.2); [1 Cor 15:1-58](1Cor.15.1-1Cor.15.58); [Col 1:18](Col.1.18); [Heb 2:14-15](Heb.2.14-Heb.2.15)).

These **godly** ones either did not enter the city until **after Jesus’ resurrection** or they were not **raised** until then, with Jesus as the firstfruits (see [1 Cor 15:20](1Cor.15.20), [23](1Cor.15.23); [Col 1:18](Col.1.18)). If that is the case, Matthew has included this episode to form a more powerful commentary on the impact of Jesus’ death.
The **Roman officer and the other soldiers** were Gentiles.

**the Son of God:** This may be an unqualified affirmation that Jesus is the unique **Son of God** (see [14:33](Matt.14.33); [16:16](Matt.16.16)) or possibly a more general affirmation of Jesus’ innocence (see [Luke 23:47](Luke.23.47)). They are responding to **the earthquake and all that had happened** as evidence of divine interest in this occasion.

In Roman crucifixion, the bodies of criminals were often left to rot. [Deut 21:22-23](Deut.21.22-Deut.21.23) prohibits a body from remaining on a cross or a gallows overnight. Joseph’s action was in accordance with Jewish law, while his motivation was probably his loyalty to Jesus.
**Pilate issued an order:** Pilate was accommodating, probably because he did not believe Jesus was guilty of insurrection (see [Matt 27:24-26](Matt.27.24-Matt.27.26)).

Burial customs were important in Judaism, especially in contrast to the Greeks and Romans, who cremated their dead. Leaving a corpse unburied was the severest form of judgment ([Deut 21:22-23](Deut.21.22-Deut.21.23); [2 Kgs 9:37](2Kgs.9.37); [Ps 79:3](Ps.79.3); [Jer 16:4](Jer.16.4), [6](Jer.16.6); [Ezek 29:5](Ezek.29.5); [Rev 11:9](Rev.11.9)). Death was lamented and mourned ([Mark 5:38-39](Mark.5.38-Mark.5.39)); the body was washed ([Acts 9:37](Acts.9.37)), anointed ([Matt 26:6-13](Matt.26.6-Matt.26.13); [John 12:3](John.12.3), [7](John.12.7); [19:39](John.19.39)), and wrapped in burial cloths ([Matt 27:59](Matt.27.59); see [Gen 50:2-3](Gen.50.2-Gen.50.3)). The body was placed in a tomb (see [Matt 23:27](Matt.23.27)) that had been tunneled into a rock or carved into the side of a cave wall. The entrance to a tomb was often closed with a huge **stone** and sealed to prevent ceremonial uncleanness or robbery.
**clean linen . . . new tomb:** Both reflect ceremonial purity. Joseph had purchased the tomb for his own family, but it had not yet been used.
This incident bolsters the truth of Jesus’ resurrection—it is inconceivable that Matthew would fabricate such a story since witnesses abounded who could have countered the claims.

The discovery of the empty tomb and the various resurrection appearances are presented with different emphases in each of the four Gospels. Matthew focuses on the reunion in Galilee, the attempt on the part of the Jewish leaders to discredit the resurrection, and the significance of the resurrection for the salvation of the world.

**Mary Magdalene** (see [27:56](Matt.27.56)): The mention of two women as witnesses lends credibility to the historicity of the account—an inventor of tales would not have used women as witnesses, since a woman’s testimony was considered less reliable than a man’s.
Such a **bribe** was contrary to the law (see [Exod 20:16](Exod.20.16); [23:8](Exod.23.8)).
**elders:** See study note on Matt 21:23.
**stole his body:** Tomb robbery was a common problem in the ancient world, so such an accusation would have been entirely believable.

**still tell it today:** Justin Martyr wrote to Jews of his day (about AD 165), “You have sent . . . men throughout all the world to proclaim, ‘A godless and lawless heresy has sprung from one Jesus, a Galilean deceiver, whom we crucified, but his disciples stole him by night from the tomb . . . and now \[the disciples\] deceive men by asserting that he has risen from the dead and ascended into heaven’” (Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* 108). This misinformation probably became widespread after the disciples began to proclaim Jesus’ resurrection (see [Acts 2:22-36](Acts.2.22-Acts.2.36)).

**some of them doubted:** This might be a veiled reference to Thomas ([John 20:24-29](John.20.24-John.20.29)), but all eleven might have experienced a mixture of both worship and doubt (see also [Matt 14:31](Matt.14.31); [Luke 24:10-11](Luke.24.10-Luke.24.11); [John 20:24-29](John.20.24-John.20.29)).
Jesus’ **authority** is power delegated from the Father (see [7:29](Matt.7.29); [9:6-8](Matt.9.6-Matt.9.8); [21:23-27](Matt.21.23-Matt.21.27); [26:64](Matt.26.64); [John 3:35](John.3.35)).

**go and:** Literally *going*, a participle that supports the main imperative, **make disciples**. Matthew probably intended **go** to be understood as a separate command (as it is translated) and not as a circumstantial modifier (i.e., *while you go;* cp. the same construction in [9:6](Matt.9.6); [Acts 10:20](Acts.10.20)).
**make disciples:** A disciple is one who repents of sin, trusts in Jesus for salvation, and obeys his teachings.

**all the nations:** The mission to the Gentile nations formally began here (see [Matt 10:5-6](Matt.10.5-Matt.10.6); [15:24](Matt.15.24); see also [1:1](Matt.1.1); [2:1-12](Matt.2.1-Matt.2.12); [8:5-13](Matt.8.5-Matt.8.13); [21:43](Matt.21.43); [24:14](Matt.24.14); [26:13](Matt.26.13)).

Two aspects of making **disciples** are **baptizing** and teaching ([28:20](Matt.28.20)).. Baptism indicates public identification with, and surrender to, Jesus and the work he has done for salvation (see [3:13-17](Matt.3.13-Matt.3.17); [10:32-33](Matt.10.32-Matt.10.33); [20:28](Matt.20.28); [26:28](Matt.26.28); [Acts 2:38](Acts.2.38); [Rom 6:1-11](Rom.6.1-Rom.6.11); [1 Pet 3:21](1Pet.3.21)).
**In the name of** means entrance into a relationship and its benefits, which come to those who truly believe.

**Father . . . Son . . . Holy Spirit:** This is a formulaic expression for the nature of God as a trinity (see also [1 Cor 12:4-6](1Cor.12.4-1Cor.12.6); [2 Cor 13:14](2Cor.13.14); [Eph 4:4-6](Eph.4.4-Eph.4.6); [2 Thes 2:13-14](2Thess.2.13-2Thess.2.14); [1 Pet 1:2](1Pet.1.2); [Rev 1:4-6](Rev.1.4-Rev.1.6)).

**Teach:** The disciples’ curriculum is comprised of **all the commands** of Jesus (e.g., the Sermon on the Mount, chs [5–7](Matt.5.1-Matt.7.29)). The church is to be marked by its obedience to Jesus’ commands ([5:17-20](Matt.5.17-Matt.5.20); [7:13-27](Matt.7.13-Matt.7.27)). Jesus’ authority and presence are the basis for the disciples’ mission (see also [1:23](Matt.1.23); [18:20](Matt.18.20)).
